A deadly Israeli strike on Deir el-Balah killed two Palestinians including a 3-year-old child. Their deaths come amid near-daily Israeli attacks despite the so-called ceasefire, with at least 1,303 Palestinians killed and 4,336 injured since it began.

World.title: Eight killed and others missing after ferry capsizes off northern Cyprus
World.content:
At least eight people have died and more than a dozen others are still missing after a passenger boat capsized off northern Cyprus, the head of the Turkish administration there has said.

Ãnal Ãstel, prime minister of the self-proclaimed Turkish republic on Cyprus, said the ferry had been carrying 259 passengers and eight crew members when it began taking on water after departing the coastal town of Kyrenia.

The ship's captain and seven crew members have been detained as part of an investigation into "how this tragedy occurred", Ãstel wrote on social media.

A search and rescue operation to find the passengers still unaccounted for is under way, which Turkish authorities have joined.

The privately owned ferry left the popular holiday resort of Kyrenia at about 12:30 local time (09:30 GMT).

Ãstel said the boat had been scheduled to travel to Turkey on Saturday, but had been delayed due to poor weather conditions.

He told Turkish media outlet TRT that the boat was hit by two waves before it capsized.

While the captain of the vessel was trying to recover from the first wave, a second wave hit and it began taking on water, he told the outlet.

World.title: US strikes Iranian launchers on Larak Island in first known attack in weeks
World.content:
Jordan's army said shortly after the IRGC statement that it had intercepted eight missiles.

"Air defense systems intercepted eight missiles that breached the Kingdom's airspace at dawn today, Monday," Jordan's armed forces said in a statement, quoting the army's spokesperson, reported by the state Petra News Agency.

The US strike is the first known attack on Iran since President Donald Trump paused a renewed military campaign in late July.

Larak Island is just offshore from the key port of Bandar Abbas and sits right on the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway for global shipping.

Iran is currently making tanker traffic pass by this island for checking and reportedly forcing vessels to pay $2m (Â£1.5m) to cross.

Hossein Mohebbi, the IRGC's spokesman called the attack a "strategic and fatal mistake by the Trump regime" and said that the "enemy will pay the consequences of this miscalculation in both the economic and military fields".

Iran's Tasnim news agency, which is affiliated with the IRGC, said earlier that the attack was carried out by drones. Reports indicate that two people were killed and two others injured, it said.

Hours later, Iranian media carried a statement by the IRGC saying it had attacked the US bases of King Hussein and al-Azraq in Jordan with ballistic missiles in response to the Larak Island attack.

The IRGC said it had caused "heavy damage" and targeted "technical infrastructure, maintenance facilities, and enemy fighter jet positions", according to a translation from the AFP news agency.

Trump âsaid last week that all minesâ placed in the Strait of Hormuz by Iran as part of its efforts to blockade the route had been detonated or removed. He said Iran had been warned that any ship âor boat deploying new mines would be âdestroyed.

Iran's Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi described Trump's claim as a "propaganda" deception.

Iran is facing renewed economic pressure after Washington announced a fresh sanctions campaign on 24 August aimed at further isolating Tehran and expanding secondary sanctions against its allies.

Iranian officials and state media have largely dismissed the campaign as a continuation of previous US economic measures, which they argue followed Washington's military failure in the recent conflict.

The US and Israel launched wide-ranging strikes on Iran on 28 February, with Iran responding by attacking Israel, US bases and allied states in the Gulf, and effectively closing the Strait of Hormuz to marine traffic. The Iran war has now crossed its six-month mark.

Some 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to travel through before the war began.

World.title: Iceland votes against restarting EU membership talks
World.content:
Iceland has voted against resuming talks on joining the European Union 13 years after they were broken off.

Public broadcaster RUV reported that 52.8% of the more than 225,000 people who voted had rejected the government's proposal, while 47.2% had backed it. Some 12,600 votes separated them.

Prime Minister KristrÃºn FrostadÃ³ttir's centre-left government promised to hold a referendum by 2027, but brought it forward because of international tensions, including US President Donald Trump's threats against Greenland.

However, debate in this island nation of almost 400,000 people centred more on its fishing industry rather than security concerns.

With some 270,000 people eligible to vote, RUV reported the turnout of 82.5% was the highest in any Icelandic election since 2009.

Already part of the EU's single market and Schengen border-free zone, full EU membership would bring Iceland into the customs union and eventually the eurozone currency union.

Iceland began its application to join the EU in 2009 in the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis and the collapse of Iceland's banking system.

Its application was already well advanced when a eurosceptic government came to power in 2013 and put those talks on hold.

Fishing rights were the biggest obstacle to Icelandic accession then - as they remain today.

Iceland fought successfully to protect its fisheries from foreign fishermen during the Cod Wars with the UK in the 1970s - shortly after gaining independence from Denmark - and the country's fish and marine industries still account for almost 40% of its exports.

Many No voters feared EU membership would mean ceding some control of these lucrative fishing grounds under the bloc's policies, which control how much a member state can catch.

"The No side was much more skillful in sort of tapping into the political national identity in Iceland, which emphasises formal independence, coming out of a long independence struggle coming out of Denmark," Eirikur Bergmann, a professor of politics at BifrÃ¶st University, told the BBC.

"And so they were able to appeal to people's very fundamental feelings."

On the other hand, the Yes campaign "ran an overtly technical campaign, never really explaining the purpose or the passion in why Iceland join the EU", he said.

World.title: Manhunt after shooting at Swiss rave kills woman, 22, and injures five
World.content:
A manhunt is under way after a 22-year-old woman was killed and five others injured in a shooting at a rave in Switzerland.

Italian national Maria Spinelli died at the scene in Aarau on Sunday morning, police said. Four men and a woman, aged between 24 and 27, were in hospital with injuries "ranging from minor to severe".

Italy's prime minister Giorgia Meloni said she was confident Swiss authorities would "shed full light on what happened and find anyone responsible".

Aarau cantonal police spokesman Michael Leupold told a news conference on Sunday afternoon that officers were "still in the midst of the operation" and had no leads on who may have been behind the shooting.

Organisers and performers said the shooting happened at a techno rave being held at a horse racing track in the town, which is located some 46km (29 miles) west of Zurich.

The force said it had received an initial report of shots fired at the Schachen race track at around 02:30 local time (00:30 GMT).

Leupold reiterated that the police were conducting a large-scale, nationwide manhunt for the perpetrator, but said that there were currently no leads on whether it was one person or multiple individuals.

They were not believed to be in Aarau anymore, he added.

The investigation is being carried out in co-operation with Freiburg police, German news agency DPA reported.

Italy's foreign ministry said in a statement that it was sending officials to Zurich "to closely follow the investigation".

It added that two other Italians "were slightly injured and have already returned home".

The Italian Embassy in Bern and the Consulate in Zurich were monitoring the situation, they said.

World.title: 15 hikers feared missing after 'terrifying' flash flooding hits Grand Canyon
World.content:
About 15 people are thought to be missing or unaccounted for after flash flooding swept through parts of the Grand Canyon.

It hit at around 14:30 local time (22:30 BST) on Saturday in Bright Angel Canyon and Phantom Ranch area, according to the National Park Service (NPS).

Sixty-two people have so far been airlifted out of the area, with more expected to follow. No injuries have been reported.

"The whole thing was terrifying," said Nikki Baggs, 41, who was among those to be airlifted out of the bottom of the Grand Canyon on Saturday alongside her two friends.

"It was a beautiful day and then people were screaming, running," she told the BBC.

Baggs said she and her friends had just dropped off their belongings at a cabin in Phantom Ranch - a remote lodge at the bottom of the Grand Canyon - when they decided to venture out to enjoy the nice day. Before they knew it, a flood of water was sweeping through the area.

As soon as the rain hit, Baggs and her friends headed toward higher ground, where they sat at a picnic table, before rangers yelled to them to run again to a different ledge, where they waited with others for hours before they were evacuated at around 21:30 local time.

Baggs said she and her two friends had been looking forward to a steak dinner at Phantom Ranch - but were now just grateful to be alive thanks to a swift response from park rangers.

"It was a really uniquely coordinated effort," she said. "That's what made us feel safe about all of it in an unsafe situation."

World.title: 'A giant leap forward': Nasa launches powerful new space telescope
World.content:
Nasa says its "crisp, sweeping surveys will help scientists investigate dark energy and dark matter, discover and characterise exoplanets, map billions of galaxies, study black holes, and explore objects from our own solar system to the edge of the observable Universe."

Dark matter, which is invisible, acts as a kind of gravitational glue, while dark energy is believed to be a repulsive force driving the Universe's expansion. Together, they are thought to make up about 95% of the Universe.

"One of our main goals at Nasa is answering the question: are we alone in the Universe?" Fox said at a Sunday morning news conference.

"With Roman, we are going to make this giant leap forward... that is going to allow us to look at these distant, distant worlds and start to really resolve the atmosphere around them to let us know: could they be habitable?"

Millard said, through the work of telescopes like Roman, scientists are hoping to create "enormous cosmic maps" of the Universe at various stages.

"They'll be almost like an onion, so you can peel back layer upon layer... and see how the distribution of galaxies changes through cosmic time," she said.

"What we want to do is use this distribution to try and figure out dark matter and dark energy because we know they exist, we see their effects, but what they are is a real mystery."

World.title: Zambian opposition leader charged with treason
World.content:
Zambian opposition leader Brian Mundubile has been charged with treason, his lawyer has said amid heightened political tensions in the country.

Mundubile was arrested on Thursday, after a deadly raid by the authorities led the opposition politician to go into hiding.

He had disputed the results of the country's recent presidential election, which saw incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema securing a second term.

The authorities then accused Mundubile's NRPUP party of planning an armed insurgency, which it denied.

On Saturday night, Mundubile's lawyer Milner Katolo announced that his client had been charged with treason. The opposition leader looks forward to answering the accusation in court, Katolo told the Zambian Eye, external.

The lawyer said 17 others, including Mundubile's running mate Makebi Zulu, had also been charged with treason.

Mundubile gained 38% of the vote in the 13 August election, while Hichilema secured 60%, official results show.

The day after the poll, security forces raided a property in the capital, Lusaka, linked to Mundubile, killing a former cabinet minister and arresting a number of other politicians.

The government said they seized weapons during the raid.

Following the raid, Mundubile and Zulu took refuge at a United Nations building in the city. The pair were detained after the president put pressure on the UN to hand them over.

The opposition was unable to mount a legal challenge to the election outcome as the courts were sealed off by the authorities on Monday, the final day that a case could be filed.

Hichilema is due to be sworn in for a second term on 1 September.

Regional and international observers described the election day as largely peaceful, but Zambia's Human Rights Commission has called for accountability over people whose whereabouts remain unknown following arrests and security operations around the elections.

World.title: Russia says it helped to repel Niger attempted coup
World.content:
The Alliance of Sahel States - composed of Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso - said the attempted coup was "a betrayal by a group of soldiers involved in an attempt at destabilisation".

The authorities have not said how many soldiers were involved in the attempted coup, nor how many casualties there were.

Niger's military ruler, Gen Tiani, who was sworn in as its president last year after he deposed its elected leader, has also not publicly addressed the incident.

The nation's state broadcaster showed footage of several alleged mutineers being arrested by the Presidential Guard.

On Sunday, Niger Press Agency reported that commercial activity was returning to normal, with petrol stations, shops and other businesses reopening.

Supporters of the government gathered at a public square in central Niamey in support of the security forces and Tiani's government.

Air Base 101, the military site attacked on Saturday, is part of the Diori Hamani airport complex.

It hosts Nigerien military aircraft and drones, as well as an Alliance of Sahel States counter-terrorism unit. Russian and Italian forces are also based there, according to news agency Reuters.

Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso are all military-ruled countries that have cut ties with Western partners and strengthened their co-operation with Russia.

But jihadist violence remains widespread in all three countries, despite the shift in alliances.

For Niger's government, Saturday's mutiny highlights that the military is dealing not only with an external insurgency, but also signs of discontent within its own ranks.

The airbase where the mutiny began had itself been targeted twice by jihadists this year â once by an Islamic State affiliate and later by an al-Qaeda affiliate.

Nigerien authorities say security forces have increased patrols around key sites in Niamey following the attempted takeover, including the main airport entrance and the presidential pavilion.

World.title: Twenty-two years to destiny: The silent sacrifices that carved my journey to the nations, By Ayo Akerele
World.content:
Continue to work hard on your business, career, and ministry. No matter how hard and bad your nation is, God’s word is not altered by human circumstances. If He has said it, you will see it. But build on the principles of consistency and faithfulness. Sit and serve in your church. Give dangerously. Watch and wait for God to blow you. For when God blows you, no man can quench you. For “whatever the Lord does shall be forever” (Ecclesiastes 3:14).

While at the university in 1993, I caught a profound vision of leaving Nigeria for America, obviously for a better life, as we would often describe it. At that time, I was actively serving the Lord under the leadership of a great ministry led by a father in the faith. This was a silent season of hidden labours in my life. I was like a madman for God. I never missed a Sunday service. I never missed a mid-week service. I was so madly in love with God that, on days when I had no money for transportation, I would walk to church and still be the first to arrive for services. We would finish our church conferences at 11:30 p.m., and I would walk back home in the thick darkness of the night, crossing dangerous bridges and neighbourhoods. The Lord kept me.

I had no time for offence. You could not offend me against my pastors or the church. I simply kept serving and serving, and while doing that, I maintained my focus on my university studies as an engineering student. There was nothing called luxury in my life.

There was nothing attractive in my life. There were no achievements. There was no money. It was a season of little beginnings. Things were really hard. These were not the days of social media or the internet. There was no external basis for motivation. But I held firmly to my conviction that God was going to open international doors for me. Right inside my small beginnings, I gave offerings as sacrificially as I could. No call for donation ever eluded me. There were times I gave out the little stipends my parents provided as offerings towards several projects in our church at that time. There was a day I packed my student stove and a few other belongings and sowed them as seeds into the missions department of our church. And I did all of these with excitement. Yet, there was no reward or visible result.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

I served God faithfully under a couple of leaders. Things were tough, challenging, and sometimes hopeless. What was that force that drove me to stick with the Lord for a breakthrough for 13 years? I cannot attribute this level of perseverance to anything normal. It must have been solely the product of divine enablement.

I am sharing these stories to connect with what some of you are going through. The enemies of the church, pastors, and church haters have told you that it is worthless and useless to go to church. You have been told that no one needs God to succeed in life. They have pointed you to many people in the world who became billionaires without God. But they have failed to tell you the hidden costs of their success, the occultic societies many of them belong to; the sacrifices performed in secret; the covenants made in dark places to secure their super-rich status. What you see is only the top of the iceberg of their success, not the lower part, which is often the largest portion. Why should Satan, the enemy of the church, be glad that you love God and love the gathering of the saints in a church community?

Everyone pays a price for success. Something for nothing exists only in the paradise of fools. You become a victim of ignorance if you allow any agent of the devil to drain out the need for God in your pursuit of success. No one succeeds in a vacuum. As Dr Olumide Emmanuel once said, “You are either backed up by the secret place or by secret cults.”

So, from 1993, I experienced a plateau, a silence. I gave and gave and gave. There was no smell or sight of any international opportunity. In fact, for the most part, from 1993 to 2001, a period of eight years, I suffered significantly. I served God with no results. I prayed with no results. I gave and became poorer. But understand something today: “Sacrifices work in silence.” Sometimes, when it appears as though God is coming late, it is because He is coming big. Dr Myles Munroe would also say, “Seeds work in silence.” My sacrifices made me look like a fool. However, from 2002 to 2005, I began to see glimmers of hope, because God began to show me favour by helping me secure some good jobs in Nigeria.

But they still fell short of what God told me in 1993: “I am taking you out of this nation.”

Then in 2005, a ray of hope sparked the birth of a torrent of light into my destiny. God miraculously connected me with some missionaries in South Africa for the final lap of my years of sacrifice. I served them faithfully. I worked with them to take many poor South Africans off the streets of Pretoria. We fed them, clothed them, and accommodated many of them. And then rays of light began to build up with a minimal level of intensity toward the end of 2005. The world’s biggest diamond manufacturing company miraculously hired me under circumstances I still cannot explain. My life had taken a new turn, I said to myself, unaware that this was just an appetizer, not the main course. And then, in 2006, the biggest miracle happened.

During my wilderness season of 13 years, I had applied for various visas. I wanted to force what God had said to happen. We’ve all been there. Haven’t you? Joseph tried to use his connection with the Butler to get out of prison, but the Butler forgot him for two years.

The US refused me a visa once; the UK refused me twice. I cannot tell the full story of what happened. But it was right in the middle of pains, regrets, and frustration in South Africa that I received a phone call from Nigeria. Before I tell you what happened, recall that I said I got a fantastic offer from a diamond manufacturing company in South Africa. It was not the deal. It was not my Canaan land. God allowed it to cool me down because I was almost running out of breath. Sometimes in life, God allows flickers of hope, temporary blessings, to cool you off so you don’t break down before the real thing happens. Within four months, that opportunity was gone, and I was back to square one.

Fast forward to after I left that organisation. One day, I sat on my bed, dejected, frustrated, and despondent. I had served God faithfully for years. “God’s word has failed,” I said to myself. Then my phone rang. Someone called from Nigeria, telling me she had received a parcel from the UK embassy, “The visa they refused two years earlier had been re-approved.” I laughed it off, insisting it was a scam. That was in 2006, the 14th year of my waiting on God. The UK visa was issued. A few weeks later, another parcel arrived: a four thousand pound scholarship was approved. I left for the UK. Just less than two weeks in the UK, another parcel arrived — you have been approved for an all expenses paid business mentorship training in France. And many more parcels arrived! Long story short, the rest is now history.

God fulfilled His word, opened international doors for me, and rewarded me massively for years of silent labours. It was as soon as God relocated me to the West that He called me into the teaching ministry. Someone reading this article today may be asking, “Is there hope for me? My case is worse than Pastor Ayo Akerele’s case.” Or perhaps you have been written off as a church slave or a church rat. You may have been labelled a madman for God. I was mad for Jesus in those days, and I am still madly in love with Him. Two things helped me, the ground into which I poured my service and my heart. If your heart is not right, or your ground is not right, you might be sowing in vain.

And to add to my points, I wasn’t just sitting in church doing nothing; I was investing the little I could into my education and career. I worked very hard. I gave God the right platform to bless and reward me, because service without work leads to frustration and woes.

My years of sacrifice were not merely from 1993 to 2006. They truly began in 1984 when I got born again, but it was in 1993 that the Lord gave me a revelation of my journey to the West for a new assignment. I served God passionately and faithfully at a Baptist church as an usher from 1984 to 1992. Not a dime of God’s money ever got stolen by me or went missing under my watch. Many times, I was left alone with the offering in the same room, and I never tampered with God’s money, even when I had desperate financial needs.

I defended my pastor and stood with him even when he was about to be voted out. It was my vote that saved his job in the heat of a gang-up against him by the elders of the church. At his funeral in New York in 2026, his daughter pulled me aside to remind me of this incident. Tears almost filled my eyes. God’s name be praised. It meant a lot to heaven, and it was written in my account.

If you are serving God at any level, do it with the right heart. Don’t gossip about your pastor. Don’t join church haters to criticise the church. The Bible says, “A mocker shall seek for knowledge and won’t find it” (Proverbs 14:6). And if you are serving God in a church founded on truth, stay there. Don’t jump from church to church. Sit and serve. Rewards are triggered by consistency and faithfulness. But if you know your pastor is not a servant of God, you may serve for 50 years and come out with regrets.

“Serve the LORD with gladness: come before His presence with singing” (Psalm 100:2).

So, if I consider all the previous years, I would say it took God 22 years to reposition me. It took Him 22 years to set me up for greatness. You are too much in a hurry with God. The God of the Christian faith does not bless or reward people in a hurry. Many people rush to the top only to be buried in the ground. Satan knows this principle very well, so he often hastens us to give up on God and accept his evil alternatives. Sit, serve, and wait for God. Today, the rest is history. Don’t believe the lies of church haters. I cannot tell you how much blessing God has brought into my life, but the greatest of them all is the oil of ministerial calling He placed on me. That alone is my greatest reward in life.

Continue to work hard on your business, career, and ministry. No matter how hard and bad your nation is, God’s word is not altered by human circumstances. If He has said it, you will see it. But build on the principles of consistency and faithfulness. Sit and serve in your church. Give dangerously. Watch and wait for God to blow you. For when God blows you, no man can quench you. For “whatever the Lord does shall be forever” (Ecclesiastes 3:14).

Ayo Akerele is the senior pastor of Rhema Assembly and the founder of the Voice of the Watchmen Ministries in Ontario, Canada. He can be reached through [email protected]. World.title: Hello, God!, By Wole Olaoye
World.content:
‘Hello God’ echoes the way she had lived her life — searching for hope during difficult times. The millions of Nigerians who adore Dolly Parton will, no doubt, find her song a good companion as they confront the ‘apocalyptic’ uncertainties of the 2027 general elections. They might even domesticate the lyrics: “Hello, God, are you out there? Will you save us from the precipice like before?”

… In memory of Dolly Parton

When the king of Afrobeat, Fela Anikulapo-Kuti, died on 2 August, 1997, the world stood still. He had conquered the music world from Africa, reinventing African jazz in his own unique way and wielding his lyrics as a weapon of social emancipation.

Michael Jackson’s death on 25 June, 2009, also shook the world, especially considering that he was at the height of his glory and only 50 years old. The King of Pop redefined the concept of dancing, revolutionising James Brown’s electric moves with a touch of the extraterrestrial.

Famous Deaths

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The revolving door between mortality and the hereafter has hosted many notable passers-through in the last 15 years: Amy Winehouse, 2011; Whitney Houston, 2012; BB King, 2015; Prince, 2016; David Bowie, 2016; George Michael, 2016; Chuck Berry, 2017; Don Williams, 2017; Aretha Franklin, 2018; Hugh Masekela, 2018; Manu Dibango, 2020; Eddie Van Halen, 2020; Kenny Rogers, 2020; Tina Turner, 2023; Quincy Jones, 2024.

Star-studded as the modern music scene has been, it will be hard to find another contemporary songwriter with as much cross-cultural and trans-ideological appeal as the woman who combined intense Christian faith with folksy fellow-feeling and a perpetual investment in everlasting youth. Her name was Dolly Parton.

In all, she wrote an estimated 3,000+ songs throughout a career that lasted a little over six decades. Out of her massive output, she has officially recorded and released around 450 to 500 of her own compositions, including such iconic tracks as “I Will Always Love You” (later famously redone by Whitney Houston), “Jolene”, “Coat of Many Colors”, and “9 to 5”. Twenty-five years ago, in 2001, she was inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame in recognition of her prolific songwriting output.



I am always fascinated by the lives of celebrities who were so rich they had more than money. What coursed through my mind when the announcement of Parton’s death hit the airwaves was the great example of generosity she left for the world to emulate in a remarkable life.



Philanthropy

Dolly Parton’s philanthropic record includes a wide range of charitable initiatives, donations, and direct community support. Her Imagination Library, which was founded in 1995 in honour of her father, mails free, high-quality books monthly to children from birth until age five. It has so far distributed over 300 million books across the United States, Canada, the UK, Ireland, and Australia.



In 2020, she donated $1 million to the Vanderbilt University Medical Center, which directly helped fund the development of the Moderna COVID-19 vaccine. She raised $700,000 to assist communities affected by the 2021 Tennessee floods. In 2024, she donated $1 million personally, matched by another $1 million from her Dollywood businesses, to assist disaster relief across East Tennessee.

She made donations towards educational support and high school retention, employee scholarships for higher education, paediatric cancer research, and wildlife conservation of bald eagles and reinvested earnings — including royalties from songs like “I Will Always Love You” — into local business properties and historic districts to support community economic development.

She was the home girl who ensured that the ordinary folk in her environment shared in her fortune. If that is the only lesson the world can learn from her, it would still have been a remarkable one. But her entire life itself was a grass-to-grace poem packaged in a curvy, buxom, mannequin-perfect visage.



Cosmetic Surgeries

Perhaps the only vanity she permitted herself was her insistence on physical perfection, which made her undergo plastic surgery several times to spruce up her looks. She viewed cosmetic enhancement as an ongoing maintenance routine, famously joking, “If I see something sagging, dragging, or bagging, I’m going to go get it stuck, tucked, or plucked.”



Ever candid in a childlike manner, she had admitted to doing facelifts, blepharoplasty (eyelid surgery), breast implants/lifts, liposuction, and excess skin removal aside from non-surgical procedures like Botox injections, dermal fillers, and lip collagen injections.



She was so light-hearted about it, quipping, “I may look fake, but I’m real where it counts.”



Her heart was where it counted. For almost 60 years, she was married to Carl Dean, an extremely reclusive man who ran an asphalt-paving business and preferred rock to country music. He rarely appeared in public, leading to persistent tabloid urban legends that he didn’t actually exist. They had no biological children.



She had enough love to share with the rest of humanity, and that is why, without ever having the benefit of personal contact, this writer, born into a different race half a world away, feels we must imbibe the deeper lessons of a life so richly blessed and so massively charitable.

Relatable Narratives

I make bold to say that her most popular song across all faiths in Nigeria is “Coat of Many Colors” because it vividly illustrates themes of poverty, love, and resilience. Interestingly but not surprisingly, it was a biographical song. Dolly was the fourth of 12 children born to Avie Lee and Robert Lee Parton who lived in a tiny, two-room log cabin on Locust Ridge in Sevier County, Tennessee, without electricity and running water.

Robert Lee Parton was a sharecropper and tobacco farmer who also worked construction jobs while his wife managed the household, cooked meals from basic staples, and made clothes for the children. Cash was always a problem, so much so that Dolly’s father paid the doctor who delivered her with a sack of cornmeal.

“Coat of Many Colors,” therefore, did not drop from the sky. It was a lived experience. In a world where about 1.1 billion people live in acute multidimensional poverty across developing countries, the song resonated well. Parton was vocalising the sentiments of the wretched of the earth, irrespective of geographical location.

Her critics argued that she was glamorising poverty. Well, what is there to glamorise about wealth in an unfeeling world of one millionaire amidst a million beggars? Parton’s ability to convert her experiences into a relatable narrative solidifies the song’s place in both music history and sociology.

Supplication

In the midst of the doom and gloom of the 9/11 terror attacks in the United States, only a Dolly Parton could have come up with the composition of ‘Hello God,’ which is at once a prayer to which everyone can relate and a passionate reaching for the celestials in the midst of profound vulnerability and inconsolable grief.



The lyrics of ‘Hello God’ need to be heard again and again by the merchants of forever wars and mass murders all over the world, lest we self-destruct. Rather than offering rigid dogma, the song voices genuine human helplessness, showing that doubting during a crisis is a universal human experience. She wonders if any human being could ever claim to be fighting for God. Apparently we have abused God’s gift of free will.

‘Hello God’ echoes the way she had lived her life — searching for hope during difficult times. The millions of Nigerians who adore Dolly Parton will, no doubt, find her song a good companion as they confront the ‘apocalyptic’ uncertainties of the 2027 general elections. They might even domesticate the lyrics: “Hello, God, are you out there? Will you save us from the precipice like before?”

Wole Olaoye is a Public Relations consultant and veteran journalist. He can be reached on [email protected], Twitter: @wole_olaoye; Instagram: woleola2021

World.title: In Anambra State, the fox now guards the chicken coop, By Chidi Anselm Odinkalu
World.content:
This week marks 24 years since Barnabas and Amaka Igwe were liquidated. It is possible that the current governor of Anambra State has lost the capacity to be affronted by the murder of a pregnant woman. If so, he should stop complaining about insecurity. But he cannot put the security of the state in the hands of a man like Ken Emeakayi and still pretend that insecurity worries him.

“The first method for estimating the intelligence of a ruler is to look at the men he has around him.” – Niccolo Machiavelli, The Prince, Chapter XXII (1513)

In April 2006, the Hamas-led new government of the Palestinian National Authority in Gaza appointed a new director-general to head the para-military “Executive Force” in charge of security in the Strip. The new director-general, Jamal Abu Samhadana, was no ordinary militant. He had lived for a majority of the preceding quarter century in exile, spent 19 months as a detainee of the Palestinian Authority, and was reportedly the second name on Israel’s “most wanted” list. Gideon Meir, spokesperson at the time for Israel’s Foreign Ministry, likened his appointment to “allowing the fox to guard the chicken coop.”

Anambra State in South-East Nigeria is an unlikely theatre for a re-enactment of this plot of the fox guarding the chicken coop. Unlike the story of Jamal Abu Samhadana, the fox in the Anambra re-make cannot be accused of a cause.

The story begins a quarter of a century ago. Nigeria had returned to elective government after 15 years of unbroken military rule. In many states of the federation, the transition threw up grave security challenges. Few states struggled with this like Anambra State.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The governor of the state was Chinwoke Mbadinuju. To address rampant insecurity in 2000, he assented to the Anambra Vigilante Services (AVS) Law. Into this new legal space, the governor invited the Bakassi Boys, a murderous gang described by Human Rights Watch at the time as a “legitimization of murder and torture.”

According to the Nigeria Police Force, a standard practice of the Bakassi Boys was “hacking suspected criminals with machetes and then setting their bodies ablaze.” They were known to be “completely unaccountable.”

The fear of the Bakassi Boys created a chilling effect conducive to keeping a lid on public criticism of the prevailing misgovernance. For long stretches from 2001, workers in the public sector in the state were routinely unpaid.

In 2002, unpaid teachers declared industrial action for the full school year. State civil servants were similarly on strike for many months, as were judiciary staff. The prolonged strike action by judiciary workers in the state resonated on the kitchen tables of lawyers in one of the most litigious states in the country.

Onitsha, the leading centre of commerce in southern Nigeria, is also the site of the largest collection of lawyers in the state. In 2002, Barnabas Igwe, a senior lawyer, led the Onitsha Branch of the Nigerian Bar Association (NBA). His wife, Amaka, was also a lawyer.

As the leader of the foremost branch of the bar in the state, Mr Igwe was under pressure from the evident stress on the livelihoods of his members. In August 2002, he called an emergency meeting of the senior leadership of the NBA in Onitsha. Invited to the meeting were all former chairmen of the branch; all Senior Advocates of Nigeria (SANs) and lawyers with over 30 years of practice experience in the city; and the elected leadership of the branch.

Two days later, both Mr Igwe and his wife were dead, hacked in a gruesome attack involving guns and matchetes on Oraifite Road on the outskirts of Onitsha. The attackers were elements from the Bakassi Boys… The double murder of the chairman of a leading branch of the NBA and his pregnant wife drew swift and widespread outrage. Inspector-General of Police, Tafa Balogun, was in his fifth month in office.

Rising from the meeting, the Onitsha Branch of the NBA issued a 21-day ultimatum to the state government to discharge the backlog of salaries owed to judiciary workers and public service workers in the state or face an escalation. If the state governor could not do so, Mr Igwe declaimed, then he should resign.

Very quickly, Mr Igwe’s leadership galvanised hitherto quiet voices around the state. The governor had a problem.

This was the situation when Barnabas and Amaka Igwe departed Onitsha in the last week of August 2002 to Ibadan, Oyo State, for the 42nd Annual General Conference of the NBA. Amaka Igwe was pregnant with what would have been her fourth child. She was already the mother of one daughter and two sons.

On the last day of August 2002, they returned from Ibadan to Onitsha. It was their last trip out of the city.

Two days later, both Mr Igwe and his wife were dead, hacked in a gruesome attack involving guns and matchetes on Oraifite Road on the outskirts of Onitsha. The attackers were elements from the Bakassi Boys.

The double murder of the chairman of a leading branch of the NBA and his pregnant wife drew swift and widespread outrage. Inspector-General of Police, Tafa Balogun, was in his fifth month in office.

In Charge no. O/60C/2003, The State v. Francis Nzekwe (alias Francis Nzewe Ibekwe), and 10 others, the government of Anambra State initiated criminal proceedings to bring to account 11 suspects in connection with the double murder.

One of the suspects was one Ken Emeakayi. At the time, he was the commissioner for Works in the cabinet of Governor Mbadinuju. His reputation around the state was settled. Witnesses appeared to have identified him as the man in command of the gang that liquidated Barnabas and Amaka Igwe.

The Onitsha Branch of the NBA secured permission (fiat) from the Ministry of Justice enabling its ablest lawyers to lead the prosecution. The case began before Kalajine Anigbogu, a judge of the High Court of Anambra State. In short order, he recused himself citing determined interference from un-named “high places” in the state.

It was thereafter reassigned to another judge in Onitsha, Peter Umeadi, before being transferred to Cecilia Uzoewulu, then sitting at the High Court in Ekwulobia.

With Mr Emeakayi now safely ensconced in his new role, those with opinions about the brutal cynicism of his rehabilitation by the governor who promised different turned mute. Such is the palpable fear around the state of his long service in the enterprise of gratuitous violence with impunity.

In 2005, the High Court inexplicably decided to grant bail to Ken Emeakayi in the double murder trial. This was most implausible because murder cases are notoriously not bailable. Around 22 February 2006, a prison break freed the remainder of the suspects from pre-trial detention in the Onitsha prison. In this engineered confusion, the records were disappeared from both the courts and the Ministry of Justice. So, the case was never brought to a conclusion.

I know because I went looking.

In 2022, the Governor of Anambra State asked me to lead a Truth, Justice, and Peace Commission (TJPC) into the unrest in South-East Nigeria. Membership of the Commission included the then Attorney-General of the State, Professor Sylvia Ifemeje. Nigeria’s current Minister of Foreign Affairs, Bianca Odumegwu-Ojukwu, served as the secretary.

The TJPC had a mandate going back to 1999, which brought the double murder of Barnabas and Amaka Igwe within its purview. When it reported in March 2024, the Commission called attention to the especially heinous character of the double murder of Barnabas and Amaka Igwe. It specifically referred to the unfinished prosecution of Mr Emeakayi and asked the state government to review the case with a view to ensuring effective accountability. It also recommended an official apology and symbolic compensation to their children.

The governor promised “swift action based on the Commission’s recommendations.”

Six months later, instead of accountability, the same governor appointed the same Ken Emeakayi as his Special Adviser for Community Security. At the beginning of 2025, the State Government created a new vigilante militia called “Agunechemba” ultimately under the command of Mr Emeakayi.

Anambra State’s road to enthroning the fox as the king of the chicken coop was complete.

With Mr Emeakayi now safely ensconced in his new role, those with opinions about the brutal cynicism of his rehabilitation by the governor who promised different turned mute. Such is the palpable fear around the state of his long service in the enterprise of gratuitous violence with impunity.

How a man credibly suspected of involvement in the murder of a pregnant woman and in orphaning her children can be enabled by a former Governor of Nigeria’s Central Bank is one of the many miracles of Nigerian politics. In normal society, that is sacrilege.

This week marks 24 years since Barnabas and Amaka Igwe were liquidated. It is possible that the current governor of Anambra State has lost the capacity to be affronted by the murder of a pregnant woman. If so, he should stop complaining about insecurity. But he cannot put the security of the state in the hands of a man like Ken Emeakayi and still pretend that insecurity worries him.

Chidi Anselm Odinkalu, a lawyer, teaches at the Fletcher School of Law and Diplomacy and can be reached through [email protected].

World.title: BBNaija S11: Sultex, Goddessa evicted from ‘Show Ya Sef’ house
World.content:
Big Brother Naija Season 11 housemates Sultex and Goddessa have been evicted from the “Show Ya Sef” house after five weeks in the reality television competition.

Their exits were announced by host Ebuka Obi-Uchendu during the fifth live eviction show on Sunday, as the race for the ₦160 million grand prize intensified.

Bells received 5.22 per cent of the votes, followed by Goddessa with 5.02 per cent and Sultex with the lowest, 4.77 per cent.

Sultex and Goddessa were among 14 housemates placed on the public voting list during Week Five, following a nomination twist introduced by Big Brother.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Their departure further reduced the number of housemates remaining in the competition.

Sultex’s journey ends after five weeks

Sultex, whose real name is Sultan Aregbe-Obanikoro, joined the competition on the opening night on 26 July.

The Lagos-based dancer, choreographer, casting director and filmmaker became known for his energetic personality, dancing ability and outspoken approach to the game.

He enjoyed a major high earlier in the season when he emerged as the ‘Most Influential Player’ of the Week during Week Three. The recognition earned him immunity from the next eviction process, as well as a tablet as part of Big Brother’s reward system.

However, his final week in the house was overshadowed by a heated confrontation involving fellow housemates Bells and Yusuf.

The disagreement started during a conversation between Bells and Sultex but escalated after Yusuf intervened. The three housemates exchanged words in the garden, with the argument nearly turning physical.

Sultex and Yusuf subsequently engaged in a heated face-off, while Bells remained involved in the confrontation. The incident became one of the defining moments of Sultex’s final week in the house.

Big Brother, making an official address, later described some of Sultex’s threatening remarks during the confrontation as “extremely dangerous” and placed him on “behavioural probation” with a final warning.

The warning came just a day before his eviction.

His departure ends a five-week stay that featured strong task performances, energetic dancing, and several moments of confrontation and strategy.

Goddessa was also sent packing

Goddessa, whose real name is Lovette Amaka, also exited the competition on Sunday.

The musician from Arochukwu, Abia State, entered the house hoping to showcase her personality and further advance her music career.

During her time in the house, Goddessa became involved in several conversations and relationship dynamics that generated reactions among viewers.

One of her most prominent storylines in the final week involved her relationship with Araga.

Following the Saturday Night Link-Up, Araga attempted to apologise to Goddessa over their disagreement, but she initially refused to engage with him. Temi Nkem later intervened as efforts were made to resolve the tension between the pair.

Goddessa was also involved in conversations following the confrontation between Sultex, Bells and Yusuf. She advised Yusuf not to let the incident damage his reputation and urged him to be mindful of what he said when angry.

Despite receiving significant support from fellow housemates during the Week Five nomination process, Goddessa ultimately remained vulnerable to the public vote and was evicted alongside Sultex.

Eviction list

Week Five was themed “Topsy-Turvy Week”, with Big Brother transforming the house into a jungle and assigning animal identities to the housemates.

The week also introduced a major change to the usual nomination process.

Rather than naming housemates they wanted to see evicted, the contestants were instructed to publicly identify two housemates they wanted to save and explain their choices.

Goddessa, Sheba and Aikou emerged with the highest number of save votes.

Chimsom Chuka, who won the Head of House challenge for the second time this season, was then given the power to break the tie and choose one of the three to receive full protection.

He chose Sheba. As a result, Goddessa remained vulnerable to the public vote despite receiving significant support from her fellow housemates.

The 14 housemates eventually placed on the eviction list were Araga, Barry, Bells, Bluethopia, Gerard, Goddessa, Keivo, Nomy, Oyin, Ricky, Sultex, Temi Nkem, Tram and Yusuf.

The public voting process then determined who would remain in the competition.

Dramatic week five

Beyond the eviction battle, Week Five was marked by several developments, including the jungle-themed tasks, relationship tensions, the Gambits’ romantic mission and disagreements over the weekly wager.

The house also faced consequences for breaches of Big Brother’s rules.

Oyin and Chimsom were sanctioned over damage to house property, while Abi and Keivo were punished for pouring water on their microphones and were barred from the upcoming Pool Party.

Nomy, who already had one strike, was also warned over repeated lateness, disobedience and selective participation in mandatory activities.

The entire house was further informed that there would be no hot water for the rest of the week and that communal areas were expected to be kept spotless.

Big Brother emphasised that “actions have consequences”.

With Sultex and Goddessa now out of the competition, the remaining housemates will continue the battle for the ₦160 million grand prize as the eleventh season of BBNaija enters another critical stage.

World.title: Group confirms security incident at car park, commends staff for ‘containing’ situation
World.content:
Filmhouse Group is deeply saddened by a security incident that took place outside the premises, in the car park of one of our locations, in the early hours of this morning, 2am to be precise. The incident was unrelated to our regular operations. We are working closely with the relevant authorities, who are leading the ongoing investigation, and have taken additional precautionary measures across our locations.

The security team stood between danger and the people in their care, and it is through their bravery that the situation was contained and safety restored. Their commitment and courage in that moment will not be forgotten.

The safety and wellbeing of our staff and guests remain our highest priority. Security across all our locations has been increased and prioritised, and the safety of our guests and everyone within our premises remains of the utmost importance to us. We continue to monitor the ongoing situation.

World.title: Tortoise and the $1bn rain that came after the harvest, By Festus Adedayo
World.content:
If you hopped onto a horse galloping in a race inside the Nigerian First Lady’s tummy, its hoof would not hit a single stumble. That was how unmistakable the air of triumph was in Abuja last week. The catalyst for this sudden, infectious jubilation was the grand launch of the $1 billion Household Prosperity and Empowerment Social Protection Project (HOPE-SP) inside the State House Banquet Hall. At the centre of the spectacle stood Pastor Remi Tinubu, whose mini – khimar – the traditional scarf covering the head, shoulders and bosom of Muslim women – flapped excitedly as she paced the rostrum. The poor velvet scarf seemed itself in a celebratory mood, synchronising perfectly with the carefully orchestrated joy hovering over the rocks of the Federal Capital Territory.

It is three years and three months after President Bola Tinubu famously declared an abrupt end to the petrol subsidy. On one of his off-cuff junkets to France, he attributed his yanking it off to a spirit that suddenly pounced on him. With the $1 billion HOPE-SP, the administration was loudly signaling to Nigerians that real, tangible hope had finally arrived.

“What’s better than money?” Crime thriller king, James Hadley Chase, asked decades ago. Madam was the pond-skater, Ìròmi, dancing on the face of the river. $1 billion was the Kongo, the drumstick, with which the drummer hit the raw face of the hide; this time, not underneath the river. You could see the drummer itself inside the Banquet Hall. You would conclude the Khimar had just won a contest. As the Pastor paced the rostrum, her Khimar, wary of being left out of the joy, disentangles from the embrace of her neck periodically. And flaps on her laps. Madam rescues the insolent folk, straps it again on her neck, like a mother forcefully hoists a needlessly crying irritant child on her back. The scarf mirrors the infectious joy hovering over the rocks of the FCT.

To the administration’s loyalists, this $1 billion gamble was the ultimate trump card, a definitive response to Atiku Abubakar, Peter Obi, and the relentless commune of ungrateful critics who have spent months hammering the President’s economic policies. Waziri Adamawa had not just become a pest to the bazaar in Abuja. He had become a piercing arrow that penetrates right inside the esophagus of the First Family. You could see the recent flurry of frenzies of presidential hirelings trying to outpace one another in the job of deflecting Atiku’s tantrums.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Lately, Atiku has adopted the posture of an unsparing Wolé-Wolé (sanitary inspector), peering into every corner of the presidential family’s cooking pot. He brings to mind Irish Assistant Commissioner of Police John Lynn, the CID official nicknamed Ọkùnrin Oníjògbòn yẹn (That Troublesome Man) by Mama H.I.D. Awolowo. During the dark political crisis of the Western Region in 1962, when Chief Obafemi Awolowo was locked in battle with the federal powers-that-be and their region accomplices, Lynn’s team relentlessly raided Awo’s official residence at No. 7 Bell Avenue, Ikoyi, and his home in Ikenne. Exasperated during one such intrusive raids, Mama H.I.D. famously marched into her kitchen, hauled out a cooking pot, and asked Lynn if he would like to inspect that as well! Today, Atiku, like Lynn, has become a piercing arrow penetrating the esophagi of Aso Rock, leaving presidential hirelings scrambling to outpace one another in deflecting his political arrows.

Predictably, on the $1b bailout purportedly for Nigeria’s suffering masses, both Atiku and Obi raced to the blacksmith’s forge for a weapon with which to attack what they view as an expensive medicine-after-death. They see the administration’s sudden benevolence through the lens of a classic Yoruba proverb: “Tèmi ò ṣòro, tí kì í jẹ kí ọmọ alágbẹdẹ ní idà” – it is the ambivalence of the blacksmith’s son, who insists that urgent tasks are simple and can wait, that leaves him without a sword when crisis strikes.

Yet inside the State House, the conviviality continued unabated. An old man sitting by the Banquet Hall doorstep eventually caught the First Lady’s attention, drawing on her Ososami, Ibadan upbringing of kindheartedness to the elderly. He implored her to take a fable to the President, which he said he amply entitled ‘The Tortoise, the Weaverbird, and the Midnight Harvest’. It goes thus:

In an ancient animal kingdom, Alábahun, Tortoise the Trickster, was king. He held suzerainty over forest activities, as well as on all crawling and flying animals. On all of them, he held supreme authority. Surrounded by all animals in the kingdom, Tortoise radiated the majesty of his regal stool.

Then, suddenly, like a child seized by an unannounced convulsion, King Tortoise announced to the generality of animals in the kingdom that he had just discovered an answer to the food crisis of the kingdom. Henceforth, he proclaimed in a sudden decree, the communal granary, forest animals’ commonwealth, would thenceforth be locked. All animals, he proclaimed, were banned from foraging in this fertile valley source of daily meal. Keeping the granary locked, said King Tortoise, would bring greater prosperity and wealth to the kingdom sooner than the animals imagined. The animals were aghast. To them, it was a case of the proverbial Weaverbird (Eye-ègà) using its beak to pull out what it had moulded, which the Yoruba translate to Ègà f’enu kó’lé, ègà f’enu è tu“. Where in the name of prosperity, does a leader kill his people in instalment?

As if the animals were seers, a terrible famine gripped the forest. It met bitter outcry. Weaverbirds (Ègà) and other forest creatures grew frail and emaciated, gathering at the palace gates to weep for their dying young. But, Alábahun remained locked inside his high stone walls. Palace canaries (Ìbákà), like Old Major in Orwell’s Animal Farm, sang loudly of a golden future time of riches more than mind can picture urging the populace to keep toiling for freedom’s sake. “…For that day we all must labor. Though we die before it break…” Once in a while, Alábahun himself walked to the palace balcony to see the starving animals. In sweet-smelling voice, he pleaded understanding, and need for sacrifice today for a better tomorrow. “Endure the dry season for a glorious harvest” was the palace mantra.

Apparently suffocated by the cries of the dying animals whose hungry voices grew too loud to ignore, Alábahun finally directed the royal guards to prize off the lock of the granary and unlock the forest’s treasury. He ordered a massive, unprecedented caravan of grain to be distributed to the starving animals.

The grand wagons finally rolled into the public square. As they did, the palace expected songs of praise for this royal benevolence. Alábahun stood upon his balcony, anticipating the forest to erupt in dance. King Tortoise stood upon his balcony expecting wild applause, but met only a heavy, mournful silence. The silence below was heavy.

“You watched us perish for seasons, and now you bring out baskets of corn. Is it for our funeral or that of our children? Is it now when hundreds of our children have already closed their eyes in life-long sleeps?” cried the older animals.

A fierce debate divided the forest. To many, it was mourning time. Palace’s grand grain distribution came at the animal kingdom’s most vulnerable time. It was a frantic afterthought that could not undo the months of harrowing pains and slow starvation. The heavy rain of abundance had finally fallen, but only after the soil had completely hardened into stone. As the old adage warns: “Òjò t’ó rò l’éyìn ìkórè kò lè gba iṣu t’ó ti joro” – the rain that falls after the harvest is over cannot save the rotten yam.

Animals who deigned to collect the grains were put off by palace couriers’ antics. They pilfered so many sacks of grains and the few left had been eaten up by weevils. They dissolved into dust even before they got to the nests of the poorest birds and holes of kwashiokor-ed animals. The wind blew the husks into the dry air, creating a golden dust storm that blurred the line between the palace and the valley. The heavy rain of abundance had finally fallen, but it came only after the soil had completely hardened into stone.

“That is the end of my story” the old man said.

And I suddenly woke up. A river-like beads of sweats cascaded off the pores of my flesh.

It was a dream!

Same last week when the $1 billion social package was launched, the administration announced that state governors will soon roll out lower transport fares nationwide. They will use Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) and electric vehicles. It will be backed by a planned network of 1,000 refueling stations and over 120,000 converted vehicles. Administration supporters frame these roll-outs as a long-awaited answer to public suffering. Like the crowd that cheered Christ’s entry into Jerusalem – where He warned the scolding Pharisees that the stones would cry out if the people stayed quiet – the First Lady’s flapping Khimar served as Aso Rock’s celebratory “stone,” cheering relief where critics saw only ruin.

To the opposition, however, this sudden rush of belated interventions by a president who fiddled for three years and three months while the people died reflects the tragic pattern of an economic wastrel. This parable of the wastrel reminds me of a musician after my heart. He was High Chief Adedara Ar’ú’nra L’ójà Oba,legendary Ijesa musician. Those days while walking the streets of Oke-Oye in Ilesa, I saw ‘Dedara, as he called himself, playing draught with country-folks somewhere close to Saint Margaret Girls’ School. He was Ijesa’s sonic signature, their musical identity and cultural signature. Adedara presented Ijesa people’s unique musical repertoire and history to the outside world.

Adedara then famously sang of the dog-in-the-manger, the wastrel who refuses to farm, prevents others from farming, and seizes both their hoe and cutlass: “Kò ṣe, kò ṣe, kò j’ólúrè se; ó gb’okọ Olúrè, ó dè gb’àḍá rè o.” The wastrel was the man who declines to embark on a productive venture and would not allow anyone to so do; he seizes the hoe of the willing and his cutlass as well.

The fundamental flaw of the Aso Rock social protection model lies in its heavy reliance on transactional optics over structural economic survival. In three years, three months, Tinubu more than quadrupled tax payments; mercilessly devalued the Naira; replaced astronomical school fees with loans; pedaled food prices to rooftop height and flushed proceeds to federal hangers-on and state governors.

Nigerians have died in their thousands; many lost their manhood as the economy castrated them from performing their household head roles; businesses collapsed; many committed suicide. High drug prices have sent many to their graves. Yet, Tinubu’s Ìbàkà bird aides reel out robust World Bank economic figures to invalidate our oozing flood of tears. If economy under this government has had positive effects on the people, why celebrate this $1b with this fanfare? Why is it now that government suddenly realizes that hopeless Nigerians need hope and buffer? What lifeline will government give the dead and their mourning families?

Distributing grains like Alábahun did – or Naira, as Tinubu proposes to the so-called poorest of the poor, turns governance into an act of emergency relief distribution, rather than sustainable empowerment. This is after after policy fires had already scorched the economic landscape. When a government inflicts macro-economic shock therapy on its citizens, without immediate, synchronized safety nets as the Tinubu government has done since May 29, 2023, any eventual palliative, no matter how grandly packaged inside state banquet halls, feels less like a lifeline, with greater optics of an afterthought. You cannot systematically subject a populace to severe economic attrition for three years and three months, yet expect a sudden shower of palliatives to convert widespread mourning into dancing as Alábahun did.

Ultimately, the $1 billion HOPE-SP initiative risks becoming another monument to misplaced timing. If the underlying cost of living remains astronomically high, temporary cash drops and subsidized transport schemes will be swallowed whole by inflation, leaving the structural roots of poverty untouched. The administration must realize that true “Renewed Hope” is not measured by the flutter of celebratory scarves in Abuja, but by whether the ordinary Nigerian can afford to eat, work, and survive without waiting for King Tortoise’s belated granary to open.

Festus Adedayo is an Ibadan-based journalist.

World.title: APC secretary Ajibola Basiru visits Gov. Adeleke, seeks cooperation to secure 1.5m votes for Tinubu
World.content:
The National Secretary of the All Progressives Congress (APC), Ajibola Basiru, visited he Osun State Governor, Ademola Adeleke, on Sunday, with their discussions during the meeting touching on the campaign for President Bola Tinubu’s re-election in the state for the 2027 presidential election.

Mr Basiru, a former Osun Central senator, was one of the vocal critics of Mr Adeleke during the campaigns for the 15 August governorship election, which the governor won.

The opposition figure’s visit to Mr Adeleke, who contested the election on the platform of Accord Party, was their first publicly known encounter since the acrimonious rivalry between their parties in the lead-up to the election.

The meeting came two weeks after the electioneering marked by widespread violence and fierce exchanges ahead of the off-cycle poll.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

It also came a day after the APC governorship candidate Bola Oyebamiji’s concession of defeat in the election.

Mr Basiru said after the visit to Mr Adeleke at the Government House in Osogbo that the governor, who had repeatedly vowed to back Mr Tinubu for second term in office, said he was prepared to campaign for the president ahead of the January 16 presidential election.

He said the cooperation between the APC and Mr Adeleke’s Accord Party in the state could help the president secure about 1.5 million votes in Osun.

“I am also here to thank him for endorsing my leader and our presidential candidate and to also assure him that we are ready to work together to ensure that we deliver Osun massively for President Bola Tinubu,” Mr Basiru said.

“The governor, during our closed-door meeting, has also said that not only is he endorsing the president, but he will also be on the field to campaign vigorously for President Bola Tinubu for the January 16th presidential election.”

APC, Accord alliance targets 1.5m votes

Mr Basiru said the APC’s defeat in the governorship election did not amount to a poor performance, noting that the party secured 46 per cent of the votes.

He argued that combining the electoral strength of the APC and Accord could significantly increase the number of votes available to Mr Tinubu in the presidential election.

“You can even see from the last contest; my party performed creditably well in that election, scoring 46% of the votes. In between the Accord and the APC, we have close to one million votes, and with the presidential election, I think we should be looking, if we worked together, at about 1.5 million votes for President Bola Tinubu,” he said.

Mr Basiru urged APC members in Osun to close ranks and work with other political stakeholders to secure victory for Mr Tinubu.

“We must close ranks and work together, work together to ensure victory for President Bola Tinubu in the January 16th election,” he said.

The development comes two weeks after Mr Adeleke secured re-election in the 15 August governorship election, defeating his closest challenger, Bola Oyebamiji of the APC.

His victory came despite the APC’s efforts to reclaim the state, which President Tinubu had described as politically significant to his administration and the wider South-West.

Osun also has a sizable voting population, making it an important battleground in any statewide presidential contest. The strength of the state’s electorate, combined with the votes secured by Accord and APC in the recent governorship election, is central to the APC’s calculation that a political alliance could deliver a significant bloc of votes for Mr Tinubu.

Mr Basiru, however, said the outcome of the recent governorship election should not divide Osun residents along party lines, urging political actors to prioritise peace and development.

He also appealed to members of the National Union of Road Transport Workers to resolve their leadership disputes peacefully, saying the post-election violence in the state had subsided.

“On the post-election violence, I think the violence has subsided, but we must sustain the peace,” he said.

“Election has come and gone; all of us belong to this place; we must work to ensure that we have meaningful infrastructure and a good living for the people of Osun.”

World.title: Nepal-China Flood: Over 800 people dead, 3,000 missing
World.content:
The death toll from the devastating floods near the Nepal-China border rose to over 800 on Sunday. Thousands of people are still missing as rescue officials race against time to locate survivors.

Authorities disclosed that more than 3,000 ‌people are still missing on both sides of the Nepal-China border.

The disaster struck the Gyirong border area in China’s Tibet region and Rasuwa district in northern Nepal, in the Himalayan region.

A torrent of ice, rock, mud and debris swept through the border area on Wednesday, swallowing towns, roads and bridges and causing significant loss of life.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The US Geological Survey (USGS) said a massive glacier collapse and landslide triggered the disaster.

Nepalese officials linked the glacial collapse to flash floods that occurred on the Nepal side of the Himalayan mountains.

Chinese authorities also disclosed that at least 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries are missing due to the disaster.

They include 104 Nepalis, 49 Indians, and 33 Latvians.

A total of 18 Americans have also been reported missing, alongside 15 Britons, 6 Canadians, 6 Australians, 3 Russians, Malaysians and Germans,

Nepal is a hotspot for climate disasters as the planet heats up. Vast swaths of ice up in the Himalayas are melting, and rocky mountainsides are becoming less solid and more fluid.

Since Wednesday, countries and organisations around the world have been sending aid to Nepal, including UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who pledged £5 million.

After complaints emerged that people were trapped inside the tunnel, the government prioritised deploying a rescue team and has been advancing work to clear the entrance by removing debris and rubble.

The office of the Nepal prime minister said late on Saturday that the rescue teams were exploring every possible option to identify and locate citizens still missing.

“To expedite the digging of the tunnel entrance and the search operations, a joint team of 82 personnel – including 62 from the Nepali Army and 20 from the Armed Police Force Nepal and Nepal Police – has been continuously deployed since last night. However, with adverse weather conditions persisting in the area, the rescue efforts have become quite challenging,” the prime minister’s office said in a statement.

According to Nepal’s Foreign Secretary, Amrit Rai, about 19,000 security personnel and 16 helicopters have been mobilised in the search and rescue operations.

Meanwhile, in China, a team of 2,141 rescuers has been deployed to the border area, including more than 500 in the worst-hit areas.

A state broadcaster, CCTV, earlier reported that rescue operations were temporarily paused due to the risk of further flooding from a newly formed lake and resumed after the lake was “discharging naturally” and had been “essentially drained.”
