World.title: A Letter to a Zambian Church Leader
World.content:
By Kapya Kaoma

My Dear Fellow Servant,

There comes a moment in the life of a nation when true leadership demands sacred, uncompromising courage. Our offices are patterned after the prophets and saints of Sacred Scripture who dared to stand against tyrants. Yet throughout history, a shadow has stalked our calling: clergy who claim the name of God while quietly serving the forces consuming God’s people. Our mission is defined by the Gospel we proclaim—by the One who called us to take up the cross, not to retreat into the comfortable sanctuaries of modern prestige.

We were called to shepherd God’s flock to protect them from wolves. Scripture warns us: when the flock is scattered and left to perish, God holds the shepherd accountable. The systemic decay in which our nation is caught is not happening in a vacuum; its weight rests upon our shoulders. For too long, we have hidden behind the sanitized statements of church mother bodies—statements our people have long stopped listening to. The flock does not follow press releases; they follow us, individually, from our pulpits and on our phone screens. That is why I address you directly.

Zambia stands at a tipping point. Just look into the faces of our youth: they are hungry, desperate, and burning with rage. Starved of opportunity, they are easily bought for a pittance to turn their hands against their own neighbors. This is more than a political failure; it is a moral catastrophe. The ongoing plunder of our mineral wealth alongside crushing youth unemployment forms a fuse that political slogans cannot extinguish.

In underdeveloped border regions like Mufumbwe, the ground is already catching fire. When state forces deploy under the premise that local miners bear arms, the risk of full-scale armed escalation becomes immediate. Left unchecked, these mineral-rich lands will inevitably attract foreign warlords and insurgent capital. Compounded by unhealed wounds like the Barotseland question, Zambia risks sliding into devastating civil conflict. Is this the heritage we intend to leave for future generations?

We have coasted for decades on the pride of our peace, but no nation is immune to bloodshed. The human heart remains capable of terrifying violence. The clashes that flare during election cycles can easily be fanned into an inferno that consumes the whole republic; it takes only one sparked spark to turn region against region. Yet we watch in silence as our people are manipulated into viewing democratic competition through a tribal lens.

Frankly, this is not about ethnic identity; it is about individual power. Tribalism is being weaponized to manufacture victimhood and justify the destruction of political rivals. It works because a victim is granted the moral right to self-defense. But exploiting tribal strongholds may secure short-term electoral victories, but it sows long-term ruin. Hyper-partisan hostility has so corrupted the body of Christ that many now prioritize their tribe over their faith. When a believer rejects a brother or sister simply because of his ancestry, we must ask: What remains of our “Christianity”? We have failed our people, and we must repent of what passes for Christian witness in our public square.

Our threats gather both within and without, yet we are afraid of confronting them. Why has there been no moral outcry over the body of the late Hon. Mutotwe Kafwaya being discarded, stripped naked in a morgue? Why did we fail to question the morality of denials that characterized his death by the state? Aren’t we Africans to know the sanctity of burial rites? And why did we look on in silence when the courts were abruptly closed for three days?

When church leaders plead for the release of opposition figures like Mundubile and Makebi, we subtly reinforce the lie that they are guilty simply because the executive says so. How many ruling party cadres brandished weapons during campaigns? How many assaulted officers of the law? Have they answered to justice? And how did president Hichilema know he won the elections from which Mundubile intended to usurp power long before the first vote was cast since the arrests began long before August 13? I believe the law is only just when it is applied without bias. Today, our legal system seems bent to serve a single man: the President. We know this. We murmur in private. Yet we are paralyzed by fear to declare it aloud. Is it not suggestive that the very actions that are treated as treason today were the very tactics utilized when the current administration was in opposition? The statutes have not changed. The judges have not changed. Only the occupant of the high office has changed.

We both know. President Hichilema is a man, not a god. He must remain accountable to the people he governs. Holding constitutional authority is one thing; but exercising it ethically is another. The power to appoint and dismiss military commanders, oversight heads, and judges is not a license to misuse national institutions for political survival. Worse still, to dismantle these pillars is to sabotage the nation’s future.

Since taking office, the President’s reach has repeatedly overstepped constitutional boundaries. We watched with heavy hearts as Constitutional Court judges were purged after ruling against his interests during previous administrations. We looked away as he militarized our recent elections. It is not that we didn’t recognize the danger; rather, like Peter at the trial of Jesus, fear paralyzed our truth—and we stepped back into the shadows as the cock crowed. When will we stand up and demand a judiciary that obeys the Constitution rather than the executive?

Ruling party cadres attack citizens, intimidate police, and disrupt gatherings while the state preaches “peace.” Law enforcement targets the opposition while the military assumes an unprecedented role in civilian life. And how does the Church respond? By calling for “calm” among the victimized.

This is not pastoral care; it is complicity. It is telling authorities that they can oppress with total impunity. This is normalizing state intimidation. We resisted this during the Kaunda era when the state became militarized. Our youth may not remember, but when the president claimed to be “the chief shushushu”—it warned of a vicious reign of terror once characterized Dr. Kaunda, the Mankangala’s era! Kumulu ni Lesa, Panshi ni Kaunda! We were all made to shout. That was the era of the shushushu–Zambians spied on each other to serve the interests of the Almighty KK. Are we walking that dark path again? Are state agencies operating under directives where political opponents are marked for elimination? Today the hammer falls on the opposition; tomorrow it will crush the ruling party’s own dissenters when they are out of power. Yet, the President is a civilician, and NOT the Chief Intelligence Officer. Unless we remind him of this fact, we risk losing more innocent lives.

The military belongs in the barracks, not patrolling public streets. The summary use of force against civilians must end. Misusing soldiers is playing with fire—the military is trained for war, not community policing. We must warn the President: preaching peace while unleashing state force against citizens is an illusion of power. State violence inevitably breeds citizen retaliation. When a people realize the system meant to protect them has become their executioner, self-defense becomes an irresistible call.

Justice and policing are inseparable: properly policed communities receive justice; militarized communities receive tyranny. The judiciary exists to shield the weak from the strong. Even autocratic regimes generally keep court doors open to preserve the illusion of order. Didn’t Jesus speak about the unjust judge giving justice to the persistent widow? To see courthouses closed across the country is a stain upon our nation before the global community. How can the executive expect citizens to respect judicial rulings when the process is so blatantly manipulated? It is like Herod delivering the head of John the Baptist on a platter to appease political convenience. Is this our vision for Zambia—a nation where justice is a favor granted only at the whim of the powerful?

As spiritual leaders, we must demand more than soothing rhetoric from an administration marked by broken promises. We must refuse to allow the Christian faith to function as the opiate of the masses—a pacifier for the broken and a silencer for the oppressed. We must stop allowing the persecuted to be stripped of their dignity in captured courts. Citizens are not rebels for challenging their government; it is their constitutional right. Sacralizing state oppression by preaching passivity while human rights are violated is an insult to the Gospel.

When citizens are unjustly arrested, beaten, and bloodied in broad daylight while others applaud, some demand a “proper theology of protest.” What they mean is quietism—doing nothing so the thrones of power remain undisturbed. Our nation does not need pious, empty prayers offered inside sanctuary walls while the streets burn; such rituals mock God. We must speak with prophetic clarity. We must look past our denominational silos and unite as the body of Christ. Our people do not need pacifying platitudes; they need moral courage. Those languishing in cells are not criminals simply because a president labels them so. Those abusing power are not gods; they are mortals accountable to the law and to God. It falls on us to call them to account.

Our ministry must remain non-partisan, but it can never remain neutral. We have grown comfortable serving the institutions we build—cathedrals that replicate the mansions of politicians. Our calling is planted in the cross—the rugged cross where our Lord bled and died as a victim of state execution and religio-political collusion.

The cross is inherently political. As theologian Evangelical Christopher Wright observed, viewing Jesus as “non-political” is a total misreading of history. The Roman Empire did not execute Jesus because he taught personal piety; they killed Him because His proclamation of the Kingdom of God exposed the illegitimacy of their ultimate authority. When we confess Christ as King of kings, we declare that no president, no party, and no regime holds absolute power. Earthly authority remains entirely subject to the judgment of God. An administration may imprison our bodies, but the Church holds the divine mandate to call thrones to repentance.

This is the baseline of Christian witness: stepping into the public vulnerability of our Lord—a vulnerability present today in the poor, the detained, and the silenced. Ever since Constantine, the Church has been tempted to trade the cross for the throne, bartering its soul for political access. Yet throughout history, God has raised prophets to break that unholy alliance, often at the cost of their lives.

Across Africa, believers have suffered martyrdom for standing against abusive power. On our own soil, those who brought the Gospel faced a choice: stand with the cross or align with the colonial oppressor. Tragically, many chose the oppressor, demanding that Africans remain submissive. The blood shed to liberate Zambia was spilled despite the prayers of complicit clergy who labeled freedom fighters as outlaws. During the UNIP era, a Roman Catholic archbishop died under mysterious circumstances because he dared to be a voice for the voiceless against a regime that sought to supplant God.

Our integrity as religious leaders is under judgment. Throughout Israel’s history, court prophets were bought with royal favors. Today, too many of us have been silenced by access and influence. We have traded the hard word of the cross for executive dinners, selling our birthright for silver—and like Judas, missing the glory of the Holy God. Those silver coins will not save us. Instead of praying to God, we offer public invocations tailored to please the political patrons who control the purse. So it was in the days of Elijah; so it is today.

As magnificent as our church buildings may be, Christ does not live in our brick and mortar. Christ is suffering in underserved compounds left without clean water. Christ is present where young people are exploited while leaders feast in luxury. He is present among political prisoners denied access to a judge or a lawyer. Even Pontius Pilate granted Jesus a formal trial; today, basic legal rights are swept away at the executive’s command. On state occasions, clergy parade alongside officials, acting as human shields for state overreach rather than heralds of Gospel liberation. They repeat the tragic pattern of Maundy Thursday, when religious authorities and imperial officers joined hands to condemn an innocent man to preserve their own status.

The theology of the cross is an act of holy resistance. It exposes the lie of tyranny and demands ethical action against systemic evil. It points to an innocent Man who walked the road to a grave, exposing the bankruptcy of human power. The victim of yesterday is the Risen Lord of today, who has empowered His Church to defend the least of His brothers and sisters.

Theologically, holiness and justice are inseparable. True worship demands righteous action. We see this in the ministry of Jesus, who broke cultural, political, and religious barriers to bring mercy, peace, and truth to the marginalized. If not a single sparrow falls to the ground without your Father’s knowledge, how much more does the blood of those denied justice cry out to Him on our watch?

It was this uncompromising truth that made Jesus an existential threat to earthly powers. When He was arrested, the crowds vanished. His followers fled; some even joined the mob shouting, “Crucify him! We have no king but Caesar!” He stood alone. This remains the brutal reality for political prisoners in our land today—they suffer isolated, mocked, and forgotten. Even religious leaders have forgotten them.

As witnesses to Christ, we cannot abandon the cross. It is our only authority. From the cross, Jesus forged a new community of solidarity: “Woman, behold your son… Son, behold your mother.” The power of the cross exposes the naked deception of political tribalism. We ignore ethnic divisions until election season, only to watch citizens prosecuted for “hate speech” while the elite exploit those same divisions to capture votes. Allowing the lie that regions vote purely by tribe is a failure of our moral and religious leadership. At the cross, tribal divisions collapse, leaving only the truth of our shared identity in Christ.

We face an unavoidable choice: uphold a corrupt status quo or bear witness to the truth. Too often, we become silent partners to injustice, watching Christ suffer in the person of the oppressed while we offer polite prayers for the oppressor. We urge the weak to submit, but fail to call the strong to repent.

Where is the spirit of Moses demanding from Pharaoh, “Let my people go”? Where is the spirit of Samuel declaring to Saul, “The Lord has rejected your rule”? Where is the spirit of Nathan standing before David, “You are the man”? As Jesus reminded Pilate, no ruler holds authority except that which is given from above. No president is above the law of God or the law of the land.

The cross is God’s protest against human cruelty, and the Resurrection is His promise that tyranny has an expiration date. A third day is coming—a day when fear loses its grip, and when bars, chains, and state power can no longer suppress the truth.

Let us reclaim the prophetic fire of our calling. We are servants of the cross, and it is from the cross that our strength flows. It is a severe indictment of our witness when secular civic groups show more courage against executive overreach than the Church of Jesus Christ. There is no neutrality in the face of oppression. The Church found its voice to speak truth to Dr. Kaunda; we found our voice during the Chiluba administration. We must speak with the same unyielding clarity to President Hichilema today: he is a mortal leader, not a deity. Political opponents do not need presidential mercy; they require impartial justice.

May the cross grant us the fortitude to stand firm, trusting in Christ as our shield. As Apostolic Father Ignatius of Antioch on his way to execution reminded us: “When Christianity is under attack, grand words are of no use—only grand actions.”

Let us move beyond rhetoric into principled, dangerous obedience. May God grant us the courage of the cross.

Many will condemn this message. But I do not fear their condemnation. I fear only the judgment of God if I remain silent.

World.title: Well done Southern Province
World.content:
By Dr. Field Ruwe

The voice of the ECZ election officer resonated ominously like a death knell:

“Thank you, chairperson. The next results are from Southern Province.”

For supporters of Brian Mundubile the mere mention of Southern Province brought about untold anguish because it represented the moment of demographically and mathematically inevitable defeat. The election officer proceeded to announce the results.

Monze District, Bweengwa Constituency: “Daniel Pule PDP=0, Richard Siamunene CDP=0, Howard Kunda ZWP=0, Richard Silumbe LM=3, Brian Mushimba OPP=1, Given Chansa MEE=8, Given Katuta Independent=4, Fred Mmembe SP=5, Kelvin Bwalya ZMP=23, Harry Kalaba CF=11, Brian Mundubile NRPUP=129, Hakainde Hichilema UPND=24,492.”

“Next,” the announcer continued. “Solwezi North: “Daniel Pule PDP=0, Richard Siamunene CDP=0, Howard Kunda ZWP=0.” Richard Silumbe LM=0.” There was laughter from the audience.

Announcer continued. “Brian Mushimba OPP=0,” Laugher. “Given Chansa MEE=0” Laughter. “Given Katuta Independent=0.” More laughter. “Fred Mmembe SP=0.” Even more laughter. “Kelvin Bwalya ZMP=0, Harry Kalaba CF=2, Brian Mundubile NRPUP=2,331, Hakainde Hichilema UPND=39,662.”

Every Zambian should tip his or her hat to the Tonga and the Bantu Botatwe for showing other ethnic groups the meaning of ethnic solidarity. Through robust intragroup ethnic capital, they have demographically and successfully executed their voting strategy with collective action like no other. Never in the history of Zambia have a people grounded themselves in a shared identity, collective action, and political cooperation to rescue one of their own sons as has been demonstrated in this year’s election.

Southern Province served as the critical counterweight in the election, with the Bantu Botatwe regions decisively wiping out or eroding the margins Mundubile was securing in his strongholds. This formidable turnout highlighted the impact of a unified electorate voting in lockstep, motivated by the acute understanding that the fate of their political leader was inextricably bound to their own fate.

What we have witnessed from the Bantu Botatwe and its affiliates is a masterclass in ethnic demographic solidarity, political unity, and collective resolve.

On August 13, 2026, more than 50 % of 2.6 million Tongas; 440,000 Lambas; 310,000 Lenjes; 215,000 Ilas; 75,000 Solis; 69,000 Totelas; 58,000 Salas; and 17,000 Fwes (Mafwe) stood shoulder-to-shoulder in endless queues outside polling stations in absolute trust and mutual reciprocity. At the end of the day, they executed a historicized subnational cohesion and a natural political strategic alignment unprecedented in Zambian politics.

This is what I meant when I penned “2026 Hunt for Successor Five.” Securing victory in an election through demographic means entails effectively forming a voting coalition that spans crucial population segments, including ethnicity and geography, which surpasses or strategically outmaneuvers the opponents’ support base within the established electoral framework.

By voting monolithically, the Tongas and Bantu Botatwe affiliates have proved that “demography is destiny,” and has nothing to do with tribalism. They have understood that winning an election relies on eroding an opponent’s traditional margins. If they are not challenged in future elections, they will do it again, and again, and again, and gladly so.

Well done, Southern Province and all your affiliates.

World.title: There’s nothing like the country is divided; it’s common practice in any democracy!
World.content:
By Prince Bill M. Kaping’a

In their desperate attempt to discredit President Hichilema, the opposition has seized every opportunity to push the narrative that HH has divided the nation. They gleefully cite the outcome of recent elections as proof.

What kind of warped reasoning is this?

In the United States — the very citadel of democracy we claim to emulate — voters have always followed predictable regional patterns. For decades, there have been solidly Democratic “blue states” and solidly Republican “red states.” The West Coast and Northeast are Democratic strongholds, while the South and Midwest lean Republican. And even within those states, the pattern flips: rural areas in blue states often vote red, while major cities in red states often vote blue.

If we took a closer near home, in South Africa, the same trend holds. The Western Cape has long been a DA base, KZN and parts of Gauteng swing between ANC, IFP and MK, while Limpopo and the Eastern Cape remain ANC strongholds.

Regional voting patterns are not evidence of a president dividing a nation. They reflect history, economics, and demographics that existed long before any one leader. To blame HH for a map that looks the same every election is not analysis. It’s cheap propaganda!

Given the foregoing, it’s obvious that the voting pattern in our beloved country shall remain the same, RED or Green, for a long time to come unless a miracle happens. There’s no need to malign or call each other names.

On the other hand, Lusaka and Copperbelt shall equally remain battleground provinces for political parties. As they are cosmopolitan by nature, they may not be easily attracted or moved by ethnic affiliations but rather party manifestos.

Have you taken the trouble to interrogate how UNZA and CBU voted for instance in the recent elections? UPND had a field day harvesting votes at these institutions as students are very attracted to the party’s education policy.

State House has dismissed as cheap propaganda claims that the Executive is pressuring Chief Justice Mumba Malila to ignore a presidential election petition, after opposition figure Clayson Hamasaaka alleged that pressure was being applied on the judiciary to have the Chief Justice sit on the matter rather than let it proceed.

Brebner Changala said Chief Justice Malila, who has acknowledged receiving the petition and forwarded it to the Constitutional Court, should resist external pressure and ensure the petition gets its day in court, according to a report carried by the Daily Nation.

The Judiciary confirmed that the petition, filed by opposition leader Brian Mundubile, has in fact been forwarded to the Constitutional Court, contradicting suggestions that it had been ignored or suppressed.

The dispute comes against the backdrop of the brief closure of courts on August 24, the very day the deadline for filing a presidential petition was expiring, a development that drew criticism from civil society and opposition figures who questioned the timing.

A Judiciary memorandum at the time instructed staff not to report for work, citing security concerns, while police presence around court premises restricted access. The Judiciary has said the closure does not establish that President Hakainde Hichilema personally ordered it, and has stressed that determining the effect of the closure would require evidence rather than speculation.

With the petition now formally before the Constitutional Court, the practical question is one of timing: the ceremony marking the start of President Hichilema’s second term falls on Tuesday, leaving a narrow window for the court to signal how, and how quickly, it intends to deal with a challenge of this weight.

Changala’s intervention places him among a small number of civil society voices who have spoken publicly on the judiciary’s independence in the days since the election, distinct from the separate legal questions raised over the conduct of the Mandevu rerun and the various election petitions already lodged at the Ndola High Court.

Government has maintained that the courts remain independent and that the petition process will be allowed to run its lawful course, with the Constitutional Court now seized with the matter.

The controversy over court access follows weeks of tension since the August 13 election, during which President Hichilema was declared the winner, opposition figures were arrested, and a raid on Mundubile’s home left former minister Mutotwe Kafwaya dead.

As the Constitutional Court prepares to consider the petition, both government and opposition supporters will be watching to see whether the process is seen to be free, transparent and untainted by outside interference.

World.title: A Day After Fresh Mandevu Order, ZCLU Questions ECZ’s Legal Authority
World.content:
LUSAKA: A day after the Electoral Commission of Zambia ordered a fresh parliamentary election in Mandevu constituency, the decision is facing a direct legal challenge, with a civil rights group insisting the Commission had no lawful basis to call the rerun.

ECZ announced on Saturday that it would conduct a fresh poll in Mandevu following a security breach at the constituency’s totalling centre on August 13. Unknown individuals attacked the centre, destroyed result transmission kits and fled with documentation, preventing declaration of results in the seat.

The Zambian Civil Liberties Union has now questioned the legal authority behind that decision. Executive director Isaac Mwanza said there is no law that mandates the Commission to cancel and conduct fresh parliamentary elections outright.

ZCLU said it had examined the Electoral Process Act of 2016, as amended in 2025 and 2026, particularly Sections 56 and 75, and found that neither provision applies to a cancellation or a fresh call for nominations of this kind. “The two sections cannot both apply,” Mwanza said, since the Mandevu incident occurred after voting and during aggregation. He argued the only proper course open to ECZ was to approach the Constitutional Court for guidance on whether a by-election could be held at all, given that no law empowers it to order one unilaterally.

Candidate reaction has hardened in the day since Saturday’s announcement. Citizens First’s Steven Mwale argued the fresh poll would impose a heavy financial and logistical burden on candidates who had already invested heavily in their campaigns, saying the commission should instead have pursued those responsible for the alleged ballot tampering rather than ordering a complete rerun.

Independent candidate Adrian Banda said he remained too disturbed to comment further, while Resolute Party’s Jean Kapata has still not spoken to journalists on the matter.

Socialist Party’s Teddy Mwaba maintained his welcome of the decision a day on, describing it as a step toward restoring fairness following irregularities in the original vote, and repeated his call for ECZ to release a full election timetable without delay.

Green Party leader Peter Sinkamba, who warned on Saturday that the disputed August 13 poll could be reduced to an academic exercise unless the manipulation that marred the process is addressed, has since gone further. He is now challenging ECZ to consider fresh mayoral elections in Lusaka alongside the Mandevu rerun, given how much the mayoral vote draws from Mandevu.

ECZ now faces a choice: defend its authority to order the rerun as announced, or clarify whether it intends to seek the Constitutional Court’s guidance that Mwanza says the law actually requires. Ten parliamentary candidates remain on standby for the reignited Mandevu seat once, or if, nomination and polling dates are confirmed.

World.title: State Agents Search Makebi Zulu’s Home As Church Denies Political Deal Claim
World.content:
Security agents have searched the Lusaka residence of opposition running mate Makebi Zulu, a search his lawyer Sakwiba Sikota says was carried out without his legal team being notified beforehand, raising fresh questions about how the operation was conducted.

The search comes as an eight-member church mediation team dismissed suggestions that it had brokered, or attempted to broker, a political settlement between government and the opposition. In a statement, the churches said their mandate was never to negotiate a political deal between the two sides, but rather to facilitate a peaceful and dignified transition through the United Nations premises to legal representatives.

The clarification followed reports that Brian Mundubile and Zulu had been handed over as part of a negotiated arrangement, a narrative the churches were keen to correct given the sensitivity of the treason case against the pair.

Sikota’s objection centres on the absence of prior notice to counsel, a procedural point that lawyers say matters regardless of the seriousness of the allegations under investigation, since it goes to whether the rights of an accused person are being observed at every stage of an operation, not only once a matter reaches court.

The search of Zulu’s home follows a similar operation at Mundubile’s Kabulonga residence on August 14, during which former minister Mutotwe Kafwaya was killed and various weapons recovered. Eleven people associated with Mundubile were arrested during that operation.

The Law Association of Zambia has continued to follow the handling of the case, with its leadership convening briefings to update the public on developments affecting the accused, including procedural questions of the kind Sikota has now raised over his client’s search.

With both principal opposition figures now facing treason charges and their properties searched, how each search was conducted, and not only what was found, is likely to feature prominently once the matter reaches open court.

World.title: Africa: Is This The Bandage For Africa's Rising Medical Fabrics Demand?
World.content:
Local cotton manufacturing moves into surgical textiles as Africa seeks import alternatives and channels more fibre into homegrown factories.

African manufacturers are increasingly turning locally grown cotton into high-value medical textiles, offering a domestic alternative to raw exports and expensive imports.

The shift is still small compared with the size of the continent's cotton industry. But it comes as countries across the region are under pressure to produce more of the health products they consume.

As demand picks up, it has drawn entrepreneurs along the continent's cotton value chain who want an early foothold in a market poised for strong growth in the next four years.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Market research firm Mordor Intelligence forecasts the Africa textile market to reach $49.41 billion by 2030, up from $39.21 billion in 2025.

Tellingly, "medical and healthcare textiles are the fastest growing segment, projected at 5.71% CAGR through 2030", the firm said, pointing to rising demand for products used in hospitals and operating theatres.

"Nigeria, Kenya, and Ethiopia are building hospitals under public-private frameworks that standardise demand for surgical drapes, fluid-repellent gowns, and certified wound dressings." Mordor Intelligence attributes this growth to Covid-era reforms which made bulk buying of protective wear more routine.

This, it says, has encouraged IFC-backed factories in Ghana and Kenya to add clean-room production lines built to meet ISO 13485, the global standard for medical-grade production.

A move toward local sourcing of medical textiles could give manufacturers a steadier market than fashion, where producers often depend on foreign buyers and shifting orders.

For cotton-producing countries, the potential is massive because much of the raw material needed for these products is already grown locally.

In Ethiopia, Adama Development has already moved beyond cotton spinning. The company now operates a medical textile business, Nazmed Medical Textiles, alongside its cotton and textile operations.

A textile industry professional working for the company describes Nazmed as part of Adama Development's medical textile operations.

The development reflects a broader change in the way African manufacturers are looking at cotton for new opportunities to cash in from the crop. For decades, much of the continent's cotton has left in relatively unprocessed form.

UN Trade and Development estimates that 70% of Africa's cotton exports are primary intermediate products such as cotton fibre. Only 12% are yarn and 18% are cotton fabrics.

The OECD-FAO Agricultural Outlook projects that Africa will export nearly 80% of its cotton production by 2035, although the textile and apparel industries are expanding in countries like Ethiopia and Benin.

But the uptake of medical textiles could see the continent convert more of its cotton into finished healthcare products as fresh focus and investment flow into manufacturing.

New ventures are adding capacity further along the chain. In Zambia, a China-Zambia joint venture began test runs at Mulungushi Textiles in Kabwe in January 2026 after new machinery was installed.

The $140 million rehabilitation aims to revive textile production and create hundreds of direct jobs, while also supporting cotton outgrowers.

Everness Nankala, a principal public relations officer at Zambia’s Ministry of Commerce, Trade and Industry, said the project was “a testament to the government’s commitment to promoting industrial growth and creating employment opportunities for Zambians.” The plant is also expected to “reduce reliance on imports, and promote inclusive development,” she said.

In Zambia, another entrepreneur is already turning cotton into a medical product. Carrivorious Simasinti began producing surgical cotton wool after seeing his country export raw cotton and then import absorbent cotton products.

Simasinti founded Premier Multipurpose Cooperative Society in 2016. His factory processes cotton lint into absorbent and surgical cotton wool for medical and sanitary use.

In 2021, when UNCTAD profiled the business, the factory was producing about 7,200 kg of surgical cotton wool a month. About 70% was sold within Zambia and the remaining 30% exported to neighbouring countries.

“Demand for the product is high,” Simasinti told UN Trade and Development.

The company had also developed an outgrower scheme involving more than 100 farmers. Together, they had covered 250 hectares and were expected to produce 150 tonnes of seed cotton. But shortages of raw cotton, limited machinery and transport problems restricted expansion.

In Kenya, African Cotton Industries Limited has produced cotton wool and hygiene supplies since 1960, operating facilities in Nairobi, Mombasa and Kampala.

The firm supplies major institutional distributors, including Mission for Essential Drugs and Supplies, the Kenya Medical Supplies Authority, and Kenyatta National Hospital.

In South Africa, Da Gama Textile now operates facilities with more than 580 employees, producing up to 15 million machine metres of fabric per month in Zwelitsha, Eastern Cape.

Its healthcare range now includes 100% cotton and poly cotton sheeting, linen, drapes, curtains, and uniforms with antimicrobial and water repellent finishes.

“Cotton-rich sheeting is in high demand from both public and private hospitals, as well as clinics and healthcare facilities to ensure patient comfort and laundering durability,” it noted.

The company says its medical fabrics are produced locally using mostly local materials and that its facilities have the capacity and equipment to make fabrics in different weights, designs and finishes.

South Africa has also moved further into specialised medical fabrics, with producers such as PrionTex entering this space. The company manufactures reusable laminates, theatre textiles, clean room suits, and procedure packs for African markets.

PrionTex also developed a breathable three-layer surgical gown fabric tested to EN 13795 standards to block fluids, viruses, and bacteria.

Zimbabwe, meanwhile, has developed another niche. Zimbabwe Hosiery now manufactures tubular medical bandages in two ranges. Its Tubidress range is made from 100% cotton yarn while its Perlon range uses cotton and polyester yarns.

“The Tubidress range of tubular medical bandages is manufactured from 100% cotton yarn,” the company said.

Such products may appear simple compared with high technology medical equipment, but they are part of the everyday supplies that hospitals need continuously.

That makes healthcare an attractive market for textile manufacturers in Africa’s cotton value chain. The demand is also being supported by a broader push to build local health production capacity.

In Morocco, the focus is already on medical goods. Chinese manufacturer Jiangsu Aishelun Medical Technology Group launched its first African factory at Mohammed VI Tanger Tech City in May 2026 through its Moroccan subsidiary, InnovMed Tech Group.

The company makes medical consumables and infection control items, from surgical gowns and drapes to ice packs, adult care products and urinary bags.

It plans to use the plant to serve markets across Europe, the Middle East and North Africa while sourcing raw materials across Africa.

Still, the World Health Organisation expects African countries to remain heavily dependent on imported medicines and health products and urges long-term manufacturing plans for countries.

Close 

Kenya’s 2026–2030 local health manufacturing plan, unveiled in June, recognises that production capacity alone will not build an industry. It calls for better use of existing factories and sustained procurement commitments that give manufacturers the certainty to invest and expand.

President William Ruto, who chairs the African Union’s push for local manufacturing, has placed the issue at the centre of what he calls Africa’s “health security and sovereignty agenda”. Kenya’s Principal Secretary for Medical Services, Dr Ouma Oluga, put the challenge more directly: “You cannot finance a healthcare system that you cannot supply.”

From surgical cotton wool in Zambia to hospital fabrics in South Africa and tubular bandages in Zimbabwe, African manufacturers are demonstrating that more of the continent’s cotton can be turned into essential medical products at home.

The decisive next step is whether hospitals, governments and procurement agencies will provide the reliable orders needed to turn those individual production lines into a durable continental industry.
