World.title: From the archive: Learning Spanish? Don’t be shy or afraid of making mistakes
World.content:
The goal of our “From the Archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Sarah DeVries article, for example — originally published in November 2019 — explores the leap of faith required when learning Mexican Spanish.

When I first arrived in Mexico, I had two years of college-level Spanish under my belt. While I was an enthusiastic learner, I was also a very self-conscious speaker, terrified of making embarrassing mistakes and generally sounding like a 2-year-old.

I did, in fact, sound like a 2-year-old at first, as there’s simply no way around being a “baby” when one is first learning. Happily, I survived that stage and now speak at least as well as a know-it-all 13-year-old.

Part of my apprehension with the language was the sense that Mexico’s love-hate relationship with the United States would lead to some situations in which I’d be mocked for my accent or mistakes that I would inevitably make.

After all, most people here know very well how Latinos are treated by certain segments of the U.S. population when they’re on the other side of the border, so I’d imagined that the temptation to dish some out to us collectively would be at least a little irresistible.

For the most part, that didn’t happen. It’s also possible that I simply didn’t realize it was happening, but I think most of us humans have a pretty good sense of when others are laughing at us.

Once in a while someone will have a longish conversation with me (in Spanish) and then say something like, “So, you don’t speak Spanish, eh?” or they’ll point out that they “could tell right away that I was American because of my accent” which always makes me bristle, as I’m pretty sure my accent is, while definitely existent, not obviously American.

(My Mexican friends may disagree with me on that one; I’d ask them, but the answer might be too painful for me to hear.)

There’s some sting in it, but I do my best to chalk up any unflattering comments about my Spanish to cosmic justice and not take it too personally.

In the part of Mexico where I live, English is not considered an essential skill the same way it is in the north or in tourist areas. Because of this, most foreigners in my area do their best with the language: they take classes, they practice, they work hard to get better.

Learning a language is sign of respect

They understand, above all, that learning the language of your hosts, if you are able, is a matter of respect.

When I traveled to Los Cabos recently to visit a friend, I saw how different things were in a town that depends on tourism from their English-speaking neighbors: I was addressed in English at all times, and if I answered in Spanish it almost seemed to startle people, as if they’d come into contact with a dog that had learned to produce human sounds.

For the most part, Mexicans are charmed when we non-native speakers at least try. They’re patient and encouraging, and try their best to be helpful. Mexico really is an ideal place to learn Spanish, as I can’t imagine another place in which more impromptu and consistent support among the general population would be given.

That said, I know many of my compatriots are shy about learning — and especially about using — the Spanish that they know already. I completely understand: there’s nothing that makes us feel quite as vulnerable as not being able to “prove” that we are smart, complex, discerning individuals.

There’s no way around sounding like a simpleton when we’re on that long uphill trajectory, and simply put, it can be a humiliating experience.

But again: at least attempting to learn the local language, if one is able, is a matter of respect. “Well then, what about all the people in the U.S. that haven’t bothered to learn English? I bet you don’t go around preaching to them about respect, do you?”

The short answer is that no, indeed I do not. Because here’s the difference: most people who go to the U.S. without already speaking English are in survival mode, just trying to make it from one day to the next, often working a dizzying number of hours both to both survive, and likely to send money back home.

Most Americans and Canadians, however, come to Mexico either in vacation or retirement mode. Some, sadly, come because their spouses or loved ones have been deported and they want to keep the family together.

If one is on vacation, of course, learning the language won’t be expected. But if you settle here, an effort must be made.

Find a school, or find a teacher. Find someone to sit and help you practice. Spend time just listening to people with no intention of adding to the conversation. One of the best pieces of advice I’ve ever received for learning a language is literally to pretend to be a baby: listen to the sounds, watch people, let whole social situations piece themselves together and come into focus slowly.

Babies, after all, spend at least a couple of years listening and observing before they try to string together a sentence with more than four words in it.

On my first plane ride into Mexico, my nervousness increased with each sentence given in Spanish by the flight attendants: the more they spoke, the more I realized I wasn’t catching anything at all that they were saying.

Since then, I’ve made about a million mistakes, linguistically embarrassed myself in every way imaginable, and surely sounded much less sophisticated than I imagine myself to be.

But I’ve gained the ability to talk to most people on this side of the world and have developed some of the closest relationships of my lifetime in this language.

Hands down, totally worth it.

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, sarahedevries.substack.com.

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: A governor takes a U-turn, CJNG loses more ground and business booms
World.content:
Listen to this article

The week of Aug. 24 in Mexico began on awkward footing following a Morena party faux pas in Sinaloa. Rubén Rocha Moya, currently under investigation in the United States for alleged collusion with the Sinaloa Cartel, briefly reclaimed the Sinaloa governorship after months on leave, only to retreat again two days later. Meanwhile, several storm systems dumped rain on most of the country, and an investigation into fuel theft in Tamaulipas turned up a startling menagerie of exotic animals.

Also this week, President Sheinbaum revealed new reforms and a US $6M windfall for Guerrero schools as she prepares to soon give her second annual report to the nation.

Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Sheinbaum weighs in on Rocha’s status in Sinaloa

President Claudia Sheinbaum spent the week fielding questions about the fallout from Rocha Moya’s brief return to the Sinaloa governorship from Aug. 21–23 and the future of Sinaloa’s leadership.

At Monday’s mañanera, as Sonora’s cattle trade with the U.S. reopened, she addressed the episode directly for the first time, saying she learned of Rocha’s Friday return through his social media post and had no prior knowledge of his plans. “I didn’t think it was appropriate, to say the least,” she said, later calling the decision “imprudent.” She credited Rocha’s renewed leave request — approved unanimously by Sinaloa’s Congress that Sunday — as “the best thing for Sinaloa,” and dismissed rumors that former President Andrés Manuel López Obrador had encouraged Rocha’s return as “political fiction.”

Sheinbaum extended the same standard to other Morena officials swept up in the same U.S. indictment. Asked on Tuesday about Senator Enrique Inzunza — one of 10 Sinaloa-linked officials accused by U.S. prosecutors of drug trafficking ties, who had signaled he might return to the Senate — she said the same principle applied. “Yesterday I gave my opinion on the case of the governor of Sinaloa, who is now on leave. I feel the same way about all 10 cases under investigation by the Attorney General’s Office,” she said. Inzunza subsequently separated from Morena’s Senate caucus on Wednesday, though he remains in office as senator.

Multiple CJNG busts across three states

Security forces delivered a string of blows against the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) this week. A coordinated operation across Hidalgo, Jalisco and Michoacán from Aug. 21–23 resulted in 20 arrests and the seizure of weapons, drugs and exotic animals tied to the cartel, with authorities raiding 36 properties and confiscating firearms, fentanyl, methamphetamine, 113 vehicles and a drone jammer.

That action followed a separate military-led operation in Michoacán targeting alleged CJNG leader Heraclio “El Tío Lako” Guerrero Martínez last week, which produced roughly a dozen more arrests, including relatives of the suspect. Combined, the two operations brought the week’s tally of alleged CJNG detentions to 32, part of what Security Minister Omar García Harfuch described as an effort to systematically dismantle the group’s operational and financial capacity rather than simply rack up arrests.

Confusion and concern in Mexicali

A U.S. security alert warning of a possible “August 25 threat” in Mexicali created a tense but ultimately murky standoff between caution and normalcy. The alert prompted the U.S. Mission to suspend official travel and activity in the border city, reportedly linked to fears that the crime gang Los Rusos might retaliate after a 120-kilogram fentanyl seizure — roughly 4 million doses — from a property connected to the group.

Mexican officials responded by increasing patrols around public buildings, but as Tuesday came and went without a major incident, the federal security cabinet said it had found no evidence of a specific or imminent threat to the public. Residents described a largely normal day, and the Mexicali-Calexico border crossing remained open throughout, leaving the alert’s basis and its practical necessity still unclear.

Economic data: Record highs alongside warning signs

Revised GDP figures showed the economy grew in the second quarter but contracted in June, with the primary sector contributing the steadiest growth. Foreign direct investment in Mexico yielded US $34.968 billion in FDI in the first half of 2026, its highest semester total ever recorded, up 2.1% year over year, even though the second quarter alone saw a 3.5% annual decline. Manufacturing captured 38.6% of that investment, and the United States remained the dominant source at $16.871 billion.

Trade data added to the good news: July exports hit a record US $81.4 billion, up 43.7% annually, driven by a 134% surge in electrical and electronic equipment shipments tied to U.S. demand for AI and data-center infrastructure inputs. At her Wednesday press conference, Sheinbaum cheered the numbers as proof of a “strong” economy, pointing to record FDI, 60 million people employed and a firm peso, and argued that years of minimum-wage increases had not triggered the inflation or capital flight critics once predicted.

That optimism gained further support when Mexico placed among the OECD’s fastest-growing economies, ranking sixth with 1.4% quarterly growth against an OECD average of 0.5%. But the jobs report complicated the picture: Mexico posted its best monthly job gain of 2026 in July, yet the increase was driven entirely by informal employment, with more than 1.08 million informal jobs added while over 412,000 formal positions vanished. Informality climbed to 56.2%, its highest level since December 2021 — a reminder that headline growth figures can mask deteriorating job quality.

This week’s investment announcements

Schneider Electric announced a major expansion of its operations in Querétaro, reinforcing the state’s role as an industrial and technology hub. Danish firms unveiled a US $510 million renewables project set to boost Campeche’s clean energy supply, adding to the country’s growing green energy portfolio. And Jalisco is set to host Mexico’s first solar panel recycling plant, a facility in Ciudad Guzmán capable of recovering up to 95% of materials from the roughly 1.6 million panels already installed statewide.

A fresh framework for environmental protection

Environment Minister Alicia Bárcena presented a bill to put environmental justice at the center of Mexican law, proposing reforms to the General Law of Ecological Balance and Environmental Protection. The initiative would require more forward-looking assessment of major projects, close loopholes that let developers split projects to dodge full environmental review, strengthen restoration and remediation requirements and add specific protections for environmental defenders and Indigenous, Afro-Mexican, rural and urban communities.

Foreign Minister strengthens ties in South Korea and Washington

Foreign Minister Roberto Velasco kept a packed international schedule this week. In Seoul, he met with South Korean officials and executives from Samsung, Hyundai, LG and Posco to promote investment in technology, semiconductors and education, part of groundwork for a 2026–30 bilateral action plan ahead of a planned visit by South Korea’s president. He then traveled to Washington, where he held his first face-to-face meeting with Secretary of State Marco Rubio. While both sides publicly stressed cooperation against drug and arms trafficking, Bloomberg reported that Washington privately pressed Mexico to do more to stop its own citizens from crossing into the U.S.

Aura farming battles debut in Mexico

A new social-media-driven trend reached Mexican public squares this week: aura farming battles, in which participants strike poses, dance and reference memes to project confidence and style while crowds judge who accumulates the most “aura.” Events popped up at Mexico City landmarks as well as in Xalapa and Torreón, though at least one Veracruz municipality banned the contests in public parks on administrative grounds.

Sheinbaum proposes dual-citizenship ban

Sheinbaum also unveiled a constitutional amendment that would bar dual nationals from running for president, governor or Mexico City mayor unless they renounce their other citizenship before registering as candidates. The government argues current constitutional language contains a loophole and that the country’s highest offices should be held only by people with unambiguous national allegiance — a proposal likely to draw scrutiny over its impact on Mexican-born citizens with binational ties.

Mexican athletes shine internationally

Cyclist Isaac del Toro won the Tour of Germany, becoming the first Latin American rider to capture the race, finishing 53 seconds ahead of France’s Louis Barré.

Mexico won two gold medals and a bronze at the World Rowing Championships in Amsterdam: Aylín Ibarra and Melissa Márquez took gold in women’s lightweight double sculls, Kenia Lechuga won gold in lightweight single sculls, and Alexis López earned bronze in men’s lightweight single sculls.

Looking ahead

The coming weeks will test whether this week’s political and security cracks widen further. In Sinaloa, the ongoing conflict between Los Mayos and Los Chapitos remains unresolved, complicating the search for a permanent successor. Pressure is also unlikely to ease on other Morena-aligned officials named in the same U.S. indictment, amid broader questions about the party’s exposure to organized crime in states beyond Sinaloa. With Sheinbaum’s second annual report to the nation approaching, how she navigates these overlapping crises could shape both her security narrative and her party’s credibility heading into the fall.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Activists rally to stop luxury project on Yucatán dunes
World.content:
A proposed luxury real estate development along a protected beach community in Mexico’s Yucatán Peninsula has sparked protests and backlash online. It’s the latest in a string of projects that activists have sought to stop, saying the developments will have detrimental impacts on their communities.

Las Dunas tourist complex is a planned luxury real estate and tourism venture that aims to encompass 92,000 square meters (more than 22 acres) of virgin beach area less than an hour’s drive from Mérida, the state capital of Yucatán, including more than 70 apartments spread across six towers.

Given its size and scope, activists say the project will have a significant economic and environmental impact on the small beach town, and that it ignores pressing issues that need to be addressed.

“In Chuburná, there are real needs – problems stemming from a lack of basic infrastructure and systematic neglect by the authorities,” Salvemos las Dunas, a local environmental activist group, told Mexico News Daily. “They want to foster the false belief that megaprojects bring economic benefits, but the question is: benefits for whom?”

‘A crime against biodiversity’

It’s not just Salvemos las Dunas that’s sounding the alarm.

Mexico’s Ministry of Environment and Natural Resources (Semarnat) denied the project’s initial proposal in December 2023, as the site was deemed highly vulnerable. However, in April 2025, after adjustments were made to the proposal, the project was federally approved.

As the Las Dunas development began to take shape, the outcry from community members and activists was swift. Salvemos las Dunas launched a petition calling for a halt to the project and an official review of the proposed plan.

“[A]bove all, this area is not just a stretch of sand; it’s the history and identity of the people who already live there,” Salvemos las Dunas said.

Their concerns were supported by a three-day inspection led by the Federal Prosecutor’s Office for Environmental Protection (Profepa) in late July. That report detailed multiple violations of federal regulations, some of which could carry criminal charges.

“Omissions, non-compliance and subsequent damage to species of wild flora and fauna protected by Official Mexican Standards may transcend the administrative scope and constitute a crime against biodiversity,” Profepa wrote in a statement shared with Mexico News Daily.

Profepa and the government of Yucatán have since paused the project while they verify its compliance. During a press conference in early August, Gov. Joaquín Díaz Mena said that the “protection of Yucatán’s natural heritage will prevail over any particular project.”

Meanwhile, Salvemos las Dunas’ petition to protect the dunes has garnered more than 140,000 signatures. A protest was also held at the Monumento a La Patria in nearby Mérida in late July.

The public opposition to the project appears to be working.

“Given the concern of citizens, the State Government formally requested, since last July 25, Semarnat and the Federal Attorney General’s Office for Environmental Protection (Profepa) to verify the timely compliance with the project authorizations and delivered all the technical information it has,” Yucatán’s government wrote in a statement.

Designia Desarrollos, the development firm behind Las Dunas, declined to comment on the ongoing proceedings.

“This project is completely contrary to environmental protection laws, contravening the human rights that guarantee access to a healthy environment, especially for the residents of Chuburná Puerto,” Salvemos las Dunas said. “The lack of regulation and the ease with which permits are granted to real estate developers have hijacked the state.”

How important are the Chuburná Dunes?

The Chuburná Dunes are an integral part of the coastal ecosystem, recognized as one of the most well-preserved in Yucatán. Hosting various endangered wildlife species, including some that are endemic to Yucatán, as well as a nesting ground for a tortoise species on the brink of global extinction, the current ecosystem is both fragile and consequential.

Among the animals that call the dunes home are the Mexican sheartail hummingbird (doricha eliza) and the Yucateca wren (campylorhynchus yucatanicus), both of which have been granted a protective status, as well as the hawksbill sea turtle (eretmochelys imbricata) and the green sea turtle (chelonia mydas).

The dunes also serve as a natural protector against wind, tides, hurricanes, erosion and other storm systems that frequently batter the area, meaning any damage to them could prove irreversible.

“We believe that progress can be achieved consciously, hand in hand with environmental protection and citizen participation, but above all, by safeguarding the interests of the people, not just a few families in Mérida,” Salvemos las Dunas said.

A stalled Royal Caribbean project

The Las Dunas tourist complex is just the latest in a string of recent developments that didn’t sit well with local activists and conservationists.

Earlier this year, a Royal Caribbean megaproject in Quintana Roo came to a halt after citizens and activists expressed concerns.

The project, known as “Perfect Day,” is a proposed amusement park in the municipality of Othón P. Blanco, in the small fishing village of Mahahual. The famous cruise line had purchased the property, located close to the port of Costa Maya, which Royal Caribbean also owns, for $292 million.

An online petition against the development has garnered more than 5 million signatures to date.

Royal Caribbean officially withdrew its environmental assessment application in May, citing Semarnat’s intentions to deny the project. The company said it was “disappointed” in Semarnat’s decision and would “respect the role of Mexico’s environmental authorities,” but stopped short of saying “Perfect Day” would be scrapped entirely.

“We continue to believe in Mexico, and are optimistic in the potential to advance our investment responsibly,” the company wrote in a statement at the time. “Over the coming weeks, we will re-engage stakeholders to move forward in a way that delivers shared prosperity through the development of essential environmental infrastructure, the creation of thousands of local jobs, and community programs that support the people of Mexico.”

Tren Maya’s 900-mile development

The activism surrounding both Las Dunas and Perfect Day is set against the backdrop of the Tren Maya megaproject, which was completed in 2024 under then-President Andrés Manuel López Obrador.

So far, the 900-mile train route spread across five states in Mexico’s southeast has failed to realize its promised financial benefits for local communities, while also understating its overall environmental impact.

Tren Maya carried its first passengers in December 2023. Since then, 42 trains have been inaugurated, traveling more than 900 miles of track across Chiapas, Tabasco, Campeche, Yucatán and Quintana Roo.

According to an August 2023 report by CartoCrítica, Tren Maya’s construction spans more than 26,000 acres, requiring deforestation efforts in 61% of the surrounding jungle. The report alleges that 87% of the deforestation was done without the necessary permits.

This, despite López Obrador’s assertions in a 2018 interview that “Not a single tree” would be cut down. Semarnat similarly released a statement in January 2023, saying that “More than 64,000 plants have been rescued with 85% survival.”

However, Priscila Alaniz Uribe, the general director for the Sélvame nonprofit, has a different take.

“About 12 million trees have been cut down, and around 125 cenotes have been damaged,” Alaniz Uribe told Sierra Club in July. “There are 15,000 piles of concrete poisoning the water in underground rivers – water we humans, animals, and plants use to live here.”

Such concerns define the environmental activism that has taken place around the Yucatán Peninsula in recent years.

“This project is completely contrary to environmental protection laws, contravening the human rights that guarantee access to a healthy environment, especially for the residents of Chuburná Puerto,” Salvemos las Dunas said of the project they’re working to stop. “If this area is cleared, it will leave the residents who have cared for their city for years unprotected; not to mention that it is home to endemic species of the area that are in danger of extinction.”

Jesse Foley-Tapia is a writer and photographer living in the Yucatán Peninsula, where he has dedicated his time and energy to shedding light on issues affecting Indigenous communities. His biggest journalistic accomplishment is interviewing Kendrick Lamar in 2010. His work has appeared in The Sun Magazine and BreakThrough News.

Paraguay · CURRENCY

Key Facts — Exchange rate The guaraní closed near 5,990 per US dollar on 28 August 2026.

— Year to date The dollar has shed about 9% of its guaraní value since December 2025.

— Twelve months The guaraní has gained about 18.4% on the dollar since 28 August 2025.

— Policy rate Paraguay’s central bank held its rate at 5.50% on 25 August 2026.

— Reserves Net international reserves stood at US$11.45 billion on 21 August 2026.

Record soybean receipts have lifted the currency, and the chambers that earn in dollars are unhappy.

Paraguay’s appreciating guaraní closed near 5,990 to the US dollar on Friday 28 August 2026, its strongest level since late 2018. The move has turned a quiet currency into the loudest argument in the country’s business chambers.

Paraguayan guaraní notes. The dollar has fallen about ten percent against them this year.

Where the guaraní now stands

The Banco Central del Paraguay (BCP) publishes a daily reference rate drawn from interbank spot trades. Market pricing on Friday 28 August 2026 put the dollar at about 5,990 guaraníes.

The last quote of 2025 was 6,575.71, set on 30 December. The dollar has therefore shed about 9% of its guaraní value so far this year.

A year earlier, on 28 August 2025, the same rate stood at 7,340.01. Measured against the dollar, the guaraní has gained about 18.4% over twelve months.

The weakest point in the whole BCP series was 8,029.54, reached on 2 April 2025. Paraguay’s appreciating guaraní has since pushed the dollar about 25% below that mark.

The guaraní was last this strong in late 2018, when the reference rate briefly dipped toward 5,911 to the dollar.

What is pulling the dollar down

Export receipts did much of the work behind Paraguay’s appreciating guaraní. Total exports reached US$12.13 billion in the seven months to July 2026, up 25.2%.

Soybean shipments led at US$2.65 billion, a rise of 49.0% on the year. Volumes climbed 40.8% to 6.83 million tonnes after an unusually large harvest.

Soybean meal added US$1.42 billion and soybean oil US$390.7 million. Paraguay ran a trade surplus of US$679.1 million, against a deficit twelve months earlier.

Beef did not help. Shipments fell 7.4% to US$1.12 billion, with volume down 23.7% to 162,200 tonnes.

A softer dollar abroad compounded the move. The BCP noted in August that the dollar index had weakened since its previous meeting.

The carry trade argument

Manuel Ferreira, a former finance minister, points to interest rates. He told Última Hora that guaraní rates in the banking market run between 10% and 14%.

Dollar rates, he said, sit nearer 5% or 6%. That gap gives investors a reason to sell dollars and hold guaraníes instead.

The BCP policy rate is 5.50%, held unanimously at the meeting of 25 August 2026. Market rates in local currency are close to double that level.

If the currency then strengthens, the trade pays twice over. Ferreira’s worked example turns US$1 million into about US$1.14 million rather than US$1.05 million.

That mechanism is one economist’s reading rather than an official finding. The BCP has not confirmed it as a driver of Paraguay’s appreciating guaraní.

Why the central bank has stayed out

Through August 2026 the BCP had neither bought nor sold dollars directly to the financial sector. Its net operations with the public sector came to US$328.4 million.

Holding those dollars rather than reselling them slowed the move. It did not stop it.

Net international reserves stood at US$11.45 billion on 21 August 2026. They had been US$11.70 billion at the end of July.

Inflation gives the bank little reason to act. Consumer prices rose 1.6% in the year to July 2026, and fell 0.1% in the month.

Core inflation was 1.3%. Both readings sit well below the 3.5% target the BCP has set, inside a two-point band.

Neighbours use pre-announced rules instead. Chile buys up to US$25 million a day under a published programme, and Peru had bought US$3.93 billion by mid-July.

Investment grade and the hunt for dollars

Two agencies now rate Paraguay investment grade. Moody’s moved the sovereign to Baa3 with a stable outlook on 26 July 2024.

S&P Global Ratings followed with a BBB- rating and a stable outlook on 17 December 2025. The BCP cites both when it explains the country’s appeal to long-term capital.

Direct investment figures lag by about ten months, so 2024 is the latest full year. It brought net inflows of US$931 million, a rise of 15% on 2023.

The stock of direct investment ended 2024 at US$10.4 billion, up 3.8%. Investors came from 68 countries, led by Brazil, the United States and the Netherlands.

A BCP study with the Latin American Reserve Fund (FLAR) was presented on 6 August 2026. It put cumulative net inflows near US$10 billion since 2008, helped by the two investment-grade ratings.

Grain exporters and industry want an answer

Hugo Pastore runs the Cámara Paraguaya de Exportadores y Comercializadores de Cereales y Oleaginosas (Capeco). He told ABC Color on 27 August that his sector has no predictability left.

He described the currency as a bottomless barrel that never settles. Machinery and freight costs are climbing in dollar terms as the soy planting season approaches.

Luis Tavella, who heads the Federación Paraguaya de Mipymes (Fedemipymes), put exporter losses near 25% over the year. He said the conversion from dollars into guaraníes is where the money disappears.

The Cámara de Industrias Sustentables del Paraguay (Cispy) went further. It said Paraguay’s appreciating guaraní is destroying competitiveness, cutting margins and putting investment and jobs at risk.

Cispy asked the BCP for real, concrete and urgent action. Property developers complained the next day that no central bank official had explained the situation.

Cattle producers lose the gain in translation

The Asociación Paraguaya de Productores y Exportadores de Carne (Appec) put numbers on the squeeze. Cattle prices rose 22% in dollars between January and August 2026.

In guaraníes the same prices rose 6%. Paraguay’s appreciating guaraní absorbed the sixteen-point difference before it reached the ranch gate.

Appec said a slower move would have left producers more of the international gain. Costs, it noted, matter as much as the headline price.

The trade data points the same way. Beef receipts fell 7.4% in the seven months to July, even as world prices improved.

Property prices are the exception

Gonzalo Faccas of the Cámara Paraguaya de Desarrolladores Inmobiliarios (Capadei) called this a very serious predictability problem. He said the guaraní has risen more than 23% while regional currencies gained about 10%.

Faccas said square-metre prices have moved from roughly US$1,500 to about US$2,000. Developers earn in dollars but pay four fifths of their costs in guaraníes.

Raúl Constantino, who chairs Capadei, said members now recalculate costs constantly. He argued that exchange-rate stability is a basic condition for committing to a project.

Faccas also pointed to an asymmetry. The BCP acted when the dollar climbed towards 8,000 guaraníes, he said, but has not acted on the way down.

Consumer prices tell a calmer story. At 1.6% a year, Paraguay’s appreciating guaraní has produced no general price alarm, whatever the property market reports.

Frequently Asked Questions

How strong is the guaraní right now? The dollar traded at about 5,990 guaraníes on 28 August 2026. That is the strongest guaraní reading since late 2018. Why is the guaraní rising? Record soybean receipts, a large trade surplus and a softer dollar abroad. High local interest rates also draw money into guaraní deposits. Who is hurt by the stronger currency? Grain exporters, cattle producers, small manufacturers and property developers have all complained. Paraguay’s appreciating guaraní cuts their dollar earnings once converted into local currency.

World.title: Peru Flags 152 Glacial Lakes at High Risk of Bursting
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

Peru · CLIMATE

Key Facts — Lakes flagged Peru’s glacial lake risk review rates 58 lakes very high and 94 high.

— Regions Áncash, Cusco, Junín, Lima, Puno and Huánuco hold most of the flagged lakes.

— Glacier loss A new national inventory puts Peru’s glacier loss at 59% over six decades.

— El Niño The national disaster risk centre places over nine million people at very high risk.

— Palcacocha Ten siphons operate above Huaraz, with maintenance funding still unresolved.

A national glacial lake risk review puts 152 lakes in the top two bands above Andean towns and farmland.

Peru’s glacier institute has put a number on the glacial lake risk hanging over its Andean valleys. Of 528 lakes judged capable of bursting, 152 sit in the two highest bands.

Peru’s Cordillera Blanca. Most of the highest-risk lakes sit behind loose moraine dams.

What the national review found

The Instituto Nacional de Investigación en Glaciares y Ecosistemas de Montana (INAIGEM) is Peru’s state glacier research body. Its national evaluation of lakes at risk of bursting is now the reference document.

INAIGEM counts 528 glacial lakes carrying some level of overflow risk. That is roughly 6% of all glacial lakes in the country.

Of those, 58 are rated very high risk and 94 are rated high risk. The combined 152 lakes define the current glacial lake risk picture.

Paola Moschella Miloslavich, INAIGEM’s director of glacier research, set out the figures this week. Most of the flagged lakes sit in Áncash and Cusco.

Where the danger is concentrated

The heaviest concentration runs through the central Andes. It lies between the Cordillera Blanca and the Cordillera Central.

INAIGEM’s ranking puts Upiscocha, in the Cordillera Vilcanota, at the top with a risk ratio of 0.99. An estimated 111 dwellings sit below it.

Palcacocha, above Huaraz in the Cordillera Blanca, scores 0.78 with 3,980 dwellings exposed. Tullparaju, also in Áncash, scores 0.75 with 4,198 dwellings exposed.

Across the 20 most dangerous lakes, INAIGEM counts more than 15,000 families in Áncash alone. That exposure is the core of the glacial lake risk problem.

How the high risk label is decided

The rating is not a forecast that any particular lake will burst. It combines physical susceptibility with the people and buildings downstream.

Moschella said the team weighed slope angles around each lake, lake size and the material holding the water back. Many Andean lakes are dammed only by moraine, the loose debris left by retreating ice.

A rock or ice fall into a lake can raise a wave that overtops or breaches that dam. The result is an aluvión, the Spanish term for a glacial mudflow.

Specialists call the same event a GLOF, or glacial lake outburst flood. INAIGEM’s report ranks Peru third in the world for exposure to it.

The nine million figure, and what it measures

A separate number has circulated alongside the glacial lake risk figures this week. It comes from the Centro Nacional de Estimación, Prevención y Reducción del Riesgo de Desastres (CENEPRED).

CENEPRED’s scenarios place 7,951,322 people at very high risk from flooding across 22 departments. Another 1.38 million face very high risk from landslides and huaicos, the local debris flows.

Together that clears nine million people, and the driver is El Niño rather than melting ice dams. It is a risk classification, not an alert level, and the two hazards are counted separately.

Response falls to the Instituto Nacional de Defensa Civil (INDECI), Peru’s national civil defence institute. INDECI estimates 1,248,412 people could be affected between October and March 2027.

El Niño is confirmed, not La Niña

The Comisión Multisectorial Encargada del Estudio Nacional del Fenómeno El Niño (ENFEN) reports every fortnight. Its technical report dated 26 August keeps the country on Alerta de El Niño Costero.

That is the top state in ENFEN’s five-level warm-phase alert system. The commission is vice-chaired by the Autoridad Nacional del Agua (ANA), Peru’s national water authority.

The Servicio Nacional de Meteorología e Hidrología del Perú (SENAMHI), the national weather service, sits on the same commission. SENAMHI grades its own warnings yellow, orange and red, with red the most severe.

ENFEN expects coastal El Niño to persist into the 2027 summer at extraordinary magnitude. Weekly sea surface anomalies off northern Peru ran near four degrees Celsius in late August.

Why 1941 and 1970 still frame the debate

On 13 December 1941 a lake dam in the Cojup valley above Huaraz gave way. The flood covered about 60% of the built-up city and killed roughly 1,800 people.

Palcacocha sits in that same Cojup valley, which is why it dominates local argument. Its volume grew roughly 34 times between 1972 and 2016 as the glacier withdrew.

On 31 May 1970 an earthquake offshore of Chimbote shook loose part of Huascarán. The rock and ice avalanche erased Yungay and a string of nearby villages.

Published Peruvian accounts put close to 4,000 people missing across those settlements. INAIGEM has since modelled how a comparable detachment would behave today.

The defences that exist, and the money

Palcacocha’s main physical defence is a set of ten siphons that draw the water level down. The regional government says all ten were working in late August.

Rafael Macedo Menacho, who runs disaster risk management for the Áncash regional government, put the volume below 15 million cubic metres. An alert level begins near 17 million cubic metres.

The early warning system above Huaraz has been the weak link. In April the provincial council said maintenance needed about S/700,000 (US$209,000) that never arrived.

Áncash general manager Marco La Rosa has since costed a full maintenance file at S/1.4 million (US$418,000). Conversions use the Banco Central de Reserva del Perú rate of S/3.348 per dollar on 27 August 2026.

Budget law blocks the region from transferring maintenance money to the two municipalities involved. The region therefore plans to take the system back and service it directly.

From siphons to permanent works

At a multisector El Niño meeting on 26 August, INAIGEM pressed one specific point. It urged authorities to move from temporary siphoning to permanent engineering works.

No funded national programme for those works has been announced. Local engineers have floated two containment dams above the Cojup valley, so far unstudied.

INAIGEM’s monitoring centre in Huaraz opened in May 2026 and watches three lakes live. Palcacocha, Upiscocha and Gangrajanca carry sensors and streaming cameras.

The institute also hands municipalities evacuation maps and marked safe zones. Macashca, near Huaraz, received its maps in July, and signage is still pending.

A new national glacier inventory is due for formal presentation shortly. It records about 4,500 glaciers left and a 59% loss of glacier cover in six decades.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a GLOF? A GLOF is a glacial lake outburst flood. It happens when a lake’s natural dam fails and releases water suddenly. How many Peruvian lakes are rated dangerous? INAIGEM lists 528 lakes with some overflow risk. Of those, 152 carry high or very high glacial lake risk. Is the nine million figure about glacial lakes? No, it is CENEPRED’s count of people facing very high risk from El Niño rains. Glacial lake risk is assessed separately by INAIGEM.

World.title: US Expands Deportation Flights to Haiti Despite Do-Not-Travel Alert
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

Haiti · MIGRATION

Key Facts — Flights The second of the widened deportation flights to Haiti landed at Cap-Haïtien on 27 August.

— Status Haiti’s Temporary Protected Status ended on 27 July 2026 for about 334,900 people.

— Advisory The State Department still tells Americans not to travel to Haiti for any reason.

— Force The UN-backed Gang Suppression Force had 1,083 soldiers against 5,500 authorised in July.

— Displacement Some 1.47 million Haitians were internally displaced in May, roughly 12 percent of people.

Deportation flights to Haiti are widening against a Level 4 warning, a terminated protected status and a UN force at a fifth strength.

The United States flew a second planeload of deportees into Haiti on 27 August, one week after the first. Washington is scaling up deportation flights to Haiti even as its own advisory tells Americans to stay away.

A market hall in Port-au-Prince. The capital now holds more than 300,000 displaced people.

A second removal flight in one week

The United States sent a second charter flight of deportees to Haiti on 27 August 2026. The Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) plane left Opa-locka in Florida and landed at Cap-Haïtien.

HaitiLibre reported that the charter carried 57 Haitians, among them several children born in the United States. The youngest passenger was a one-year-old US-born child, according to information given to Haitian authorities.

That flight followed a 20 August removal that brought more than 160 people to the same airport. Deportation flights to Haiti had until then run at roughly one a month.

The Haitian Times reported that the administration is moving those flights toward about one a week. Officials in Port-au-Prince say they have received no formal notice of the new schedule.

Washington’s own advice is to stay away

The State Department keeps Haiti at Level 4, the highest rung on its four-step scale. The advisory was last updated on 10 July 2026 and opens with a blunt instruction.

It tells Americans: “Do not travel to Haiti for any reason”. The same page cites crime, terrorism, kidnapping, unrest and limited health care.

US commercial flights to Port-au-Prince remain barred into early September because of gang violence. That is why deportation flights to Haiti now land at Cap-Haïtien in the north.

The gap between that warning and the removals is the heart of the dispute. Homeland Security argues that conditions have improved enough for Haitians to go home.

How Haitians lost their protected status

Temporary Protected Status, or TPS, lets nationals of unsafe countries live and work legally in the United States. Haiti was first designated after the 2010 earthquake and held the status for most of the years since.

The Department of Homeland Security published a termination notice in the Federal Register on 28 November 2025. It set the end of Haiti’s designation for 3 February 2026.

A federal judge in Brooklyn had already pushed back an earlier termination date in July 2025. That case, Haitian Evangelical Clergy Association v Trump, delayed the removals for months.

The Supreme Court cleared the way in June 2026, and the termination took effect on 27 July. Pew Research Center counts 334,900 Haitian recipients, about a third of everyone stripped of TPS in this term.

Who is on the planes

Haiti’s National Office of Migration said the 20 August flight carried people facing removal orders and former prisoners. It said none of those passengers had held TPS.

Wire reports from the same airport said the group did include TPS holders. That contradiction remains unconfirmed, and the two accounts have not been reconciled publicly.

On 27 August a Bahamasair flight returned 104 more Haitians to the same terminal within hours. Haitian officials and the International Organization for Migration struggled to process both arrivals.

That organisation, known as IOM, is the United Nations migration agency and meets returnees at the airport. Of 42,778 Haitians forcibly returned in April and May, 99 percent came from the Dominican Republic.

The force that was meant to secure Haiti

The Multinational Security Support mission, a police deployment authorised by the Security Council in 2023, never grew as promised. On 30 September 2025 the Council folded it into a new body.

Resolution 2793 created the Gang Suppression Force for an initial period of twelve months. Twelve members voted in favour, while China, Pakistan and Russia abstained.

The text set a ceiling of 5,550 people, of whom 5,500 are soldiers and police officers. As of 8 July 2026 the force fielded 1,083 military personnel and 16 civilians.

The Council also created the United Nations Support Office in Haiti to supply logistics and camps. Personnel costs come from voluntary donations rather than from assessed United Nations dues.

By 8 July, 15 member states had pledged US$223.5 million, of which US$184.2 million had arrived. Only US$67.5 million of that money had actually been disbursed.

What the humanitarian numbers show

IOM counted 1.47 million internally displaced people on 13 May 2026, about 12 percent of the population. Women and girls made up 54 percent of that total.

The Port-au-Prince area passed 300,000 displaced residents for the first time, driven by fighting in Cité Soleil. Most displaced people in the capital now live in improvised sites.

The Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, the UN aid coordination body, says 6.4 million Haitians need assistance. Its 2026 response plan sought US$880.3 million and was 25 percent funded by mid-June.

The Integrated Food Security Phase Classification is the standard international scale for measuring hunger. Its April analysis placed 5.8 million Haitians, or 52 percent, in crisis-level food insecurity.

More than 1.8 million of those people were living in emergency conditions. Aid agencies warn that fuel and food price rises could reverse fragile gains.

Gangs, ground truth and the return risk

Gangs control an estimated 70 percent of Port-au-Prince, according to reporting from the capital. The Secretary-General’s July report describes gang influence across Carrefour, Cité Soleil, Gressier and Croix-des-Bouquets.

Clashes in the Cul-de-Sac plain killed at least 542 people and injured 355 others. At least 176 women and girls were raped during that fighting.

A massacre in Kenscoff between 23 and 25 August displaced 2,647 people, IOM reported. Local outlets put the death toll above 60.

Deportation flights to Haiti therefore arrive in a country that aid agencies still describe as an emergency. Cap-Haïtien absorbs the arrivals because the road south is frequently cut by armed groups.

What it means for the wider region

For employers in Florida and Ohio, the end of TPS strips work authorisation from thousands of staff. ICE arrested 49,571 people nationwide in July, its highest monthly total of this term.

The Dominican Republic remains by far the largest single source of forced returns to Haiti. Its expulsions dwarf the American charters in raw numbers, though not in political weight.

The Gang Suppression Force mandate runs out at the end of September 2026 unless the Council renews it. That vote will land while deportation flights to Haiti are still increasing.

Travellers and investors should note that the advisory has not moved at all. Level 4 remains in force, and commercial flights to the capital are still barred.

Frequently Asked Questions

Has Haiti’s Temporary Protected Status been terminated? Yes. Homeland Security terminated the designation, and it took effect on 27 July 2026 after the Supreme Court cleared the way. Where do deportation flights to Haiti land? They land at Cap-Haïtien in the north. The main airport in Port-au-Prince is closed to US commercial traffic because of gang violence. How large is the UN-backed force in Haiti? The Gang Suppression Force had 1,083 military personnel and 16 civilians on 8 July 2026. Its authorised ceiling is 5,550.

World.title: The Week Ahead for Latin American Markets: US Jobs, Brazil GDP
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Rio Times Markets · The Week Ahead

Key Facts —US Payrolls Friday’s August jobs report follows a July in which American employment fell by 23,000. Consensus looks for a return to growth at 58,000. —Euro Area CPI Tuesday’s flash estimate is seen jumping to 3.3 percent from 2.9, while core holds at 2.5 percent. The gap is energy. —Brazil GDP Tuesday brings second-quarter output, with the economy having grown 1.1 percent in the first quarter and 1.8 percent over the year. —RBNZ New Zealand’s central bank is expected to raise its rate to 2.75 percent from 2.50, one of the few tightening moves left in the developed world. —Bank of Canada Wednesday’s decision is seen holding at 2.25 percent, with the Beige Book from the Federal Reserve arriving four hours later. —Benchmark Revision The BLS marked payrolls down by 79,000 for the year through March, and private employment by 178,000, on 28 August. —ISM Surveys Manufacturing on Tuesday and services on Thursday frame the American economy either side of the payrolls report.

The Latin American markets week ahead is built around Friday’s American jobs report, with a euro-area inflation jump on Tuesday and Brazil’s second-quarter growth figure giving regional desks their own reasons to watch the calendar.

A week of global data and central-bank decisions for investors in Latin America. (Photo internet reproduction)

American employment contracted in July, and the composition explains why the headline was worse than the underlying picture. Private employers added 30,000 jobs while government payrolls fell by 53,000. The two combine to the reported loss of 23,000. Friday’s August report carries a consensus of 58,000 in a Reuters poll of economists, with published forecasts running from roughly 45,000 to 62,500. No comparable consensus for the private component is widely published, which leaves the split between private hiring and any further government drag as the report’s genuine unknown.

That distinction matters for Latin America because the two readings point to different Federal Reserve paths. A private-sector slowdown argues for easier policy and a softer dollar. A public-sector payroll adjustment does not. The unemployment rate is forecast to hold at 4.1 percent, but participation entering the week at 61.4 percent means a stable jobless rate is not on its own evidence of a stable labour market.

Those figures now carry an asterisk. The Bureau of Labor Statistics published its preliminary benchmark revision on 28 August, marking down payroll employment for the twelve months through March 2026 by 79,000 and private employment by 178,000. The revision does not alter July’s reported decline, but it lowers the level from which August is measured and is the main reason Friday’s print will be read as a check on a weaker trend rather than as a single month.

Three Themes for the Week

The American labour market is the week’s organising question, and the answer arrives in three instalments. Job openings on Tuesday are forecast at 7.39 million against 7.359 million, a marginal increase. Private hiring on Wednesday is seen at 45,000 against 44,000. The payrolls report follows on Friday. Each is a partial view of the same problem.

Euro-area inflation is accelerating, and the open question is whether core follows. Headline is forecast at 3.3 percent for August against 2.9 in July, the upper end of a provider range that starts nearer 3.0. Forecasters divide on core: some see it steady at 2.5 percent, others at 2.6. The steady case leaves a gap of 0.8 percentage points that energy has to explain. Producer prices on Thursday are seen rising 1.3 percent in a single month after a 0.3 percent decline, which is the same story one stage earlier in the chain.

Latin American activity data lands without a single rate decision to anchor it. Brazil publishes second-quarter growth on Tuesday and July industrial output on Wednesday, having fallen 1.8 percent on the month in June. Chile reports July copper production, manufacturing, and retail sales on Monday, and Colombia’s unemployment rate follows the same afternoon, having last printed at 8.0 percent.

The Week, Day by Day

Monday, August 31, 2026

Britain is closed for the summer bank holiday, thinning European trading. German inflation at noon is the session’s most consequential release ahead of the euro-area figure on Tuesday, with the harmonised measure forecast at 3.0 percent. Chile publishes three July indicators at 1.00 pm, and Colombia’s unemployment rate follows two hours later.

The Week in Context

Latin American assets remain sensitive to the dollar and to American real yields, which makes the payrolls report the week’s transmission channel into the region regardless of what the local calendar contains. A firm dollar tightens conditions and can override decent domestic fundamentals; a softer one gives the Brazilian real, Mexican peso, and Andean currencies room to appreciate.

The euro area presents the sharper contradiction. Headline inflation is forecast at 3.3 percent while core sits at 2.5 percent and unemployment holds at 6.3 percent. Producer prices are seen rising 1.3 percent in July alone. That combination, a stable core with an accelerating headline and a rising cost pipeline, is the same configuration that preceded the European Central Bank’s June rate increase, and it will shape expectations for the rest of the year.

Regional activity is uneven. Brazilian manufacturing entered the week at 47.5 and services at 49.7, both in contraction, while the composite reading of 48.8 suggests the second-quarter growth figure on Tuesday may prove to be the high-water mark. Chile reported annual economic activity of 2.4 percent and manufacturing output down 3.2 percent, a split between mining strength and industrial weakness. Colombia’s unemployment rate of 8.0 percent is reported as the lowest for a June since 2001, though above the series low near 7 percent recorded in November 2025, which complicates the case for faster easing there.

The Bottom Line

Friday’s payrolls report is the week’s decisive release for Latin American portfolios, and the private component deserves more attention than the headline. July’s decline of 23,000 was the arithmetic result of 30,000 private jobs added and 53,000 government jobs lost. The August consensus of 58,000 in a Reuters poll says nothing about that split, and with the preliminary benchmark revision having marked private employment down by 178,000 in the year to March, the private component is where the information sits. Brazil’s second-quarter growth on Tuesday and euro-area inflation the same morning give the week two further pivot points, and the Bank of Canada and the Beige Book fill Wednesday. No Latin American central bank sets rates, though Colombia’s board holds a scheduled non-rate session on Monday. For desks planning the Latin American markets week ahead, Friday at 12.30 pm UTC is the fixed point.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the most important event in the Latin American markets week ahead?

The American jobs report on Friday at 12.30 pm UTC. Payrolls are forecast at 58,000 in a Reuters poll after a decline of 23,000 in July, with unemployment holding at 4.1 percent. The result drives the dollar and American real yields, which in turn set financial conditions across the region.

Why did American employment fall in July?

The decline was concentrated in the public sector. Private employers added 30,000 jobs while government payrolls fell by 53,000, and the two combine to the reported loss of 23,000. Private hiring continued, but at a pace too slow to offset the public-sector reduction.

What should I watch in Brazil this week?

Second-quarter growth on Tuesday at noon and July industrial production on Wednesday. The economy grew 1.1 percent in the first quarter and 1.8 percent over the year, but manufacturing entered the week at 47.5 and industrial output fell 1.8 percent in June, so the forward-looking indicators are weaker than the growth figure.

World.title: What’s On in Latin America: the week of August 31 – September 4
World.content:
Latin America · What’s On

Key Facts — What happened Argentina’s lower house approved the central bank charter reform 144–102 on 26 August; the bill now moves to the Senate, where Milei’s bloc does not hold a majority (US$0, but your peso purchasing power is watching).

— How big a jump Rock in Rio 2026 opens on Friday 4 September at Cidade do Rock with Foo Fighters, Rise Against, The Hives and Nova Twins — the first of seven nights that will draw more than half a million people to Barra da Tijuca.

— What it signals Colombia and Israel restore reciprocal visa-free travel from 1 September, fourteen months after it was suspended, following a diplomatic thaw signalled in June.

— The catch Registration for Belo Horizonte’s first Instituto Capim Santo free cooking course closes at midnight on 31 August for classes that start 3 September — only twenty places, and the form is in Portuguese.

— Who it touches Brazil’s Q2 GDP print lands Tuesday 1 September; a strong number supports the real, which in turn makes your reais go further if you are paid in dollars.

— What comes next Bogotá’s Gastrofest runs eighteen days from 3 September to 20 September at Feria del Hogar with twelve curated establishments, while the Territorios routes spread up to sixty venues across the city all month. Dishes are typically in the COP 12,000 to 15,000 range, about US$3.85 to US$4.80.

Your Latin America week ahead for 31 August to 4 September is bookended by two of the biggest events of the year: a reopened visa corridor between Colombia and Israel, and the opening weekend of Rock in Rio. In between, a free professional cooking course launches in Belo Horizonte, a food festival takes over Bogotá, and Argentina’s Senate decides whether to reshape the institution that prints its currency.

Here is what is on, drawn from our coverage across the region, with every date checked against the source reporting and local-currency prices carried at the conversions each report published.

Cerro de la Silla, Nuevo León. (Photo: The Rio Times.)

Culture and events this week

The week belongs to Rio de Janeiro. Rock in Rio 2026 opens its first weekend on Friday 4 September at Cidade do Rock in Barra da Tijuca, and the opening night is the hardest-rocking of the seven. Foo Fighters headline the Palco Mundo, with Rise Against, The Hives and Nova Twins on the same bill. Gates open in the early afternoon; the headline act takes the stage after dark.

The full festival runs 4, 5, 6 and 7 September, then 11, 12 and 13 September. Saturday 5 September brings Avenged Sevenfold and Bring Me the Horizon; Sunday 6 September is Calvin Harris and Black Eyed Peas; and Monday 7 September — Brazil’s Independence Day holiday — pairs Elton John with Gilberto Gil, a one-off bill that will not be repeated. Weekend two adds Stray Kids, Maroon 5, Demi Lovato, Twenty One Pilots and Halsey.

Day tickets are sold through the Rock in Rio Card, a limited-edition product priced at R$795 full and R$397.50 half-price, about US$154 and US$77. Standard daily gramado (lawn) tickets cost R$870 full and R$435 half-price, about US$169 and US$84, with Itaú cardholders eligible for a discount to R$739.50. As of late August, the Saturday 6 September and Saturday 12 September dates are sold out; tickets for the opening weekend and the second Sunday remain available through Ticketmaster Brasil. If you are travelling for it, Barra da Tijuca is closest to the venue, though many visitors prefer Ipanema or Copacabana and budget extra time for the drive.

In Bogotá, Gastrofest 2026 opens on Thursday 3 September and runs eighteen days to Sunday 20 September. The flagship event is the Feria del Hogar edition, with twelve curated establishments at the fairgrounds. Alongside it, the Territorios Gastrofest routes spread across the city throughout September with up to sixty restaurants, cafés, bakeries and breweries in the Centro Histórico, Chapinero and satellite corridors. Dish prices at the festival venues are typically in the COP 12,000 to 15,000 range, about US$3.85 to US$4.80, though individual restaurants set their own prices. The Cámara de Comercio de Bogotá publishes the full venue list at gastrofest.com.co. No reservation is required for the public routes; you buy a dish at each stop and move on.

Belo Horizonte gets its first Instituto Capim Santo “Cozinha do Amanhã” cooking course, with classes starting Wednesday 3 September. The programme is free, runs one hundred hours over roughly two months, and meets Tuesdays, Thursdays and Fridays at the UniBH kitchens on Avenida Mário Werneck, 1685, in the Estoril neighbourhood. There are twenty places in the first class, open to residents of Belo Horizonte aged eighteen and over with a family income of up to two minimum salaries. The curriculum covers kitchen technique, food safety, waste reduction, and workplace readiness. In 2025, participants reported an average income increase of 88 per cent after completing the course. Registration closes at midnight on Sunday 31 August through institutocapimsanto.org.br/cozinha-do-amanha; the form is in Portuguese only.

In Santiago, the Puerto Rican reggaeton artist Arcángel plays three consecutive nights at Movistar Arena — Monday 31 August, Tuesday 1 September and Wednesday 2 September. Also on Tuesday 1 September, the K-pop group Ikon performs at Teatro Coliseo. Both venues are in the downtown–Providencia corridor, served by the Santiago metro. Tickets are available through Punto Ticket.

Buenos Aires closes its Tango World Championship on Wednesday 2 September, the final day of a festival that has turned the city into the global capital of the dance since 19 August. Competitions in Tango de Pista and Tango Escenario run at venues across the city, free to watch, alongside milongas and classes. The closing gala is typically the hardest ticket of the fortnight; if you want to catch the end of it, check tangoba.org for the final schedule. On the music front, the ArChiDrama Invita festival at the Chilean Embassy’s Centro Cultural MATTA in Palermo wraps its three-day run of Argentine, Chilean and Brazilian theatre on Tuesday 1 September; admission is free on a first-come, first-served basis.

In São Paulo, the Associação Brasileira dos Captadores de Recursos holds its Festival ABCR 2026 on Thursday 3 and Friday 4 September at the Centro de Convenções Frei Caneca, with more than seventy talks across nine simultaneous stages. It is aimed at the nonprofit and social-impact sector, and tickets are available through the ABCR site. For music, the 37th Curta Kinoforum short-film festival continues to 30 August — so its final sessions fall on the Saturday and Sunday before this week begins, but if you are in the city over the weekend, the last screenings at MIS on Avenida Europa are free and handed out at the box office one hour before each session.

Further south, the Curitiba Biennial runs until 15 November with more than three hundred artists from thirty-eight countries at the Museu Oscar Niemeyer and satellite venues. Entry is free every Wednesday, which falls on 2 September this week. In Montevideo, the city’s spring cultural season begins to warm up in early September with open-air concerts in the Ciudad Vieja on Thursday and Friday evenings, though the full programme is typically published only a few days ahead; check the Intendencia de Montevideo site if you are passing through.

Politics you will feel on the street

Argentina is the one to watch. On Wednesday 26 August, the Chamber of Deputies approved President Milei’s proposal to reform the Central Bank’s charter by 144 votes to 102, with nine abstentions. The bill strips the BCRA of its current mandates regarding economic and social equity, leaving its sole responsibility as preserving the value of the currency, and bans the central bank from financing government spending.

The Senate is the harder chamber. Milei’s La Libertad Avanza bloc does not hold a majority there, and the opposition has signalled it will fight the bill. If it passes, the reform would be the most significant institutional change to Argentine monetary policy in two decades. If it fails, the government will likely look for executive workarounds. For foreign residents paid in dollars and spending in pesos, the question is whether the reform stabilises the exchange rate or triggers another cycle of pressure. The Senate session has not been formally scheduled as of 30 August, but the governing bloc is pushing for a vote this week.

In Colombia, the diplomatic thaw with Israel becomes practical on Tuesday 1 September, when the reciprocal visa waiver takes effect. Colombian passport holders can enter Israel without a visa for up to ninety days, and Israelis can do the same in Colombia. The arrangement was announced by both foreign ministries in mid-August and follows fourteen months of suspended visa-free access after the Petro government broke diplomatic relations with Israel in May 2024. President de la Espriella’s administration restored ties in June 2026. For Colombian expats with Israeli connections, and for Israeli travellers and digital nomads considering Medellín or Bogotá, the change removes a bureaucratic barrier that had become a genuine obstacle.

The backdrop remains the earthquake recovery in Chocó. The death toll stands at 329, with 247 still missing, and reconstruction is being costed at up to US$12.9 billion over as much as six years. The government has declared an economic emergency and says it will follow the 1999 Armenia model. For foreign residents in the major cities, this changes little day to day, but it is the fiscal backdrop to every tax promise and infrastructure decision below.

Two further Colombian changes are worth noting for anyone employing locally. The military high command was replaced in full following the earthquake, and a set of Petro-era labour rules was scrapped by decree, which matters if you run a business or employ staff in Colombia.

In Brazil, the Q2 GDP print lands on Tuesday 1 September. The figure matters for the real, which has been one of the better-performing emerging-market currencies this year. A strong number supports the currency; a miss weakens it. For foreign residents paid in dollars, that translates directly into purchasing power. The print follows the Q1 surprise and will be watched closely by the Central Bank ahead of its next rate decision.

Deadlines and money

The one hard deadline inside the window is the Capim Santo registration in Belo Horizonte, which closes at midnight on Sunday 31 August for classes that begin Thursday 3 September. The form is at institutocapimsanto.org.br/cozinha-do-amanha and requires proof of residence in Belo Horizonte and a declaration of family income.

For Rock in Rio, day tickets for the opening weekend were still available as of late August, but the Saturday 6 September and Saturday 12 September dates are sold out. If you are planning to attend the second weekend, the Friday 11 September and Sunday 13 September dates still have tickets at the time of writing. The Rock in Rio Card is the only entry format; single-day tickets at the gate are not sold.

In Chile, the IPSA index rebalances on Tuesday 1 September, gaining a member and changing hands. The details are published by the Bolsa de Comercio de Santiago. If you hold a Chilean index fund or ETF, your portfolio shifts on that date.

On the tax front in Colombia, President de la Espriella announced the intention to abolish the wealth tax on 7 August, but no bill has been filed and the 183-day tax-residency test remains unchanged. Plan on the current rules until legislation exists. The finance ministry has also said it will not fund earthquake recovery with new taxes, which limits the immediate revenue pressure but does not eliminate it.

Heads-ups for travellers and new arrivals

Aeroparque is open again. Buenos Aires’ downtown airport reopened on Thursday 27 August after a fifty-five-hour runway maintenance closure that moved about nine hundred flights to Ezeiza and cancelled the rest. If you were caught in the disruption, normal service has resumed, though it is worth confirming any bookings made during the closure window in case of residual schedule changes.

Colombia-Israel visa waiver takes effect on 1 September. If you are an Israeli citizen planning to enter Colombia, or a Colombian citizen planning to enter Israel, you no longer need a visa for stays of up to ninety days. The change is automatic at the border; no pre-registration is required. If you already hold a valid visa, it remains valid but is no longer necessary for tourist entry.

For Brazil, Rock in Rio is not the only reason to check your travel plans. The festival coincides with the run-up to Independence Day on 7 September, which means public offices close and many Brazilians take the Monday off, extending the weekend. Hotels in Rio spike in price for the festival period, and transport in Barra da Tijuca is heavily congestued from Thursday 3 September through the weekend. If you are not attending the festival, consider arriving in Rio before Thursday or after Monday to avoid the crush.

Anyone who has flown LATAM should continue to check their statements. The data breach disclosed on 19 August exposed names, addresses, birth dates, emails, phone numbers, LATAM Pass details, and partial card data. Full card numbers and CVVs were not exposed, but the combination of partial card data and itinerary information is enough to fuel convincing scams. Treat any unexpected call about a LATAM booking as hostile.

For Mexico, our guide to reading a travel advisory without cancelling your trip remains the best antidote to the headlines: the country sits at Level 2 overall on the US State Department scale, but every state carries its own rating from Level 1 to Level 4, and the difference between Yucatán and Michoacán is the difference between a normal trip and a reconsideration.

Three service pieces are worth an evening if you are still choosing a country. Retiring abroad on a fixed income sets the average US retired-worker benefit at US$2,084.40 a month as of June 2026 and notes that most Latin American retirement visas ask for well under half of it. Alongside it, why spending US dollars in Costa Rica is harder than it looks and how not to get scammed buying property in Mexico as a US retiree cover the two mistakes newcomers make most often. And for the remote-work crowd, São Paulo has just placed eighth in a new digital nomad city index.

Looking ahead

Beyond this week, Creamfields Argentina lands on Saturday 14 November at Parque de la Ciudad in Buenos Aires, with tickets from 180,000 pesos including fees, about US$122 at the rate the announcement used. The Curitiba Biennial runs until 15 November, with free entry every Wednesday. And in Medellín, the Feria de las Flores is already on the horizon for mid-August 2027 — if you are planning a year ahead, it is the week that books out first.

Rock in Rio is one of the world’s largest music festivals, with a permanent venue at Cidade do Rock that functions as a temporary city. Yes, but it ends on Wednesday 2 September. The championship began on 19 August and runs competitions in Tango de Pista and Tango Escenario across venues in Buenos Aires, free to watch. The closing events on 1 and 2 September are the highlights. Check tangoba.org for the final schedule and any last-minute venue changes. Has Argentina reformed its central bank? Partially. The reform would strip the central bank of its social-equity mandate and ban it from financing government spending. It has not yet become law. Is Gastrofest in Bogotá free? Entry to the public Territorios routes is free, but the food is not. You pay per dish at each participating restaurant, with prices typically in the COP 12,000 to 15,000 range, about US$3.85 to US$4.80, though individual establishments set their own rates. The Feria del Hogar flagship event runs 3–20 September with twelve curated venues; the wider Territorios routes run throughout September with up to sixty establishments across the city. No reservation is required for the routes. The full list of venues is at gastrofest.com.co.
