World.content:
Families scour Pokhara morgue for loved ones swept away by flood

More than 1,000 relatives of missing people arrived on Saturday as authorities display photographs of 102 bodies recovered far downstream, with some identified by school ties, tattoos and jewellery.

Over 1,000 relatives arrived in Pokhara on Saturday to scour a display of photographs of 102 bodies recovered downstream from the recent floods. Post Photo

World.title: Before flood catastrophe, Nepal asked China for early warnings as risks mounted
World.content:
Three months before a wall of water, mud and rock killed hundreds when it hurtled down a Himalayan valley bordering Nepal and China, experts and officials from both countries met in Kathmandu to discuss the risk of such disasters.

At the May 27 meeting in Nepal’s capital, 10 officials from Nepal and about a dozen from China, including the Tibet region where the disaster struck, discussed strengthening cooperation to monitor and respond to floods, weather and glacier-related hazards, according to an agenda prepared by the Nepali side.

The participants called for joint risk-reduction measures, including inventories of glacial lakes and hazard mapping.

World.title: Star defensive tackle Aaron Donald ends retirement to rejoin Rams
World.content:
The Los Angeles Rams defense will now feature two players who have combined to win five NFL Defensive Player of the Year awards.

The Rams announced on Sunday that defensive tackle Aaron Donald has ended his retirement and will return to the only team he played for over 10 spectacular seasons. The contract terms were not disclosed, though multiple reports say it’s a one-year, $20 million deal with playoff incentives.

Donald, 35, will join two-time Defensive Player of the Year and newly acquired Myles Garrett to form an intimidating defensive line.

Donald retired in March 2024 after spending all 10 of his NFL seasons with the Rams. He recorded 111 sacks, earned eight first-team All-Pro selections and was named to the Pro Bowl in every season of his career.

The possibility of a comeback emerged after Los Angeles began considering a trade for star pass rusher Myles Garrett. Head coach Sean McVay contacted Donald to get his opinion of Garrett, and the conversation eventually shifted to whether Donald might be interested in playing alongside him.

The Rams acquired Garrett in June, adding the reigning Defensive Player of the Year to a team that reached the NFC Championship Game in 2025.

“He’s put himself in a position to be able to say yes or no,” McVay said about Donald’s potential return after the Rams’ 20-12 preseason victory over the Kansas City Chiefs on Aug. 15.

Prior to his retirement, Donald recorded 543 tackles, 24 forced fumbles and seven fumble recoveries in 154 career games (150 starts) with the Rams.

World.title: Scottie Scheffler rallies to win second FedEx Cup title to join elite company
World.content:
Scottie Scheffler has joined elite company.

Tiger Woods. Rory McIlroy. Scheffler. That’s it. That’s the list.

Scheffler joined golf royalty as the only players to win multiple FedEx Cup championships when he came from behind to capture the Tour Championship in the finale of the FedEx Cup playoffs Sunday at East Lake Golf Club.

World.title: Trump’s Iran war sets test for Xi and Putin’s security club
World.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump’s intensifying economic campaign against Iran is testing the limits of the security grouping Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin have spent years expanding as a counterweight to U.S. power.

The Chinese and Russian presidents will gather with their Iranian counterpart, Masoud Pezeshkian, for the first time since the start of the U.S. and Israeli war against the Islamic Republic at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit that starts Monday in Kyrgyzstan. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi will also attend along with leaders from Central Asian states, Pakistan and Belarus.

“The message is getting clearer and louder each year that there’s emerging a new security bloc,” said Henry Wang Huiyao, founder of the Center for China and Globalization research group in Beijing. The unipolar world dominated by the U.S. “is gone,” he said.

World.title: Iceland votes to reject the EU as fisheries worry prevails
World.content:
Icelanders narrowly turned down reopening membership talks with the European Union in a divisive referendum, as concerns over retaining control of the island nation’s natural resources eclipsed the case for closer alignment with Europe.

After a night of see-saw tally, the “no” camp scored 52.8% support against 47.2% for the “yes” side when all ballots were counted, a somewhat larger victory than projected by polls in the run-up to the vote, according to the final results presented by the electoral commission on Sunday.

For the EU, the result dealt a symbolic setback to efforts to revive interest in enlargement just as it’s seeking to kick the process out of a 13-year hiatus.

World.title: U.S. forces strike two Iranian launchers on Iran’s Larak island, U.S. official says
World.content:
U.S. forces struck two Iranian launchers on Iran’s Larak island on Sunday, a U.S. official said, marking the first known American strikes on Iran since late July.

“I can confirm that earlier today U.S. forces struck two Iranian launchers on Larak Island. Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps forces were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into Strait of Hormuz,” the U.S. official said.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said the attack killed and wounded several soldiers and citizens and would be met with a “response and punishment” from Tehran, Iranian state media reported.

Iran’s semi-official Tasnim news agency reported the U.S. carried out a drone strike on the island.

U.S. President Donald Trump said last week that all mines had been detonated or removed from the international waters of the Strait of Hormuz and Iran has been told that any ship or boat placing new mines will be destroyed.

The last known U.S. strikes on Iran were in late July as the war has reached a stalemate in recent weeks with Washington threatening to impose costly sanctions on countries that support Iran.

The U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on February 28 and Iran responded with its own strikes on Israel and Gulf states that host U.S. bases. The Iran war has now crossed its six-month mark.

U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran and Israeli attacks on Lebanon have killed thousands and displaced millions. Eighteen U.S. service members have been killed in the conflict.

The war has led to the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, which before the conflict used to see a transit of about a fifth of the world’s oil barrels consumed.

World.title: Nepal races to find missing amid threats of further flooding
World.content:
Nepal raced to find thousands still missing as rising water levels and worsening weather threaten to hamper rescue efforts, five days after a glacial collapse unleashed catastrophic flooding along the border with China.

More than 8,700 people have been rescued with almost 20,000 security personnel mobilized, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said on X. Six surgical teams are operating in affected areas, it said.

Rescue personnel and those providing relief services in regions surrounding the Bhote Koshi river’s path were told to exercise “utmost caution,” the agency said early Sunday.

World.title: Realism and research underpin film with autistic protagonist
World.content:
Medical melodramas are a staple film genre in Japan. As a producer once told me, these narratives are a good box office bet because Japanese audiences love to cry.

But domestic films that address illness or disability can also be unblinkingly realistic and populated by characters who are flawed humans, rather than stainless victims or selfless saints. And if tears come, they are earned, not extracted.

The latest in this line is “Lives at Right Angles” by Syoutarou Kobayasi (as he prefers to romanize his name). The director sat down with The Japan Times for a wide-ranging interview about the development of the film and the experiences and ideas that guided his approach to its subject matter.

World.title: Don’t leave Hong Kong parents to their own devices on child social media use
World.content:
Hong Kong, a city of overachievers, especially when it comes to the young, is also filled with children who take to social media early . Almost 35 per cent of kindergarten pupils log at least one hour of recreational screen time daily. By the junior forms, 60 per cent exceed the international two-hour daily limit.

The time children spend on screens creates friction at home, accounting for 85.5 per cent of family disputes. Governments must look into whether they are adequately protecting children from screen time addiction – the bread and butter of social media platforms – or if parents are being left to their own devices.

A little over a week after the Hong Kong Institute of Family Education released findings that reaffirmed what most of us already know, Meta announced that it has started sending alerts to parents if it is found that their children have been repeatedly searching for content about suicide and self-harm on Instagram.

I have my doubts that this is because Meta cares about our children.

Last December, Australia became the first country to ban social media for children under 16. Youth are more susceptible to the systemic features that make social media harmful, such as algorithms designed to feed viewers content likely to hook them and the lack of safeguards against inappropriate content.

While a ban by one country will hardly rein in social media’s damaging effect on young people, it is a way to hold social media platforms accountable for their reckless pursuit of profit at the expense of our children’s mental health.

World.title: At your service: Hong Kong welcomes first humanoid robot-run convenience stores
World.content:
Hong Kong’s first convenience stores operated by humanoid robots will open on Tuesday, with the Beijing-based company behind it planning to establish about 10 more outlets locally as it makes the city its first stop in “going overseas”.

Following an opening ceremony on Monday, the first “Galbot stores” will open in Hung Hom, Kai Tak and Wan Chai the next day, marking the company’s first outlets outside mainland China.

The embodied-intelligence robotics company launched its first store on the mainland last August and has since expanded to about 200 outlets across 50 cities nationwide.

“This is a genuinely important step for us in going overseas as Hong Kong is an important window and platform for [mainland] China facing the international market,” said Zhao Yuli, chief strategy officer of Galbot, noting that the business had operated a Hong Kong office since 2024.

She said the company planned to open about 10 more Galbot stores in the city over the coming years, in high-footfall districts.

According to Zhao, each Galbot store is run by wheeled humanoid robots powered by the company’s embodied foundation model, AstraBrain.

The robots can take orders, deliver goods and prepare drinks using a linked coffee machine, though a human attendant is still needed for certain store operations, including some replenishment tasks, with full automation expected eventually.

World.title: ‘Zero sense’ to view Hong Kong, Singapore as enemies in changing world: envoy
World.content:
Singapore and Hong Kong do not view each other as enemies, but rather admire one another’s accomplishments, the country’s top envoy to the city has said, calling for greater cooperation between the two jurisdictions often cast as fierce rivals.

Eric Teo Boon Hee, Singapore’s consul general in Hong Kong, said Asia was big enough to accommodate two financial centres and that both sides should work together to “expand the pie” as capital rushed into the region.

Speaking exclusively to the South China Morning Post shortly after marking his first anniversary in the city, Teo pushed back against the prevailing narrative that Hong Kong and Singapore were locked in a zero-sum race for the crown of Asia’s top financial centre.

“The way we see it, healthy and natural competition between the two cities is not necessarily a bad thing,” Teo said.

“Actually, it is healthy and constructive competition to actually improve both sides, and allow us to do better for our people, for our businesses.”

He said that in all his conversations with local officials and business leaders over the past year he had “zero sense” that they viewed Singapore as an enemy.

World.title: Hong Kong WhatsApp hijacking scams surge 170% to nearly 2,000 cases
World.content:
WhatsApp account hijacking scams in Hong Kong surged by nearly 170 per cent to almost 2,000 cases in the first seven months of this year, with one victim losing as much as HK$12.2 million (US$1.55 million).

Police said the 1,993 cases logged from January to July represented a 169.7 per cent increase from the 739 cases recorded over the same period last year. The figure also surpassed the 1,669 cases recorded in all of 2025.

The cases over the first seven months resulted in losses of HK$146.3 million, down by 22.7 per cent from HK$189.2 million over the same period last year.

Despite the lower total loss, police warned that the threat was far from subsiding, noting that some victims lost between HK$1 million and more than HK$10 million.

“The rise in cases was related to the habits of our residents using these social media or instant messaging platforms,” said Superintendent Hui Yee-wai of the force’s cyber security and technology crime bureau.

“On the other hand, we have also seen that artificial intelligence is a factor. Every scam involved fake websites, while AI has made generating these fake websites significantly easier.”

World.title: Reusable rocket milestone opens a door for Hong Kong’s space ambitions
World.content:
On the morning of August 19, LandSpace’s Zhuque-3 Y2 rocket lifted off from the Dongfeng Commercial Space Innovation Test Area. After deploying its second stage and payload into orbit, the rocket’s first stage touched down softly at a recovery site in Gansu province using deployable landing legs.

It was China’s first successful land-based recovery of an orbital-class rocket booster that had just completed an orbital mission – a feat previously achieved only by SpaceX.

Just over a month earlier, on July 10, state-owned China Aerospace Science and Technology Corpartion recovered the first stage of a Long March-10B rocket using a sea-based net system. In less than six weeks, China displayed two distinct recovery methods – a rapid succession of milestones that underscores the country’s space ambitions.

The benchmark for reusable rockets remains SpaceX’s Falcon 9, which pioneered vertical landing after launches of this kind and has conducted hundreds of recoveries. Through first-stage reuse, Falcon 9 has driven its launch price down to about US$2,700 per kg (US$1,225 per lb) – a reduction of 85 per cent from an average of US$18,500 in the pre-reusable era. In contrast, China’s commercial launch prices hover at between US$8,000 and US$14,000 per kg, depending on rocket type and mission profile.

The Zhuque-3 is explicitly designed to close that gap. Standing 66 metres tall with a lift-off mass of roughly 570 tonnes, its first stage is powered by nine methane-liquid oxygen engines. Its stainless-steel structure – a deliberate departure from Falcon 9’s aluminium alloy – offers better heat resistance at a lower manufacturing cost. The booster is designed to be reused at least 20 times.

But while the China-US technology gap in reusable launch vehicles has narrowed, it remains substantial. As a Zhuque-3 team engineer acknowledged anonymously in 2024: “China may have its own Falcon 9 rocket in five years and Starship in 20 years. We need to work hard to catch up.”

World.title: Pioneering Care After Crisis: It All Starts with the People
World.content:
In this instance, that ethos translated into speed. The resilience lecture was held just days after the fire. Senior management, academic staff and technical support units worked across time constraints and boundaries. “This kind of interdisciplinary, cross-departmental collaboration … happened in a minute,” Tam recalls. In governance terms, that agility matters. Complex crises rarely fit neatly into existing silos. CityUHK’s response showed how mission-driven institutions can act responsibly across established structures.

Tam resists the language of “strategy”. The response, she insists, was embedded in CityUHK’s DNA. “At CityUHK, we have the very important mission to engage with the community ... we generate knowledge and we need to contribute to society,” she says.

Within five days—by 1 December—the university had organised a public lecture on resilience, mobilised psychosocial support for affected primary school pupils and begun planning trauma-informed workshops for frontline professionals. What started as an instinctive response soon evolved into something more ambitious: the CityUHK Community Chilling Hub, an innovative model demonstrating the synergies among private and public sectors, academia, public health and social care in Hong Kong. At its heart, the new model demonstrated how crisis exposes the urgency of human care and how universities can help innovate the possibilities. From Academic Department to First Responders

When the devastating fire broke out at Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po on 26 November, the response from City University of Hong Kong (CityUHK) did not begin with a strategy memo. “In fact, since the very beginning, it was not a strategy,” says Professor Cherry TAM, Associate Professor from the Department of Social and Behavioural Science (SS). “We viewed it as our expertise, our responsibility … our aim is to care for people and society.”

[The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.]

Beyond public messaging, the department provided direct psychosocial support, particularly for affected primary school pupils. “When we provide professional services for this kind of traumatic experience, the very important first step is to understand, to listen,” Tam explains.

Her team, partnering with an NGO and the University’s senior management, invited students onto campus, offering distance from the disaster site and emotional breathing room. Using adapted cartoon storytelling, facilitators helped children externalise their fears. “Let them know that their reaction is common, it’s normal,” Tam says. Artistic drawing allowed quieter students to express what words could not: “Silence is a very, very important signal.”

This layered approach—listening, normalising, identifying and referring—demonstrates sustainable recovery at the human scale. Rather than imposing solutions, the team built support around lived emotional realities.

Hope, Tam emphasises, is central to recovery. “Hope is very important. Without hope, maybe they would keep declining.” Bringing children to campus was therefore symbolic as well as being therapeutic.

“Even though university feels like it’s a long way off,” she says, “bringing them onto campus gives them hope for the future.” Exposure reframed identity not around trauma, but possibility.

A hand-made thank you card presented by the pupils of Tai Po Baptist Public School. Building Sustainable Capacity: Training the Trainers

It is understandable that the fire’s psychological impact extended beyond residents. “Even many helping professionals felt it was totally out of their capacity to handle such a big trauma,” explains Tam. By early January, the department launched a full-day trauma-informed workshop using a “train the trainer” model. The aim was not just immediate intervention, but strengthening the professional ecosystem.

“This kind of training is very sustainable,” Tam explains. “With more professionals equipped, when we have other issues they can take action more immediately.” Rather than relying solely on centralised emergency responses, the university invested in distributed capacity—networks of practitioners ready to respond to future crises.

From Fragmentation to Integration

The early initiatives made clear post-traumatic recovery after such an unprecedented fire was not short-term but challenging. Long-term and continuous support to guide affected people to overcome and develop post-traumatic growth is indispensable. With this mission—and made possible through the generous and timely contribution of China Hongqiao Group Limited—CityUHK established the Community Chilling Hub, drawing on interdisciplinary expertise in social work, counselling, psychology, criminology and sociology, as well as technologies in health screening, to offer longer-term and sustainable support for the affected communities in a welcoming, stigma-free space.

“The services nowadays in Hong Kong to handle mental wellness-related issues are quite fragmented,” Tam says. Many are limited by age or socioeconomic criteria. The hub aims to be different: “Without age limit, without economic limit. Anyone can come here. It is a very inclusive service.”

The hub’s model integrates physical health screening, mental health support, social services and spiritual well-being. “It’s a one-stop shop—physical, social, mental and spiritual wellness support,” Tam says. This integrated design aligns with sustainable development goals: breaking down silos, reducing inequalities in access and addressing well-being holistically.

Beyond the Medical Model

Central to the hub is social prescribing, first developed in the United Kingdom. Traditionally, mental health systems have been “very diagnostic oriented, very medical oriented”, Tam says, but after acute intervention, people need community and social support. Social prescribing connects residents not only to therapy, but to social resources through trained community link workers—volunteers drawn from university students and residents.

“We provide basic volunteer training,” Tam explains, linking them with families to co-design tailored “social prescriptions”. The volunteers also build social capital, becoming “the pool of resources in the community to serve in Hong Kong”.

If evidence demonstrates effectiveness, the university hopes to present the model to the government as a scalable alternative. “We can prove the model … and let the government have more alternatives to improve the existing services,” she says.

Enhancing Human Care Through Community

Innovating for better human care is often framed around digital platforms or policy reform. CityUHK’s Community Chilling Hub suggests another path: human care with community capacity, interdisciplinary collaboration and human dignity. “It’s in our DNA … to work with the community, to break through existing silos. Unfortunately, people fall through these cracks,” Tam reflects.

The hub is an attempt to close the cracks. If it succeeds, it may offer Hong Kong—and beyond—a blueprint for human care that is responsive, more inclusive and more sustainable because it begins where all sustainable development must: with people.

World.title: Social Transformation in the Sands
World.content:
Yuen began exploring desert restoration in the late 2000s and formally established Alxa League Springfield Forest Limited in 2011 to scale the Malan Lake initiative. When he first surveyed the site around 2010, he encountered moving dunes up to 30 metres high, advancing roughly 12 metres a year.

Malan Lake lies along an ecological corridor where unchecked expansion can intensify sandstorms and push degradation outward. Greening this frontier, Yuen argues, helps “hold the desert expansion” at a critical point. His aim is afforestation, which is the process of planting trees where there have not been any for a long period of time, as opposed to reforestation where new trees are planted to replace old or missing ones in existing forests.

“Countries, cities and villages have been annihilated by the desertification,” Yuen says, describing the stakes in stark historical terms and adding the spread of desert conditions affects communities “very, very much” and must be stopped.

On the southeastern rim of the Tengger Desert, where dunes can rise 30 metres high and advance significant metres a year, a private afforestation effort is attempting something larger than tree planting. At Malan Lake in Alxa, Inner Mongolia, founder Mr YUEN Shu Wah is testing whether desert restoration can succeed by redesigning not only landscapes, but also livelihoods and governance.

[The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.]

Early planting efforts revealed how technically complex the terrain was: seedlings on the windward side could be uprooted, while those on the leeward side risked burial. After more than two years of experimentation and hesitation, Yuen committed significant capital in and around 2013–2014, shifting from small-scale trials to systematic afforestation.

The project has since expanded dramatically. At its most intensive recently, it reported planting up to 150,000 mu—approximately 100 square kilometres—of desert in a single year. Planting density is intentionally low, at about 50 plants per mu (roughly 750 per hectare), reflecting dryland forestry practices designed to maximise survival under limited rainfall.

Yet Yuen is quick to temper any sense of triumph. Against the vastness of the Tengger Desert, he says, even these gains remain “a drop in the bucket”. Nevertheless, what began as a cautious pilot has evolved into a structured operation involving partnership between full-time staff, seasonal workers, university, research organisations and government, demonstrating both scale and organisational maturity.

A Private Model with Public Purpose

What distinguishes the Malan Lake model is not only its scale but its structure. It is largely privately funded, operating with the discipline of a business while pursuing public ecological objectives.

“The unique point is, firstly, it comes from a private source of funding,” Yuen explains. In addition, the emphasis is very much on keeping costs down and maintenance needs low. The team focuses on planting indigenous, drought-resistant species capable of surviving harsh conditions with little or no irrigation. “The plant needs to survive on its own,” Yuen says, adding that the aim is to tackle “the most harsh conditions” at minimal cost.

This technical discipline is matched by a social one. For Yuen, desertification cannot be separated from human behaviour. Overgrazing has long contributed to land degradation, but simply restricting herds without offering alternatives risks undermining livelihoods. “We try to green the desert and keep the people happy,” he says. “We need people to look after the land.”

That philosophy has led to the development of what he calls a “sand industry” - economic activities adapted to arid conditions. Cultivating Tremella mushrooms, using local shrubs as a growing medium, has become one example of an alternative income stream. The initiative also promotes indigenous plant propagation and cultivating medicinal species suited to desert environments. These ventures are designed to reduce dependence on expanding herds while giving residents a stake in ecological recovery.

“In order to let people stay there without relying only on overgrazing, we developed a sand industry,” Yuen says. “Since we're able to develop the Tremella industry, this is an innovative sort of livelihood for the local people.”

He acknowledges that policy efforts to curb overgrazing face limits if livelihoods are not addressed, pointing out that without viable alternatives, behavioural change is difficult to sustain. Yuen has called on enterprises and educational institutions to help develop more desert-based industries that align economic incentives with conservation.

“The government also knows that they need to change the herdsmen’s habit of overgrazing. But if they cannot find a good livelihood for the herdsmen… their achievement is limited,” he says.

Participation extends beyond local communities. Universities have reserved plots of land where students can take part in greening efforts over several years. Corporate partners contribute not only funding but also procurement support, for example by purchasing desert-grown products as gifts. In this way, ecological restoration is woven into supply chains and ESG strategies.

Technology and Governance

Technology is increasingly central to the project’s governance model. In its early years, operations relied heavily on field experience and practical experimentation. Now, in collaboration with City University of Hong Kong (CityUHK), the team is introducing environmental sensors and exploring satellite assessment to monitor larger areas. The goal, Yuen says, is to improve predictive capability, to understand better what can and cannot be done under volatile desert conditions, and to make the project more productive.

“We always wish to make better predictions of what we can do, what we cannot do. I think it helps to make the project more productive,” he explains.

He situates the work within a broader ESG and SDG framework. Environmental gains include biodiversity restoration and carbon sequestration; social benefits include employment and education about sustainable land use; governance innovation lies in cross-sector collaboration between private funders, public institutions and research partners.

“To find out ways and means to do this is by itself an achievement,” he reflects.

A Model for All

The project has made considerable progress, but Yuen acknowledges its limitations and emphasises that the ambition is not to conquer the desert single-handedly, but to demonstrate that restoration is possible—and replicable.

“We want more companies, enterprises, foundations, individuals to realise it is possible to forest the desert land,” he says, “and hopefully they can chip in and do the same.”

After more than a decade of work, Yuen believes the team has gradually found its way. Malan Lake now stands as more than a green patch against a shifting horizon: it is a test case for how ecological engineering, economic incentives and institutional cooperation can reinforce one another.

In a landscape defined by wind and sand, the project suggests that the more durable force may be governance—the careful alignment of people, capital and purpose towards a common environmental goal.

World.title: Data to Direction: How Vietnam is Reinventing the Strategic State
World.content:
The investment in data infrastructure has paid off. Few developing countries have built such an extensive system so quickly. Yet success has created a new challenge: turning operational strength into strategic direction.

“Vietnam has mostly focused on its operational capacity,” says George. “But now we have performance indicators across provinces, cities and central ministries.”

But, according to Professor Bert GEORGE, Professor at the Department of Public and International Affairs (PIA) and Associate Dean for the College of Liberal Arts and Social Sciences (CLASS) at City University of Hong Kong (CityUHK), the big question is no longer about how much data Vietnam collects, but about what strategic value the data can bring.

For more than a decade, Vietnam has built one of Southeast Asia’s most data-driven public administrations. Ministries track performance indicators. Provinces report standardised metrics. The central government aggregates information from different localities.

[The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.]

George suggests that the next emphasis of reform lies in shifting from measurement to data empowered national strategy. At the centre of that transition is the formation of a consolidated strategic commission, designed to align government activity around national priorities.

“They’ve done several initiatives which have been very successful, including appointing a central commission for strategy and policy,” George says. Rather than allowing ministries and provinces to pursue disconnected agendas, the commission links countrywide goals directly to Vietnam’s data systems.

“They’re not measuring for the sake of measurement … it’s really about embedding data strategies into the overall whole-of-government strategic approach.”

George describes the shift as “quite a game changer”, and one that has been particularly evident over the past two years.

Governance Intelligence

Moving from operational to strategic capacity also requires a new kind of thinking. “Policymakers are looking for governance intelligence,” George explains. That means drawing insight not only from central ministries but also from local governments, universities, businesses and civil society.

Many countries struggle with siloed bureaucracies and fragmented data systems. Vietnam’s reform effort has connected actors—which include corporations, politicians, academics and participants from the public and private sectors—while also standardising data flows and building oversight into the

system itself.

Entrepreneurship in a One-party System

These reforms are unfolding within a one-party political system often portrayed as rigid. George points out, however, that the reality is more pragmatic.

“A big part of what they’re doing is also empowering the private sector,” he says, adding that the broader strategy is to reduce the dominance of the public sector and create more space for entrepreneurs and innovation.

Universities and international partners have also been brought into the process. “They have several universities and international partners working with them … and I think that has really been a recipe for success,” says George.

At the same time, officials insist that modernisation must reflect national identity. “We’re not just trying to implement Western systems,” he adds. “They are creating a Vietnam system which reflects its values.”

Strategy, People and Trust

George describes the country’s emerging model as a whole-of-system approach built on three pillars: integrated strategy, talent development, and trustworthy institutions.

Regarding the first pillar, George explains: “One of the mistakes many countries make is that they have hundreds of strategies. Everyone has a plan, and often these plans contradict each other.” Vietnam’s response is integration—aligning actors around a shared purpose.

The second pillar is talent development. “You want to have the best people,” he says. Effective reform implementation requires a professional and strategically-minded civil service that can compete effectively with the private sector for skilled workers.

The third is trust. “What do international companies like the most? Stability, clarity, transparency.” A predictable regulatory environment, George argues, is essential for both domestic confidence and foreign investment.

He is candid on corruption, admitting that it remains a “huge issue”, but he believes that tackling it requires not only enforcement, but also the use of incentives, proper compensation,

and professionalisation.

Despite Vietnam’s progress, George warns against being hyper-focused on key performance indicators (KPIs).

“They have a KPI-driven system,” he says. Metrics can strengthen accountability, but too much reliance on them can also discourage experimentation. “KPIs have their value, but reformers should be very careful about what you’re throwing away.”

Continuous Strategising

In today’s rollercoaster environment, George believes Vietnam’s reform will depend on continuous strategising: “Keep stable what ought to be stable, and keep flexible what ought to be flexible.” That means protecting long-term values while allowing policies and systems to evolve. Governments, he argues, need dynamic capabilities and flexibility rather than rigid multi-year plans.

He explains that the collaboration between Vietnamese leaders and academics and expert support from the likes of CityUHK and AVSE Global is a key enabler to them. Mobilising support from Vietnamese academics and experts abroad is a

smart strategy.

Lessons Beyond Hanoi

Vietnam’s political system is unique, but George believes its experience carries broader lessons for other countries.

First, sequence matters: build operational capacity, then connect it to strategy. Data should serve purpose, not replace it.

Second, integration is essential. Without it, agencies will optimise for narrow indicators instead of national outcomes. Third, governments should seek governance intelligence, not just tighter central control. Finally, it's vital that stability and flexibility coexist.

Vietnam still faces challenges, from corruption risk to bureaucratic rigidity, but its shift from measurement to meaning offers a compelling case study in governance innovation.

At a time when many governments are awash in data yet struggle to act decisively, Vietnam’s experience suggests that the future may belong not to those who collect the most information, but to those who can turn it into strategy and adapt when the world changes.

World.title: Education, health fees among key concerns
World.content:
China to legislate on preschool education

China will push for legislation on preschool education to provide a legal guarantee for the operation and management of such institutions, Vice-minister of Education Tian Xuejun said on Nov 30.

Tian made the remarks at a news conference organized by the State Council Information Office regarding a child abuse case at RYB Education New World Kindergarten in Beijing that received widespread attention in November. He said the Ministry of Education was already doing research on the legislation.

"The ministry will also complete the requirements on qualifications of teachers engaged in preschool education and is considering formulating a code of ethics for them," Tian said.

He also said a plan is on the way to step up supervision of kindergartens and solve the problem of insufficient resources for preschool education. Tian said the case exposed the conflict between public demand for preschool enrollment and insufficient development of preschool education.

"It also showed that some local authorities and kindergartens still have problems of unsound management and failure to implement or fully implement regulations," he said.

Rural health fee increase explained in detail

The National Health and Family Planning Commission recently responded to public concern of newly increased fees for a new rural cooperative medical system.

Fees charged in the new rural cooperative medical system have recently been raised from 30 yuan ($5.5) to 180 yuan.

The NHFPC explained that while fees for individuals have been raised, government financial subsidies to individuals have also been raised accordingly in recent years from the previous 20 yuan per person to 450 per person. At the same time, the government has a comprehensive medical assistance system for those unable to afford such fees. Also, the reimbursement proportion for hospitalization costs for those in the new rural cooperative medical system has also been raised from 35 percent to 75 percent.

Anti-espionage law will help national security

The State Council issued a circular on China's anti-espionage law on Wednesday with detailed rules for implementing the law.

The circular explains several terms in the law, including overseas institutions and organizations, individuals, spy organizations, spy organization agents and hostile organizations. It was made clear that national security departments under the State Council will identify unacceptable behavior.

According to the circular, providing funds, venues and materials to spy organizations and individuals will be identified as helping them.

Conducting espionage activities in the territory, accepting overseas funds to endanger national security or connect them for spying activities will also be deemed as collusion.

Staff members at national safety departments are authorized to arrest and hunt criminal suspects, and their anti-espionage activities will not be interrupted by any other illegal actions.

It said that Chinese people and organizations retain the right and privilege to secure national safety, and their contributions such as providing clues about spying activities, collaborating with national security departments and fighting espionage activities will also be rewarded.

World.title: International group praises green revival
World.content:
High-level advisory panel pitches 15-year pollution fight, but holds China up as model

A high-level international advisory body applauded China's efforts to improve the environment and suggested a 15-year strategy against pollution in a draft recommendation report on Monday.

China has made building an ecological civilization an important goal and has taken comprehensive measures to improve the environment. This has resulted in positive results, including improved air quality, Vice-Premier Zhang Gaoli said when chairing the annual meeting of the China Council for International Cooperation on Environment and Development, a high-level international advisory body.

Like Zhang, Erik Solheim, executive director of the United Nations Environment Programme, said he was impressed by China's tremendous achievements regarding its environment in recent years, in particular curbing much of the smog problem.

"China is capable of solving the environment problems themselves," said Solheim, the council's vice-chairman, adding the best practices taken by China could provide guidance to other areas facing similar issues.

His praise of China's approaches to move toward being an ecological civilization won wide support from other members of the environmental council, which includes senior officials and experts from home and abroad.

The council's draft recommendation presents highlights of the war against pollution in air, water and soil, and suggests the creation of a 15-year strategy that will be "focused on cost-effectiveness, synergies and ways to build public confidence about eventual results".

Ideally, the integrated rollout should be ready before 2020, to be in line with the 2035 pivot point, when China expects to be a "basic modern country", the draft said.

Solheim said he is confident that China can reach the 2035 goal to build a "beautiful China", considering the determined and effective efforts adopted in recent years.

Along with the longer-term strategy to curb pollution, council members suggested creating conditions for fair competition and incentives for green industries.

Based on the input from Monday's meeting, the advisers and their support teams will modify their proposal and provide a final version to the State Council through the Ministry of Environmental Protection.

zhengjinran@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Beijing, Moscow drill for potential missile warfare
World.content:
China and Russia kicked off their second joint computer-assisted anti-missile drill on Monday, a move experts said could deter potential missile threats amid rising tensions on the Korean Peninsula.

The drill began on Monday in Beijing and is expected to conclude on Saturday, China's Defense Ministry said on its website on Monday. "This is a practical measure in fulfilling the important consensus reached by both countries' leaders on deepening Sino-Russian antimissile cooperation," it said.

"It will strengthen Sino-Russian mutual strategic trust, improve anti-missile cooperation between the two militaries and has great significance in jointly dealing with regional ballistic and cruise missile threats," the ministry said.

The exercise does not target any third party, it said. "China and Russia oppose the development of global anti-missile systems. The two militaries will increase practical cooperation in anti-missile defense, and jointly safeguard Chinese and Russian security interests and regional strategic balance."

The goal of the exercise is to "jointly train for anti-missile combat planning and preparation, launch command and firing coordination," Senior Colonel Wu Qian, the Defense Ministry spokesman, said in a news briefing in November.

Tension on the Korean Peninsula has been mounting since the Democratic People's Republic of Korea launched its Hwasong-15 intercontinental ballistic missile in November. DPRK media reported the missile could carry nuclear warheads and reach the continental United States.

Su Hao, a professor at the China Foreign Affairs Academy, said that it is crucial for China and Russia to bolster strategic trust and cooperate in anti-missile defense to protect their nations from potential threats.

zhangzhihao@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Memorial Day a time to 'remember', 'inspire'
World.content:
A memorial service to mark the 80th anniversary of the Nanjing Massacre committed during the War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression (1931-45) brought together hundreds of activists and members of the Chinese and other Asian communities on Sunday in San Francisco.

The memorial, organized by the Rape of Nanking Redress Coalition, the Committee to Promote Reunification of China, the Alliance for Preserving the Truth of Sino-Japanese War and Comfort Women Justice Coalition, has been held annually for the past 20 years with the aim of exposing the Japanese Imperial Army's war crimes and encouraging people to understand and never forget the dark chapter of history.

"The Japanese army blatantly violated international conventions and committed the extremely cruel atrocity in Nanjing, where 300,000 Chinese were murdered and one-third of the buildings were destroyed," Zha Liyou, acting Chinese consul general in San Francisco, said at the service.

Japanese troops captured Nanjing, which was China's capital at the time, on Dec 13, 1937. It then began a slaughter that lasted more than 40 days. Tens of thousands of women were raped.

"Our stories are linked. The fate of over 400,000 women sexually enslaved by the Japanese Imperial Army during World War II is part and parcel of what happened during the Nanjing Massacre," said Judith Mirkinson, president of the Comfort Women Justice Coalition.

She said the 20th century has been called the most violent century in the history of the world, and that one way to ensure peace in the 21st century is through truth and reconciliation.

"Reconciliation does not come without truth. So the Japanese government must acknowledge their crimes," she said.

"They must give justice to those few people who still survive from the Nanjing Massacre and to the memory of what happened there," she said.

From the time that Japan invaded Northeast China in September 1931, followed by a full-scale invasion that started on July 7, 1937, around 35 million Chinese soldiers and civilians were killed or injured during the occupation, which continued until 1945.

To honor the victims and the survivors and to pursue justice and an enduring peace, the Chinese community worldwide joined hands this year to commemorate this historic event, which was designated by the Chinese government as National Memorial Day for Nanjing Massacre Victims.

"To remember the atrocities committed by the Japanese army during World War II does not mean to pass on the enmity but rather to remind people not to forget the history and inspire them to love peace," said Zha Liyou.

In 2015, the Nanjing Massacre was entered onto the UNESCO Memory of the World Register, a compendium aimed at preserving documented heritage of universal value.

liazhu@chinadailyusa.com

World.title: More military technologies targeted for civilian sector to boost economy
World.content:
Greater integration will spur innovation and cultivate new engines of growth

China will strengthen innovation by developing high-tech industries with military technologies to boost military-civil integration, a move that aims to cultivate new growth drivers and boost the economy, said a recent State Council guideline.

This was one of the seven key tasks set by the guideline on deepening the military-civil integration in the defense technology industry, which was released by the State Council, China's Cabinet, on Monday last week.

The guideline targets sharing technological innovation bases and facilities between military and civilian sectors while more efforts will be made to apply military technologies to non-military areas.

The military integration will also focus on key areas such as space, cyberspace and maritime sciences, while private capital is encouraged to enter military industries, the document said.

The guideline was the latest move by the central government to promote the military-civil integration to widen military contract orders to civilian sectors and apply high-end military technologies for civilian purposes as part of the supply-side structural reform.

In June, the General Office of the State Council released a guideline on civil aviation development to open airspace less than 3,000 meters in altitude and other industries such as cybersecurity and satellite navigation.

Shi Haiming, an associate professor at the National University of Defense Technology, said the guideline brings benefits for both private and military enterprises while pre-entry approvals will be changed into post-entry reviews to streamline administration, except those linking strategic weapons.

Meanwhile, Shi said the guideline lowers the access threshold for enterprises to enter the field of weaponry equipment and will make the process more transparent.

The document also will further reduce institutional costs for private enterprise by building better platforms to promote military-civil integration, he said.

In fact, many developed economies are highly reliant on military-civil integration.

For example, the United States' airplane maker Boeing sells China civil aviation aircraft worth billions of dollars each year and is known for its high-end military aircraft. Many Japanese multinational companies such as Toshiba and Mitsubishi have a department to take military orders.

The integration is a worldwide trend to fully improve the national defense capability, said Jiang Luming, a professor at the National Defense University of the People's Liberation Army.

In countries such as the US, the United Kingdom and Germany, less than 15 percent of military technologies are solely for military purposes and more than 80 percent are used for civilian purposes, Jiang said.

Jiang said in October last year that China has about 290,000 national defense intellectual property rights not being used due to the previously separated military and civil industries.

For example, breakthrough technologies such as engines and aluminum alloy materials can help ease production overcapacity and transform China's economy, he said. These new technologies can essentially boost economic growth and national defense, Jiang said.

The military industry has the priority to apply cutting-edge technologies and also make breakthrough innovations, Lu Guangshan, chairman of the Avionics System Co under the Aviation Industry Corporation of China, was quoted by Shanghai Securities News as saying.

"For example, virtual reality headsets were first used in helmets for fighter jets and my company has developed six civilian industries such as virtual reality, drones, robotics and smart wearing," Lu said.

Military companies are encouraged to work with local governments to promote their advantageous expertise and develop a large number of new high-tech industries, Long Hongshan, chief engineer at the State Administration of Science, Technology and Industry for National Defense, told a news conference last week.

These new industries will play a vital role in promoting local economic growth and creating new employment opportunities, Long said.

Currently, 30 percent of products made by China's military companies are for military purposes and the other 70 percent for civilian purposes, he said.

In the future, high-tech industries will cover half of the military-related economy, Long added.

World.title: Dangerous stunts get thumbs-down from video platforms
World.content:
Multiple social media and video streaming platforms will limit who can view videos that depict dangerous stunts - and may even prohibit such material - in an effort to discourage imitators.

In November, daredevil stunt climber Wu Yongning fell to his death while scaling a skyscraper in Changsha, Hunan province. Wu, 26, had more than 1.3 million followers on social media who regularly devoured his breathtaking videos and photos. He climbed with no protective gear.

Last month, Wu's account on Sina Weibo stopped updating, leading followers to worry about his well-being.

On Friday, Wu's girlfriend confirmed on social media that the "rooftop daredevil" had fallen and died.

"Today is Dec 8. It makes me think of Nov 8, the day that you left us, left this world," she wrote.

Wu's family also confirmed his death to Jiefang Daily, a newspaper in Shanghai.

Meipai, Kuaishou, Xiaohuoshan and other video platforms on which Wu posted content, expressed their condolences, according to ThePaper.cn. Platform representatives told the news outlet that China currently has no law regulating extreme stunt videos, but each platform will update its content policy to discourage imitators.

Kuaishou said Wu's account had been restricted - meaning that only the uploader can see it - in September because of its depictions of dangerous acts.

Xiaohuoshan said it will ban video livestreams of dangerous stunts because live interactions between the performer and the audience could be a distraction and lead to catastrophic results.

The platform also said it will respect the desires of Wu's family in dealing with the videos.

All of Wu's stunt videos on the three platforms had been restricted or taken down as of Monday. A cellphone video of Wu performing his last stunt and falling to his death on Nov 8, has also been taken down.

Wu was part of an informal community of young thrill-seekers around the world who engage in "roof-topping" - climbing to the top or to high ledges of buildings, often without a permit or protective gear, to take stomach-churning pictures and videos. The activity is generally illegal.

In January, an 18-year-old identified as Alexander Sh, fell to his death from Europe's second-tallest building - the 350-meter OKO Tower in Moscow. He was trying to take a selfie when he slipped and fell, Russian media reported.

zhangzhihao@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Taiwan's New Party vows to help improve relations
World.content:
Delegation to Beijing reaffirms support for one-China, rejection of agitators

Top political adviser Yu Zhengsheng met with a Taiwan delegation representing the island's New Party in Beijing on Monday to discuss the peaceful development of cross-Straits relations and how to achieve the "great rejuvenation" of the Chinese nation.

Yu praised the New Party's unbroken stance upholding the 1992 Consensus, which embodies the one-China principle, since the party's establishment, as well as its peaceful approach to relations.

The 19th National Congress of the Communist Party of China, which was held in October, further clarified the guidelines and policies addressing Taiwan, Yu said.

In his opening address to delegates during the congress, Xi Jinping, general secretary of the Central Committee of the CPC, called the one-China principle the political foundation of cross-Straits relations, and said that attempts to move toward "Taiwan independence" in any form will be defeated.

Taiwan will share development opportunities on the Chinese mainland, and its residents will enjoy the same treatment as mainland people as they pursue studies, start businesses, seek jobs or come to live on the mainland, Xi said in the address.

Yok Mu-ming, chairman of the New Party and head of the Taiwan delegation, said the party has firmly upheld the one-China principle and promoted peace.

The delegation also met on Monday with Zhang Zhijun, head of the State Council's Taiwan Affairs Office.

Zhang and Yok agreed that the one-China principle must be upheld going forward, expressed firm opposition to separatist activities and vowed to make efforts toward peaceful relations.

Both sides agreed to establish and improve mechanisms of communication, share opinions on major issues in the relationship and promote exchanges and communication in all fields - especially between youth. They further agreed to create a constructive and convenient environment for the development of Taiwan youth on the mainland.

Zhang said cross-Straits relations have faced challenges because the island's Democratic Progressive Party has refused to clearly express support for the one-China principle, which led to the mainland suspending official communications with the island.

He said that a "Taiwan independence" force had recently stirred up the island, proposing the removal of Chinese mainland elements in a variety of fields.

"Its aim is to cut the historical ties between Taiwan and the mainland, reduce public awareness that Taiwan people are part of the Chinese nation and limit many cultural influences on the island," he said.

Some people advocating "Taiwan independence" have pushed for amending the law, and have proposed changing the island's constitution. "This shows that separatist activities and the group supporting 'independence' pose the most serious threat to the peaceful development of cross-Straits relations," Zhang said.

He warned that people from both sides should be vigilant and firmly oppose such activities.

luowangshu@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Former Chongqing political official facing corruption investigation
World.content:
Sun Zhengcai, the former secretary of Chongqing Municipal Committee of the Communist Party of China, has been placed under investigation on suspicion of accepting bribes, according to the Supreme People's Procuratorate on Monday.

According to the procuratorate, Sun has been placed under "coercive measures", which may include summons by force, bail, residential surveillance, detention and arrest.

The investigation is underway, the procuratorate said in a statement released on Monday.

In July, the CPC Central Commission for Discipline Inspection launched an investigation into Sun for "serious violations of Party discipline".

The CCDI said in a news release that Sun betrayed Party principles and ignored the Party code of conduct and rules.

He was found to have seriously violated the CPC's eight-point code on frugality and maintaining close ties with the masses, seeking pomp, ostentation and privileges, according to the CCDI.

The CCDI said he was guilty of nepotism and seeking benefits in selection of officials. He was found by the CCDI to have leaked confidential Party information and seriously breached Party rules on integrity.

Moreover, he abused power and used his job to gain benefits for others, then accepted their huge bribes in return, either paid in cash or properties, the CCDI said. He was found to seek substantial benefits for his relatives' businesses and accepted valuable gifts, the CCDI said.

The anti-graft inspectors also accused Sun of bureaucracy and sloth in work and degradation and power-for-sex trades, according to the CCDI.

Sun totally deviated from the Party spirit and political requirements of senior officials, the CCDI said in the statement, adding that his misconduct betrayed the trust of the CPC Central Committee and the public, inflicting huge harm to the Party and the country with "extremely bad" social influences.

The CCDI transferred the criminal evidence involving his case to judicial authorities for further investigation.

In September, the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee expelled Sun from the Party and dismissed him from public office.

China Daily - Xinhua
