World.title: Indigenous numbers in the AFL are down, but there’s talent in the Top End
World.content:
A couple of years ago Hawthorn's Kaitlyn Ashmore, a Dja Dja Wurrung woman, spent some time in Alice Springs.

She was immediately taken by the gift for footy so many kids had up there, but knew the pathways for development were limited.

"I've been out to the communities … the talent up there is incredible," Ashmore said on the eve of the AFLW's Indigenous Round.

"But it's just getting them down here, or getting them in a program, and then keeping them in there and making them feel culturally safe."

Loading Instagram content

She was in the Red Centre in support of the Dreamtime Academy, an initiative founded by AFLW player Lulu Pullar along with fellow First Nations players Courtney Hodder, a Badimaya and Whadjuk woman, and Ally Anderson, a Ghungalu and Wakka Wakka woman.

There are 22 Indigenous players listed across the AFLW competition, down from 26 in 2023. In the men's competition the number has dropped from 87 in 2020 to 62 this season.

Ashmore said that was why the Indigenous Round was so important.

"It's honestly representation," she said.

"If we keep doing that, and celebrating Indigenous people, culture and stories like that, then hopefully we can get some more girls that want to join us."

'Work to do': AFL targets Indigenous player boost The AFL is considering a range of measures to boost the number of Indigenous players in the league following a significant decline in recent seasons.

On Sunday night more than 4,000 people packed out the stands at Marrara Stadium to watch Richmond beat Essendon in the Dreamtime match.

Among the spectators were diehard Tigers and Bombers fans and some who had never seen an AFL game before.

Last year the marquee Indigenous Round match was on a Friday night in Darwin and attracted almost 6,000 people.

But the game was fixtured around the men's wildcard round on a day with six AFLW matches and many locals said Sunday's 6:50pm time slot may have led to lower attendance than last year.

Richmond beat Essendon in front of a 4,000-strong crowd in Darwin. (Getty Images: Celina Whan)

Match gets young fans dreaming

The elite game in the Top End was one part of nurturing football in the Northern Territory and helping to grow grassroots participation.

Top End Youth Academy head coach Ben White said just a couple of years ago most kids did not have an answer when he asked who their favourite AFLW player was.

He said now they were naming players such as Richmond's Monique Conti and Sydney's Zippy Fish.

"We've got those figureheads of the AFLW that girls can look up to and see that pathway. It's amazing," White said, crediting the Dreamtime match for bringing the game closer to community.

The crowd in Darwin for the Dreamtime game was a mix of diehard footy fans and new supporters. (Getty Images: James Wiltshire/AFL Photos)

This has also been helped by the recent Northern Territory inclusions to the AFLW of Annabel Kievit, who plays for the Gold Coast Suns, and Dom Carbone, who was elevated to Collingwood's senior list for this season after playing for the Darwin Buffettes.

Essendon captain Bonnie Toogood said one of the most pleasing parts of coming up to the Top End with the Bombers was seeing the next generation of Indigenous kids in the stands.

Essendon has a strong connection with the Tiwi Islands. In April this year, AFLW players Mia Busch and Amy Gaylor, alongside The Long Walk's Jack Peris, ran footy clinics across the Tiwi Islands and West Arnhem Land.

Bonnie Toogood (right) says the Dreamtime game in Darwin is special for the players and competition. (Getty Images: Celina Whan)

The Essendon players and staff will visit schools in Darwin on Monday.

Toogood said it was important to the team to connect with the community.

"It's the main reason as to why we want to come up here and celebrate Dreamtime," she said.

The Top End Youth Academy is fostering young talent and aiming to improve the standard of the game in the NT. (AFLNT Media: Tymunna Clements)

AFLNT launched the Darwin-based Top End Youth Academy this year in response to years of community demand for development opportunities and to strengthen existing talent pathways.

In a matter of months more than 400 players attended academy trials and more than 270 participants were picked up.

Youth Academy manager Josh Kleine was not surprised by the interest.

"Where those numbers might be higher than we expected, it doesn't shock me because there is that love and passion for the game up here," he said.

The AFLW has shown young kids that there is a pathway to the elite level. (Getty Images: Celina Whan)

Kleine said there were a few times during the trials when he and White looked at each other and thought "we've got a fair bit of work to do here'".

But within a matter of months the skills of the kids, aged 10-15, improved out of sight.

"We were actually sitting here in this room and watching them do their warm up and they're just kicking in lanes, getting ready for the game, and nearly every target was being hit," Kleine said.

"We've done some work on things like leg drives and different things. And to see someone who was struggling to get the concept, panicked a little bit, and sort of rushed handballs out, to see that then translate into a game where they're actually taking the tackler on and driving through the contest, it's amazing to see.

"They're the moments that really get you. When you've had that time with the kids and you're coaching them, and you see those things where it's a kid who might have been struggling in this area, you put in the time on the track and then you see it translate on the field.

"It's those little moments that you find really touching."

There are more than 270 players in the Top End Youth Academy. (AFLNT Media: Tymunna Clements)

Kleine said the Darwin kids had a bit more access to programs and competitions than those in other parts of the NT, but the plan was for the academy to expand to places such as Tiwi, Katherine and Alice Springs.

"One thing with our academy [that] we always talk about is, we've only got you for an hour and a half a week on the track with training … we're limited with the time we have," he said.

"So our encouragement is take the lessons we teach you and do the work away from on during the week as well.

"And the girls, the work they're putting in on the track, you're definitely seeing it. You can see when they come back the next week — they've gone away and they've worked on these things. They've done their extra 100 kicks or whatever it is."

Documentary follows young Indigenous women chasing AFLW dreams Arthurina Moreen's desire was so great to play footy, she'd practice kicking bottles with her bare foot. A new documentary has shone a light on her resilience, and that of three other Tiwi Islander women as they chase AFLW stardom.

Kleine said he hoped to see more local talent make it to the elite level, but the goal was also to strengthen the game in the NT.

"Ultimately, not everyone's going to make it, but we're creating stronger territory football off the back of it," he said.

"Half our kids, we hope they become the future captains, the future coaches, all those sorts of things, and that the local clubs are here in the next 15 years.

"It's a flow-and-effect to make Territory footy stronger in the long run … it is a tumbleweed-type thing, where it just flows on, and everyone's continually growing and improving.

"Hopefully it helps close those gaps."

World.title: NASA's new telescope to test whether scientists have dark energy wrong
World.content:
In the late 90s, a space telescope helped flip our understanding of the universe on its head.

Data from the newly minted Hubble Space Telescope, along with a range of ground-based telescopes, showed the universe's expansion was not slowing down as previously thought.

It was speeding up, driven by a shadowy phenomenon dubbed "dark energy".

The astrophysicists who discovered this acceleration, including Australian Brian Schmidt, won the 2011 Nobel prize for their efforts.

But data from our latest galactic maps suggest even the small amount we think we know about dark energy could be wrong.

Nearly 30 years after the dark energy discovery, NASA's new telescope, which was launched overnight, may help solve the mystery.

Loading...

The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope may even drive the next dramatic shift in our understanding of the universe.

"Roman will be a discovery machine that will bring us closer than ever before to answering humanity's most profound questions about our cosmic history," Nicky Fox, associate administrator for NASA's Science Mission Directorate, says in a statement.

NASA astrophysicist Ami Choi says scientists will be able to use Roman to check their results from other telescopes.

If the results are confirmed, scientists will need to toss out their working model for the universe and come up with a new one.

"Dark matter and dark energy are mysterious enough that it's really helpful to have these different views," Dr Choi says.

Elusive dark energy permeates the universe

Studying dark energy and its equally mysterious counterpart, dark matter, is a major objective of the Roman mission.

Neither interacts with ordinary matter in ways that make them easy to observe.

But physicists know both phenomena exist because they can see their effects in how galaxies move through space and time.

NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope explained The Roman telescope is a repurposed spy satellite which will accompany the James Webb Space Telescope. So what is it, and why is it being used?

Cullan Howlett, an astrophysicist at the University of Queensland, says galaxies are distributed across the universe in clusters, connected by filaments across empty voids of space.

"We call it the cosmic web," Dr Howlett says.

"That pattern encodes the ingredients that you need to make a universe, and also how fast the universe has expanded over time since the big bang."

Researchers have been building three-dimensional maps of the universe that show how the cosmic web has formed.

The more detailed the map, the easier it is to judge how dark energy and dark matter have influenced it.

Are we wrong about dark energy?

For the past 20 years, astrophysicists believed dark energy was constant from the big bang to today.

But Dr Howlett says a few recent experiments, including the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) and the Dark Energy Survey, hint otherwise.

"We basically found some tentative hints, I would say, of time variation," he says.

Map of the universe hints dark energy is weakening Physicists may need to come up with a new theory for how the universe works, after a dark energy experiment has produced confounding results.

Instead of being constant, driving the universe into ever-accelerating expansion, dark energy might be getting weaker.

"What we predict the universe might look like in the future will change very dramatically based on what dark energy actually is," Dr Howlett says.

"If dark energy is weakening, eventually the expansion rate of the universe slows down. And if it accelerates faster, eventually the universe could potentially rip itself apart."

If these results pan out, physicists would need to discard their current model of the universe's origin, called the Lambda-CDM model, and develop something new.

Dr Choi compares dark energy research to huge shifts in our understanding of gravity as we went from Newton's laws of motion to Einstein's theory of general relativity.

"We could be at a similar point, I think, where we've been seeing hints of some not full understanding of the physics," Dr Choi says.

These dramatic upheavals in scientific thought are known as "paradigm shifts".

But the paradigm on dark energy hasn't shifted yet.

"It could be that the results that we found are due to some quirk of how DESI's measurements have been made," Dr Howlett says.

While the hundreds of astrophysicists working on these projects have been thorough, it's possible the instruments they've used, or the portions of the sky they've studied, are misleading them.

"If you detect something really exciting with one telescope or one experiment, you want to be able to confirm that with an independent dataset," Dr Howlett says.

Enter Roman.

The telescope is named after NASA's first chief of astronomy, Nancy Grace Roman. (Supplied: NASA/Joel Kowsky)

Roman's tools for probing the dark universe

While it's not as powerful as the James Webb Space Telescope, Roman's infrared camera is designed to capture much larger images so it can see many more distant and ancient galaxies in one shot.

It will send back its first images and begin science operations in about three months.

Once it's operating, Dr Howlett wants to add Roman's data to observations from other ground and space telescopes to understand the cosmic web.

"We take as much data as we can from all these different telescopes and stitch them together and make, hopefully one day, the complete map of the universe and all the galaxies it contains."

The Roman telescope will head to the same part of space as the James Webb Space Telescope. (Supplied: NASA)

Brad Tucker, an Australian National University astrophysicist, says Roman's wide-angle camera will help spot a specific type of supernova.

These stars explode in a very consistent way, so observing them can help to calibrate distances; this was how Professor Schmidt and his colleagues originally realised the universe was accelerating.

But since the explosions are rare and fleeting, finding them can be hard. Roman's large shots have a much higher chance of spotting them.

"For supernovas and dark energy, it's a numbers game," Dr Tucker says.

Roman will also allow researchers to make more observations with "gravitational lensing": using the gravity of massive objects to distort light from distant things.

This deep-field image from the James Webb Space Telescope, released in 2022, shows stretched and distorted galaxies being "lensed" by the gravity of galactic clusters in front of them. (Supplied: NASA)

Confirming or refuting the findings on dark energy

Roman will use its space vantage point to see further back into time than ground-based telescopes can.

Its results will help physicists confirm or refute their other findings in its first five years of operation.

Dr Choi is excited for both options.

"Anytime you get a different answer from another experiment, you learn something," she says.

"Either you learn that there's something that you didn't quite understand before about the ongoing experiment, or the one that came before.

" Or maybe it's something more fundamental, like there's something in our underlying understanding of physics which needs to be revised. "

World.title: Modelling finds 'outdated' law costing teens $411m in superannuation
World.content:
Thousands of teenage Victorian workers are missing out around $115 million in superannuation due to a law which excludes some under-18s from guaranteed super, according to new modelling.

The peak body representing profit-to-member superannuation funds, the Super Members Council, said under-18s were excluded from guaranteed super unless they worked more than 30 hours a week for one employer.

The council said its analysis found about 156,000 teen workers will miss out on an average of $735 in super in 2026-27, adding up to $115 million across the state.

Misha Schubert from the Super Members Council says currently the law discriminates against young people. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Super Members Council chief executive Misha Schubert said that figure was the highest of any state in Australia.

"Teenage workers in Victoria are being denied a basic workplace right that 17 million other working Australians enjoy — and that's just not fair," she said.

"A young person who earns a wage should also be paid super.

"Yet this outdated and discriminatory law treats teen workers differently just because of their age and their hours."

The Super Members Council says its analysis shows 156,000 young workers are missing out on super due to the law. (ABC Gippsland: Bec Symons)

The Super Members Council found young workers in NSW would miss out on $105 million, out of a nationwide total of $411 million in missed super this financial year.

Its analysis found 91 per cent of under-18s worked fewer than 30 hours a week.

It said the average teenage, part-time worker could miss out on $2,500 in super contributions by age 18, which could compounds to $11,000 by retirement.

The council is calling for the law to be scrapped and said it was "out of step with community expectations".

"Many teenagers have their first jobs in retail, hospitality, care and community services. These are real jobs, with real wages, and they should come with real super," Ms Schubert said.

Loading...

"The earliest super contributions matter because they have the longest time to compound.

" Missing out on hundreds or thousands of dollars as a teenager can mean losing much more by retirement. "

Labor members vote to extend compulsory super payments

A push to reform the law is being led federally by the Greens, which introduced an amendment bill into parliament earlier this month.

The party also secured a Senate inquiry on the issue, which will report to parliament in November.

"For too long, Australia's superannuation system has failed young workers. It's time for young workers to be paid the super they deserve," a Greens spokesperson said at the time.

"The continued exclusion of workers under 18 who work fewer than 30 hours per week is a clear case of legislated age-based discrimination that no longer has any defensible policy rationale."

Federal Treasurer Jim Chalmers has expressed support for reform of superannuation laws affected under-18s. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Federal Treasurer Jim Chalmers has previously expressed support for reform, saying it was an "important" issue, but is yet to make any legislative moves.

"We are always looking at ways to strengthen the superannuation system and make it deliver for more workers," he said in June.

Delegates at Labor's National Conference last month voted to include a policy to extend compulsory superannuation payments to under-18s, regardless of how many hours they worked.

The Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry said it was concerned by the push for reform, saying it would have "very serious consequences for the small business community and the broader business community".

World.title: Body found in High Country river where kayaker went missing
World.content:
Human remains have been found in a north-east Victorian river six weeks after a kayaker fell overboard while fishing.

The remains, which are yet to be formally identified, were found in the Goulburn River at Ghin Ghin on Sunday near the Ghin Ghin Road.

Police believe they belong to Shane Wilson, 53, who fell overboard while fishing from his kayak on July 18.

Emergency Services were called to the river after a witness on the riverbank raised the alarm about Mr Wilson.

Victoria Police, the Country Fire Authority, Lifesaving Victoria and the State Emergency Service (SES) were involved in the search.

An SES spokesperson had said Mr Wilson was a "strong swimmer", but was not wearing a life jacket and the current was flowing rapidly.

Remains have been found weeks after a kayaker fell into the Goulburn River at Ghin Ghin. (Supplied: Greater Shepparton City Council)

At the time, Mr Wilson's sister, Melissa Teague, said her family was "incredibly disappointed" that the search was ending.

"It feels like the search is being scaled back before we've had the chance to bring Shane home, and that's devastating for us," she said.

Ms Teague previously told the ABC that she had a close relationship with her brother, who was 13 years older than her.

"Ever since I was little, I couldn't say 'brother', so I called him 'brudda'. It just stuck," she said.

" Those everyday conversations are what I miss the most. He wasn't just my big brother … he was my best friend, "

The death is not being treated as suspicious.

World.title: Nepali teacher saved hundreds of students from flood, minutes before it arrived
World.content:
Hundreds of Nepali schoolchildren were saved by their teacher shortly before the school was inundated in last week's devastating floods.

A Trishuli local, Surinder, said the floods "swept away the entire building".

"Here used to be a three-storey school building in front of a temple and there was a market nearby," Surinder said.

"When floods hit this area, the teacher evacuated all the students and saved their lives."

Nepal flash floods updates: Follow this story as it unfolds with our live blog.

Surinder said Rajendra Dawadi, who is head teacher at Tribhuvan Trishuli Secondary School in Nuwakot, saved the lives of about 1,600 students.

Houses sit partially submerged in Trishuli, in the Nuwakot district, where the Tribhuvan Trishuli Secondary School is located. (Reuters: Adnan Abidi)

Mr Dawadi told the BBC he received calls warning of the incoming disaster.

"If we didn't make a quick decision, if it was 10 minutes later, we all, including the students and me, wouldn't be able to speak to you today," he told the BBC.

"A parent came and told me that 'a big flood was coming, I am here to take my daughter, I will take her'.

"Parents don't rush without a strong reason, so it was confirmed that I shouldn't waste a second to evacuate the children.

"I decided I shouldn't delay any more. Even if the flood was not coming, it was just a matter of a single day's classes.

" I feel proud that we saved so many lives. "

Mud covers a classroom at the Shree Bagheswori Madhyamik School, damaged in flash flooding. (AP: Niranjan Shrestha)

Saved by a lunchbreak

In one of the areas worst hit by the floods, at another school, a group of schoolchildren managed to survive when they happened to leave their classroom for their lunchbreak.

Children attending other classes at the Shree Bagheswori Madhyamik School in Galchhi also escaped because teachers told them to quickly evacuate their classrooms shortly before the waters came crashing in.

"The teachers said, 'There is a flood and you should leave bags and tiffins [lunch boxes]'," said Lakshmi Shrestha, the mother of a student attending the school.

" That's how they managed to survive. "

Shrestha was among mothers and children who began to return to their school on Sunday to find the kids' belongings and see what could be salvaged.

The majority of the children at the school appeared to have survived the floods, the families said.

A mother searches for her child's bag from a pile extracted from the mud. (AP: Niranjan Shrestha)

Thick brown and grey mud coated the surfaces of school benches, walls and notebooks, while the school's courtyard was filled with sediment.

Lines on the walls showed how high the water rapidly rose.

A pile of small mud-caked backpacks, some with colourful key chains, were on the benches and floors, waiting to be claimed.

A student smiles after locating her bag. (AP: Niranjan Shrestha)

Kopila Mizar, the mother of a student, was unable to find her son's backpack, but remained positive.

"My son is alive, that is my biggest happiness," she said.

At least 69 schools in Nepal's flood-devastated districts have been destroyed or damaged, putting education at risk for nearly 19,000 children, according to the non-profit Save the Children.

Those numbers are likely to rise as rescue teams reach more areas, they said.

Students' lunch boxes covered in mud. (AP: Niranjan Shrestha)

The government ordered schools and universities to shut down for three days following torrential rains that triggered severe flash floods and landslides across parts of the country.

University exams were also paused.

With communities still receiving constant flood warnings advising them to move to higher, safer areas, it's unclear when classes will be able to resume.

The disaster has killed at least 794 people and more than 2,500 people are unaccounted for in Nepal, according to the latest figures released by the Nepal police.

Chinese authorities said 16 people were killed in Gyirong County, Tibet and 546 are missing.

AP/Reuters

World.title: 'Which limb am I willing to lose': Sydney mum recalls shark attack
World.content:
Shark attack survivor Leah Stewart has described the moment "a left hook" punch and her sheer will to watch her daughter grow up saved her life.

On June 13, the 35-year-old was finishing up her swim at Coogee Beach in Sydney's east when she was mauled by four-metre-long great white shark.

The attack left her on life support and she required multiple operations, including the amputation of her left arm.

Leah Stewart, comforted by her partner Fernando. (Supplied: Nine)

In an interview with Nine's 60 Minutes program on Sunday, Ms Stewart said when she came face-to-face with the shark she asked herself: "Well, which limb am I willing to lose."

"I'm right-handed, so I decided, 'Let's do a left hook'," she said.

She said survival mode kicked in when the shark pulled her underwater and was only "30 centimetres" from her face.

"In my head, I was like, 'You ugly f***er, you are not taking me away from my daughter'," she said.

"And I twisted myself around and I just started punching it over and over and over again. Just punch, punch, punch.

"It was like fighting a dinosaur. It was so big. It was like punching a brick wall.

"I think I must have got a really good one in. And so it let me go."

Off-duty volunteer lifeguard Charlie Verco was training for a paddleboarding competition when he saw Ms Stewart thrashing in the water.

Despite her severe injuries, the 25-year-old was able to get Ms Stewart to cling onto a drink bottle holder on the front of his board.

Mr Vecro previously spoke with the ABC about the moment he saw the shark, saying it "was so big and powerful".

"The water got very bloody and she got taken under and after a few seconds, popped up again, and the shark had let her go," he said.

'Second chance at life'

The 35-year-old teacher from Coogee has spent months recovering from the attack, being bitten across her arms and legs and suffering extreme blood loss.

Ms Stewart is a teacher and a Coogee local. (Supplied: Stewart family)

When pulled to shore she regained consciousness, with lifeguards and an off-duty doctor performing CPR as they waited for an ambulance.

Officers from the riot squad, who had increased patrols in the area after the Bondi terror attack, had tourniquets they applied to help stop the blood loss.

Ms Stewart was placed in a medically induced coma for over a week at St Vincent's Hospital.

More than $550,000 was donated on a fundraising site to support Ms Stewart and her family.

In an update posted on the site last week Ms Stewart wrote: "I feel like I've been given a second chance at life, and I'm not going to waste it."

Preparation for approaching swimming season

The release of the interview comes as new shark mitigation measures are rolled out along the New South Wales coast in time for the start of spring.

For the first time, two shark detection buoys have been installed in Sydney Harbour, near Balmoral on the lower north shore and Lady Bay in the harbour's east.

Revealed: Sydney's new shark listening station locations Sydney's lower north shore and eastern suburbs are likely locations for two new shark listening devices following a spate of attacks earlier this year.

From tomorrow, there will be expanded shark drone surveillance at more than 90 beaches, with the head of the state government's shark management program Marcel Green saying the state will have the most comprehensive drone coverage in the world.

"Every weekend, at least one drone in every LGA is now going to have weekend coverage, and one drone in every LGA will be covered 365 days of the year from dawn til dusk," he said.

Agriculture Minister Tara Moriarty said shark nets will be also be re-installed at 51 beaches tomorrow.

"We are of course sharing the ocean, none of this is ever going to be perfect, but we're doing everything we can to embrace new technology to provide people with real time information," she said.

World.title: Why the NT struggles with mental health and suicide prevention
World.content:
Dieri/Kauna man Spike has a distinctive beard, long and wrapped into a thin ponytail in string, the ends bleached white.

Warning: This story contains references to suicide and self-harm.

He calls it a reminder of his time in hospital, when he received care for depression and anxiety.

Spike has been around suicide from a young age.

"From primary school to high school, I had friends' parents and friends commit suicide," he said.

" I thought I was drawn to this magnet of suicide. "

The tipping point came while he was living in Adelaide in 2018.

A close friend of his died by suicide, with Spike being the one to find his body.

He said the death hit him hard, and his mental health slowly deteriorated.

"I wasn't coping well and a lot of people didn't see that either," he said.

"I came up to Darwin thinking I could leave that behind — but I couldn't, and it didn't work."

Spike moved to Darwin after a close friend of his died by suicide, but says he still felt lost until he started healing in hospital. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

In Darwin, Spike said he felt lost.

He struggled with depression and anxiety, and tried to find help.

"I went to a couple of [doctor's] surgeries and basically they were like, 'We can't help you right now, come back in a couple of weeks'," he said.

He went home after being waitlisted but without access to care, his condition rapidly worsened.

"I was basically found unconscious," Spike said.

Following the advice of a supportive friend, he then went to "stay in hospital for a while".

Services stretched to capacity

Spike's struggles finding mental health support in the NT is not an isolated experience.

The Northern Territory has the highest rates of suicide, self-harm hospitalisation, and acute mental illness in the country, according to Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) data.

The NT lost 52 people to suicide in 2024 — the most recent year covered by the ABS data — putting its suicide rate at 19.3 per 100,000, far above the 11.9 per 100,000 national average.

It also has 1.7 times the national rate of self-harm hospitalisations, while 51.7 per cent of Territorians aged 16-85 have a lifetime mental disorder.

But mental health sector workers say the NT's limited services designed for early intervention and prevention are struggling to resource the high demand.

Rina Bruinsma, chief executive of Territory-wide mental health care service TeamHEALTH, calls it the "missing middle" — the group of people, like Spike, who often miss out on mental health services because their needs aren't considered acute enough for emergency care.

Rina Bruinsma says services in the NT are designed for early intervention and prevention, creating a support gap that means many miss out. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

She said the organisation's residential service — which accommodates people before and after hospital stays — is at 97 per cent occupancy all the time.

Ms Bruinsma said the gap in care was felt in urban areas, but the divide was even wider in remote communities, which often had to rely on visiting physicians or telehealth appointments.

"Whilst we have good services, there is a group of people that often receive support too late and get [airlifted] into the emergency department," she said.

" [It's] because of a lack of early intervention and prevention that might have otherwise been available. "

NT Chief Psychiatrist Dr David Mitchell said mental health services outside of hospital settings needed to be better funded in the Territory.

There are calls to invest more funding in mental health services for the Northern Territory. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

"It's not rocket science — we know if people get care early then it doesn't fester, it doesn't become more severe," he said.

"An investment in early intervention and prevention is not just the right thing to do, it's the sensible and pragmatic thing."

He called on the federal government to increase the level of investment for those services.

"I do think that there is a moral imperative for the Commonwealth to be investing," Dr Mitchell said.

TeamHEALTH offers a variety of community supports, including a weekly collaboration with Balanced Choice to deliver court-side cook outs for local youth. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Federal Mental Health and Suicide Prevention Assistant Minister Emma McBride said the Australian government was investing in mental health services across the Territory, as part of a $1.1 billion spend on the sector nation-wide.

New Darwin service provides parents with mental health support Expectant and new parents in the Northern Territory suffer from some of the country's highest rates of depression and anxiety, but mental health services for those seeking help are sparse.

She said the recent opening of the NT's first perinatal mental health centre, with a second centre to come, and a free walk-in mental health clinic in Alice Springs added to "a growing network of mental health supports across Darwin, Katherine and Alice Springs, including headspace centres, Kids Hubs and Medicare Mental Health Centres".

"We know many Territorians face additional challenges accessing mental health support, particularly in rural and remote communities, which is why we are investing in services across the Territory," Ms McBride said.

Recovery support essential

Spike's story didn't end in hospital.

He completed two stints in one of Royal Darwin Hospital's mental health wards, commonly known as the Cowdy Ward.

It was there that he dyed his beard white.

Geographic isolation, paired with an overwhelmed mental health sector, are presenting access barriers for Territorians in need of support. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

"That was two years ago," Spike said, motioning to the bleached end of his beard.

"Everyone keeps saying to me, 'Why don't you dye it the same colour as your natural hair?'"

"Now, that's a memory that I'm not going back," he said, triumphantly tugging on his beard.

After leaving hospital, Spike also accessed TeamHEALTH for mental health care and the service also helped him gain employment.

He now works in aged care and at TeamHEALTH, where he uses his lived experience to help others manage their mental wellbeing.

Like Spike, Darwin resident Maria also spent time in Cowdy Ward after she was diagnosed with postpartum psychosis a few years ago, following the birth of her first child.

Maria says doctors and TeamHEALTH support workers have helped her achieve a more regular medication routine after she was diagnosed. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

She described having to complete multiple stays at the ward, and struggling to stay on her medication at the time.

"I remember I went to a party with my friends, I said farewell — they thought I was going to Melbourne, but they don't know that night I was really planning to end my life," she said.

" I'm glad my friend picked it up, so she never left my side. "

Maria has since been diagnosed with bipolar disorder and anxiety.

She said doctors and community services like TeamHEALTH, who she now works for, had helped her stay regular with medication ever since.

"My studies [are] now slowly getting on track and my boy is in my care now," she said.

Maria says her studies and home life are back on track, now that she's in a better place mentally. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Community-based groups key to saving lives

Executive director of sector advocacy with Suicide Prevention Australia, Chris Stone, said community-based services and settings saved lives.

"What we hear over and over again from people who have been in suicidal distress, when they're in that situation, is an emergency department is not the best place for them," he said.

He called for a greater focus on prevention prior to crisis — but also said that when people reach a crisis point, the system should immediately be helping.

"When people are in suicidal crisis, an appointment tomorrow is not good enough," he said.

"Many of our member [organisations] in the Northern Territory are in this position where they're sometimes overwhelmed."

Chris Stone says community-based mental health services can save lives, but many of them are overwhelmed by demand in the NT. (Supplied: Suicide Prevention Australia)

He said growing the workforce to a size that can adequately respond to the crisis "sits at the heart of it".

Ms Bruinsma agreed, and said one of the solutions, alongside funding, was to train people with lived experience to work in the sector — like Spike and Maria.

She said those workers were often able to apply their own knowledge to speak from experiences and help others.

Workers with lived experience 'give hope' to others

Astrid, a terror attack survivor, also uses her experiences to guide her work as a TeamHEALTH peer support worker, helping others to navigate a system that she once struggled to get help in herself.

She said navigating the healthcare system as an immigrant was difficult — figuring out what services were available on different visas, communicating with thick accents, and even overcoming cultural stigma about reaching out for help.

Astrid remembers having difficulty navigating the healthcare system herself. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

"To go to different doctors to get a mental healthcare plan, and tell the story and assessments — one time, two times, three times — it's triggering," she said.

"It has a name — it's re-traumatisation. That's very, very hard for us."

She said the TeamHEALTH role gave her the opportunity to use her own experience "to give hope" to the people she cares for.

World.title: Israel banned Palestine 36. Then it landed on an Oscars shortlist
World.content:
There's one scene director and writer Annemarie Jacir fought tooth and nail for in her latest movie, Palestine 36.

The historical epic encapsulates the 1936 Palestinian revolt against British colonialism, and contains lavish sets, gunfire battles and grand explosions.

But the scene Jacir needed to include in her vision is of a little girl, running along the walls of Jerusalem; an arresting shot that came within a hair's breadth from not existing at all.

In 2023, weeks before Jacir and her crew were to begin filming in her home country, the October 7 Hamas terrorist attack on Israel shut production down.

"I was getting a lot of location images of Cyprus, of Greece, of Malta, old cities. Many, many places have old cities and old city walls," Jacir tells ABC Arts.

Palestine 36 writer and director Annemarie Jacir has been working in independent film for more than two decades. (Getty: Gareth Cattermole)

"The producers were like, 'You just really need to think at this point with what's happening, that this is what we have to do.' I kept saying, 'I'm not going to film anywhere except Jerusalem. It really means something to us. It might look like another old city to you, but to us, it's not another old city.'

"A lot of things I had to compromise because of the political situation and what happened to us. But there are certain things I wouldn't compromise. That was one of them."

Jacir was committed to her vision, relocating to Jordan to complete additional scenes before being allowed back into Palestine a year later to wrap shooting.

"I think in a way it was a survival mechanism, like we just have to keep doing it. We all felt that way. It felt more important, though.

" It was already important, but then suddenly, it just had a different meaning. All of it had a different meaning. "

Going back

Palestine 36 is the only feature film to be shot in the country in the past two years, and one of just a few films to put 1930s Palestine on the big screen.

Bubbling over three years from 1936 to 1939, the uprising marked a violent time in the country's history as Palestinian Arabs sought to gain independence from British colonial rule which saw locals pushed out of their land and homes, alongside an influx of European settlers escaping the horrors of World War II.

An armoured car of The British Palestine Mandate of the League of Nations drives past a crowd in Nazareth during the 1936-39 revolt. (Getty: Heinrich Hoffmann/ullstein bild)

Tens of thousands of people were killed or wounded, with the uprising providing important context for the current Israel-Gaza war.

"It's surprising how few people know about it. It's so critical to understand and talk about this period if we are to talk about anything else that comes afterwards, the Nakba and [the war in] 1948" Jacir says.

"It's very hard to do that without understanding what happens here in '36."

UN inquiry accuses Israel of deliberately targeting and killing Palestinian children The Israeli government is condemning the inquiry and rejecting its findings, labelling the United Nations report "deeply flawed" and full of "errors and distortions" designed to push a "politically driven anti-Israel narrative".

Jacir's movie is not a single story but an amalgamation of many: the young Arab pulled into an armed rebellion; the farmers of the local village who find themselves under siege; the Oxford-educated journalist bound by truth; the British representative torn between duty and morality; the Palestinian children born into violence.

Jacir says she felt the pressure in balancing her duty as an artist to create a story and her responsibility as a Palestinian to educate others.

"We're putting something on screen that hasn't been put on screen before. It's our story and we have to honour it," she says.

"Everybody on the film had a family member that was alive during '36. The cast, they thought about it a lot. Saleh Bakri, who plays Khalid, brought to me a picture of his grandfather who worked in Yafa on the docks, actually, as Khalid does [in the movie].

'He said, 'I want to look like him. Can I look like him?' So we modelled his look after his grandfather."

Saleh Bakri as Khalid (centre) in Palestine 36. (Supplied: Nixco)

Coming back to Palestine to film was a sobering experience for the cast and crew with deep roots in the region.

"It was very difficult and very painful and I think you see that on screen. I think you see that the cast is in pain because we're performing acts of violence while there was real violence happening around us," Jacir says.

"We were already trying to get through checkpoints every day and we were getting stopped by settlers but we already had this mentality that nothing was going to stop us."

Rebel, Rebel

Palestine 36 premiered to a 20-minute standing ovation at the 2025 Toronto International Film Festival.

It then picked up Best Film at the Tokyo International Film Festival, and by December had secured a spot on the prestigious Best International Feature Film shortlist for the 2026 Academy Awards.

"I don't like being silenced and my voice should always be heard." Twelve-year-old actor Wardi Eilabouni accepts an award on behalf of Palestine 36 at the Tokyo International Film Festival. (Getty: David Mareuil/Anadolu)

A month later, Jacir and her team released a statement saying a screening of Palestine 36 at Yabous Cultural Centre in Jerusalem had been shut down by Israeli police, and that an "an official notice prohibiting any future screenings of the film" had been issued.

"Honestly, I wasn't expecting that because there are no Israelis in the film," Jacier says.

Loading Instagram content

"It's about a Palestinian village and the brutality of the British. Yes, there's political Zionism and we understand the whole political context that's happening in the film.

"But it's a really a pity that the film was robbed from its audiences, and it is really interesting and telling that they put a notice on the door saying the film is forbidden from being seen because it violates some anti-terrorism law."

Despite being one of the most difficult films she's worked on, Jacir is proud to bring the story of the 1936 rebellion to cinemas around the world.

"It's important that we remember as people in the world that we have a voice … we have agency and that is something even though these are the darkest times," she says.

The power of a unified people is the reason Palestine 36 has no main characters, but is instead a "collective story", Jacir says.

"That's why the British started the idea of collective punishment; there's power in the collective," she says.

"That was our superpower, that is our superpower."

Palestine 36 is in Australian cinemas now.

World.title: Oscar Jenkins gives first interview from Russian prison
World.content:
NationalVictoriaRussia-Ukraine war Oscar Jenkins gives first interview from Russian prison Eleanor Campbell Updated August 31, 2026 — 11:30am ,first published August 31, 2026 — 8:47am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australian Oscar Jenkins has described surviving four days alone in a trench inside enemy-controlled territory with an injured arm and leg, and detailed why he joined Ukraine’s military, in his first interview since being jailed for 13 years in a Russian prison. The former teacher from Melbourne, captured in December 2024 while serving in Ukraine’s military, is seen wearing a green prison uniform and makes an extraordinary offer to now fight for Russia, in an interview first reported by the ABC. Australian Oscar Jenkins (right) has given his first interview since he was sentenced to 13 years’ imprisonment in Russia after being captured while fighting for Ukraine. The former cricket coach was found guilty of acting as “a mercenary in an armed conflict” by a court in the Russian-controlled Luhansk region of eastern Ukraine in May. Jenkins said in the interview that American, French and British volunteers had fought his “foreign” unit, alongside Ukrainian soldiers, under a commanding officer who was a 24-year-old Brit with some fighting experience.



Related Article Russia-Ukraine war ‘Your typical Aussie cricket boy’: Why Oscar Jenkins went to fight in Ukraine He said he went on about 10 missions, including the one where he lost touch with the rest of his unit and fell into enemy hands. “Things felt a little bit hodgepodge, not a lot of resources to work with, but enough to get to the front and just sort of get yourself in a hole and maybe just hold the line if possible,” Jenkins said. “I had water, I had a backpack in position,” he said of being in the trench he had dug. “The weather sort of cleared up; the next night I worked up the courage to move a little bit forward. There’s a lot of snow in this area – and then I changed my mind. There’s nothing I can see here; it all feels very dangerous. Jenkins when he was captured by Russain soldiers.



“There were drones – a drone dropped a grenade. Broken arm here, problem with the left leg, moved back into the same hole, waited another two days [...] not much sleep, but there was food and water for me.” Jenkins said a man approached to ask if he needed help before three Russian soldiers captured him. He was bound and filmed being subjected to harsh interrogation by Russian officials after his capture. Jenkins, a former biology teacher in China, said his decision to travel to Ukraine was spurred by Russian President Vladimir Putin’s full-scale invasion in 2022. “It felt like the right thing to do if a country invades another country, why, and if there’s not a good reason for that – like Taiwan – then that’s something I should stand up for,” Jenkins said. “I’m a young guy. It’s not that my life doesn’t mean anything to me, but sacrifices might need to be made. That’s still the attitude I have.”



Related Article Exclusive

Russia-Ukraine war ‘It’s just cold. I don’t like the cold’: The haunting plight of Oscar Jenkins During the interview, Jenkins – who did not have a military background – revealed he had appealed to Russian authorities to allow him to now enlist in the Russian military. “I’ve written a statement saying I’d be happy to fight as a soldier for Russia. But if they don’t trust me for whatever reason or don’t want me then I can understand,” he said. He said he had previously considered fighting in Myanmar against the military junta and also joining the Israeli Defence Forces, before settling on Ukraine because the country was easier to fly into. He said he flew from Australia to Poland, then took a bus to the Ukrainian border and approached officials there with an offer to volunteer. He was told he would be a machine gunner at the front.



Australian Mark Lowe, who has lived in Russia for four years, conducted the interview inside the Russian maximum-security prison over two days, according to the ABC. Lowe told the ABC he had made attempts to interview Jenkins for over a year and used relationships he had with government officials to secure the interview for an upcoming documentary. Loading The ABC said it was unable to independently verify the circumstances under which the interview was conducted, nor Lowe’s claims that there were no conditions or pressure from Russian authorities. However, it acknowledged that Lowe runs a website that reports sympathetically on Russia and the Putin regime.



In a statement, Foreign Affairs Minister Penny Wong said the Australian government was “appalled” by the “sham trial” and sentence imposed on Jenkins. The Albanese government has since repeatedly called for Jenkins to be treated as a prisoner of war and afforded protections. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said last year his government would continue to make representations to the “reprehensible regime” of Russian President Vladimir Putin on behalf of Jenkins. Assistant Minister for Foreign Affairs Matt Thistletwaite declined to answer whether a prisoner swap was on the table while speaking to ABC news breakfast. “Obviously, we try and negotiate as best we can on behalf of all Australians who find themselves in difficulties such as this,” he said.



“We obviously have to abide by international laws and we always uphold them. But the Australian officials on the ground will work with their counterparts to ensure that, hopefully he’s returned to Australia safely.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: These luxury Brunswick homes were already approved. Now they’re in a flood zone.
World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaCity life These luxury Brunswick homes were already approved. Now they’re in a flood zone. Cara Waters August 31, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Pre-sold developments already under construction are facing fresh assessments by Melbourne Water after sweeping changes to flood mapping pushed the properties into flood zones. In Brunswick, diggers are busy at work excavating underground carparks from the dark brown clay for a new $40 million townhouse development, but the homes, many of which have been pre-sold, are now subject to an overlay to minimise flood impacts. Flash flooding on Sydney Road, Brunswick, in 2017. Justin McManus Planning experts warn the changes to flood mapping are long overdue but a slow rollout and a lack of co-ordination between planning and building approval systems are creating uncertainty for home buyers around Melbourne. Among the developments potentially affected by the flood mapping changes are 24 luxury townhouses under construction at 144-146 Union Street in Brunswick, a suburb where development has continued to surge after severe floods along Sydney Road in 2017.



The Neometro development received planning approval from Merri-bek council in June last year, and was previously issued a building permit by a private building surveyor. Related Article Development Resident with disability stranded for days after floods hit apartments But in January, the site became subject to a special building overlay requiring a planning permit to ensure new buildings are designed to minimise flood impacts. Planning permit applications under the overlay include a statutory referral to Melbourne Water, the floodplain management authority. Melbourne Water has since assessed the development and given advice on minimum flood protection and floor-level requirements.



“Flood mapping does not create risk; it identifies the risk that already exists,” Chris Brace, executive general manager for service futures at Melbourne Water said. It is unclear what the full effect will be on the development, but according to Melbourne Water, Merri-bek council has advised that permit amendments and further statutory processes are required. Diggers at work excavating basement car parks for the Neometro townhouse development in Brunswick. Chris Hopkins “Mapping flood-prone land through the special building overlay gives property owners and developers clear information about flood risks and the requirements that must be addressed during the planning process,” a council spokesman said. s for the townhouses, priced from $1.6 million to more than $2.2 million each, showcase architecturally designed three-bedroom homes clad in brown brick.



Neometro director James Tutton declined to say whether any alterations would be made to the development as a result of the flood-mapping changes or whether buyers had been informed. Tutton said rigorous multi-stage approvals, such as statutory referrals to various authorities, were standard procedure in property development, with local government planning schemes continually updated. “As is always the case, our expert design team proactively made all relevant applications and technical amendments to meet regulatory obligations,” he said. “This covers the full gamut of issues including flood risk.” One potential buyer, who asked to remain anonymous, put down a deposit on one of the townhouses before the application of the overlay, prior to deciding not to proceed with a purchase for reasons unrelated to the flood mapping.



“We had a serious look at four of the units,” he said. “We eventually withdrew, but we never had anything mentioned about flood risk or flood mapping.” Planning experts warn that what is happening in Brunswick is playing out around Melbourne. Cleaning up in the aftermath of flooding in Maribyrnong in 2022. Luis Enrique Ascui “The reality is that there are many parts of Melbourne and Victoria that are and will be subject to flooding,” said Jane Keddie, vice president of the Victorian chapter of the Planning Institute of Australia. Keddie said many of the areas had not been previously identified because the flood models were not up to date and the planning overlays were not in place.



“Because of the delay and the outdatedness of a lot of the current modellings, there will certainly be a difficult transition period where we do have development that’s been approved in what are essentially floodplains,” she said. Keddie said changes brought in by the state government meant that when a residential development under seven storeys came before a council, the council could not consider flood risk as part of its decision-making process when overlays were not in place. An artist’s render of the exterior of the Neometro townhouse development in Union Street, Brunswick. Melbourne Water can consider flood risk, but it is only involved at the building approval stage. “At the moment, we have a significant disconnect between the planning approval stage and the building approval stage,” she said.



Keddie said this situation was likely to continue to occur as flood mapping was brought up to date, but would hopefully become less frequent. Related Article Floods Flood risk hits 32,000 more homes in Melbourne’s north and south-east A Department of Transport and Planning spokesman said development could still occur in flood-prone areas, subject to meeting appropriate design, construction and flood protection measures. The number of developments in Melbourne affected by the updated flood mapping is unknown: Merri-bek, the City of Yarra and the City of Melbourne were all unable to provide any figures for their municipalities. “Until the final maps are incorporated in the planning scheme, council is limited to making landowners and permit applicants aware of the proposed mapping and to contact Melbourne Water for advice,” a spokeswoman for the City of Yarra said.



Just down the road from the Neometro development, neighbour Rob Veitch said he had not had any issues with flooding but was surprised to find sitting water when he had to dig a hole for a retaining wall in his backyard. A recent letter from the council informed him that the flood mapping for his home had changed. “My understanding is just if it rains, there is nowhere for the rain to go,” he said. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Brunswick East pass-in sells for $1.15m after vendor drops price
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions Brunswick East pass-in sells for $1.15m after vendor drops price Elizabeth Redman August 31, 2026 — 11:29am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

First-home buyers paid $1.15 million for a single-fronted terrace in Brunswick East in post-auction negotiations on Saturday, as the vendors cut their reserve price to sell. The three-bedroom, two-bathroom Victorian home at 209 Glenlyon Road came with an upstairs main bedroom and en suite, an updated kitchen and a grassy backyard. The property was one of 638 scheduled to go to auction in Melbourne last week. By Saturday evening, Domain recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 60 per cent from 450 reported results throughout the week, while 62 auctions were withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate. The Brunswick East home was listed with a price guide of $1.09 million to $1.18 million.



It drew only one party at auction and one genuine bid of $1 million, which was below the bottom of the price guide. A vendor bid was then placed at $1.09 million, the lower end of the price range. Related Article Victoria residential property Melbourne’s typical home is now worth less than it was five years ago But with no further bidding, the home was passed in and negotiations ensued. Barry Plant Brunswick Coburg selling agent Ben Calcagno said the vendors had set their reserve price at the top end of the range, and were hoping for $1.19 million, but also gave some negotiating room to their agents. After negotiations, the home sold to a pair of young first-home buyers for $1.15 million.



“The owners were quite rapt, they were over the moon with that price,” Calcagno said. “It was on a main road, quite a busy road. It was quite a small parcel of land.” He said the new owners of the home are local and “absolutely love it, love the area”. There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide. Calcogno said it was not unusual for auctions to go uncontested in this market, which has been dampened by interest rate rises, economic uncertainty and investor tax changes.



“It is tough, it is really tough. It feels like for every property you will be lucky to have one genuine buyer,” he said. “What I am hearing from buyers in the marketplace is people definitely have money to spend, but they are more likely to spend it on really good quality stock.” Elsewhere, a mother bought a Glen Waverley townhouse as a surprise for her son, paying $1,718,000 at auction. The new, five-bedroom home at 7A Clivejay Street had been offered with a price guide of $1.65 million to $1.75 million.



Three bidders registered for the auction, beginning at $1.6 million and rising at first in $25,000 increments to the reserve price of $1.7 million. Related Article Auctions ‘Pretty anticlimactic’: Inner-west Victorian passes in after one bid Then a further $10,000 bid was placed, and the parties continued in $1000 rises. A woman who inspected the home for the first time that day made one bid and won the keys. “When we called the son, the son was shocked. He was very excited,” Jellis Craig Glen Waverley selling agent Tori Liu said.



“You never know what is going to happen at an auction.” He said the market broadly had been a little slow but transactions were still happening, and noted the clearance rate edging up from its low of a few months ago. “A lot of vendors are starting to realise the market is changing,” he said, adding that buyers also realise they have more options and are more cautious about not bidding above their limits.

World.title: Joyce denies claims of MP’s One Nation exit as Hanson fires back at Albanese
World.content:
PoliticsFederalOne Nation Joyce denies claims of MP’s One Nation exit as Hanson fires back at Albanese Nick Newling August 31, 2026 — 11:29am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce has rubbished claims his parliamentary colleague David Farley is considering quitting the party after less than three months in the role, as Pauline Hanson accuses the prime minister of stoking political violence. Hanson’s comments come just days after her party’s first successful foray into Labor heartland outside Queensland – winning the West Australian state byelection in Secret Harbour – and a Victorian campaign event where she drove a nail into, and later buried, a coffin labelled “net zero”. One Nation leader Pauline Hanson and Farrer MP David Farley. Dominic Lorrimer A report that Farley was “poised” to quit the party and sit as an independent was published in The Saturday Paper. The One Nation MP was elected in May at the Farrer byelection, the first time the party had won a seat in the House of Representatives. “I had a conversation with him nearly a day or so ago, and that was completely the opposite of what he said to me,” Joyce told ABC radio on Monday.



“He’s incredibly competent ... he’s an asset to the party. Of course, the media have a lot of fun with people if they can smell blood on the waters.” One Nation won the West Australian state byelection in the previously safe Labor seat of Secret Harbour on Saturday, with an enormous swing towards new MP Luke Herdegen. Loading Speaking the next day at Labor’s Queensland state conference, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Hanson sought “to divide Australians” and “talks Australia down both here and overseas”. “Parties like One Nation have no serious answers to our problems,” Albanese said. “Their own divisions and disagreements are now showing through. They think Australians are lazy and overpaid. That people working from home are bludging. That domestic violence is sometimes a woman’s fault. That we should, somehow, become a monoculture.”



Taking to social media on Monday morning, Hanson said Albanese’s speech had crossed a line, arguing his rhetoric had become “increasingly desperate”. Related Article Analysis

Political leadership Secret Harbour shellacking a warning for Labor, Coalition “No matter how worried Jim and Albanese are about losing their jobs, telling Australians that their democratically elected opponents are ‘dangerous’ and a ‘threat to our country’ invites people to treat them as a threat. Words have consequences. That is how political violence is incited,” Hanson wrote. Hanson cited the death of conservative British politician Ann Widdecombe as a warning over the danger of violent political rhetoric. Widdecombe was found dead in her home in July, having suffered a serious injury to her head. A man has been charged with her murder and is expected to face trial next year. Threats against MPs have been steadily escalating recently. There are about 20 ongoing court matters across the country in which people are accused of making violent threats against Albanese. Nearly 40 people have been charged with Commonwealth crimes since September last year for threatening MPs and other high office holders.



One of the threatened MPs, Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie, has been afforded additional security. Sources told this masthead Hastie believed the decision was driven by an orchestrated campaign against him online that had been fuelled by One Nation and its supporters over the Ben Roberts-Smith saga. Appearing on News24, formerly Sky News, on Monday morning, Joyce would not say whether Albanese had incited violence against One Nation representatives, instead pointing out he thought the prime minister was a liar. “I just don’t believe them. It’s like listening to a crazy man in a park. What’s the point? You know, when people have proved themselves to be liars and they don’t basically ask for forgiveness on that, you just dispense with them and say everything they say is irrelevant,” Joyce said. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Australian wildcard Preston scores gritty US Open win, but Gibson falls short of upset
World.content:
SportTennisUS Open Australian wildcard Preston scores gritty US Open win, but Gibson falls short of upset Marc McGowan Updated August 31, 2026 — 11:17am ,first published August 31, 2026 — 8:23am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Taylah Preston has capped her rapid rise to the world’s top 100 and ended Australia’s barren start to the US Open with a second grand slam match win this year. The 20-year-old wildcard backed up winning for the first time in a major at the Australian Open in January with an impressive 6-3, 6-3 victory over big-hitting American Alycia Parks on Monday (AEST). Wildcard Taylah Preston advanced to the second round of the US Open with a win over local hope Alycia Parks. Getty Images There might be a dearth of men’s prospects in Australia beyond Cruz Hewitt, but Preston is part of a youth-led uprising on the women’s side, alongside the likes of Maya Joint, Talia Gibson and Emerson Jones. Preston, who made her top-100 debut last week and is up to No.89 in the live rankings, is so far the sole victor on a challenging first day for Australians. Gibson, Adam Walton and Storm Hunter exited in the opening round.



Two other Australians, Aleks Vukic and Kim Birrell, also face being out of the tournament early. Vukic trailed Japan’s former world junior No.1 Rei Sakamoto, 6-4, 6-7 (5-7), 6-4, 3-6, 4-3 (Sakamoto was 30-15 on serve), when rain caused officials to suspend play, while Birrell is a set down and locked at three-all in the second-set tiebreaker. Loading Coached by Brett Hunter and Ash Barty’s former mentor Craig Tyzzer, Preston overcame deficits in each set to eliminate Parks in what is her second main draw appearance at the New York slam. The West Australian wriggled out of a 0-40 hole in the third game before riding a break in the fifth game to a one-set advantage over Parks, whose waywardness contrasted greatly with Preston’s composed play.



However, an aggressive crosscourt backhand secured Parks an instant break in the second set as she tried to lift in front of her home fans. Parks had a game point on serve for a 3-0 lead, but she repeatedly was her own worst enemy, whether double-faulting, spraying shots wide or long, or simply fluffing straightforward volleys. It was the latter that saw Parks gift Preston the break back in the second set. Talia Gibson fell narrowly short in her US Open first-round clash with Donna Vekic. Getty Images Preston had to dig deep after double-faulting to slip to 15-30 at two-all, but her emotions never wavered in a mature performance. Parks called for the trainer to have the strapping on her right shoulder readjusted, but it did not help her cause. Another double fault from the American on break point in the next game put Preston on the brink of victory – and the world No.100 completed the job.



Preston hit only eight winners compared to Parks’ 22, but crucially committed 20 fewer unforced errors. Earlier, Gibson threatened to cause an upset before losing 6-2, 4-6, 6-3 to Croatia’s Olympic silver medallist Donna Vekic. Loading Gibson, 22, has experienced a breakout year, earning a Billie Jean King Cup call-up and storming into the top 100 for the first time after a blistering few weeks at the Indian Wells and Miami Masters events, where she eliminated five top-20 stars. She even briefly became Australia’s top-ranked woman, but quickly found herself a set and 4-1 down to Vekic – by a double-break deficit – in an error-strewn start before staging a mid-match revival.



Related Article US Open As the US Open begins, all eyes are on the big problem hurting tennis Vekic’s serving woes helped open the door as Gibson claimed 10 points in a row to grab one of the breaks back, hold serve then reduce her former top-20 opponent to 0-30 in the eighth game, which turned into an enthralling back and forth. Eventually, an increasingly agitated Vekic wilted on Gibson’s second break point in the game, delivering her sixth double fault for the match and fourth in the second set to leave the set tied at four-all. Another Vekic double fault two games later sent the match to a decider. Everything seemed to be going Gibson’s way when she escaped from 0-40 in the opening game of the final set with some excellent first serves and a wonderfully struck forehand winner from deep in the court to get on the board first.



Her big opportunity came in the ensuing minutes. A tense Vekic began spraying even the easiest of shots, offering two more break points to Gibson that could have split open the match. Instead, Gibson let her off the hook with some loose errors, which became an unfortunate theme. Storm Hunter qualified for the draw, but was no match for Marta Kostyuk. Getty Images Vekic finally made it out of the game on a mishit backhand that snuck inside the sideline and evaded Gibson’s racquet. The stroke of fortune seemed to embolden the Croatian, who secured the break on her third chance in Gibson’s next service game, which lasted more than 10 minutes and involved five deuces.



Related Article US Open Demon’s tough draw and Tiley’s $150 million US Open splash All was not lost. Gibson brought up two consecutive break points to get back to three-all, only to again bail Vekic out as her last opportunities came and went. “It’s a hard one to swallow,” Gibson said. “Most of the time it’s who makes the most unforced errors on the court who comes away with the loss, and today that was me, so it’s just something to learn from.” Hunter qualified for a grand slam main draw for the sixth time in her career, but was no match for Roland-Garros and Wimbledon semi-finalist Marta Kostyuk, the No.11 seed.



Kostyuk needed only 67 minutes to breeze past Hunter 6-4, 6-1, while China’s Wu Yibing thumped 43 winners in downing Walton 7-6 (7-2), 6-2, 7-5 to prevent the Australian from reaching the second round again. Among the players to advance to the second round were 2024 runner-up Jessica Pegula, 2021 champion Daniil Medvedev and fellow seeds Tommy Paul, Jasmine Paolini, Jiri Lehecka, Leylah Fernandez and Arthur Rinderknech. However, dual grand slam winner Barbora Krejcikova lost 7-6 (7-4), 6-2 to Uzbekistan’s Kamilla Rakhimova, and British 29th seed Cam Norrie bowed out 6-7 (6-8), 6-2, 6-2, 6-3 to French up-and-comer Luca Van Assche. with AAP News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: ICAC Operation Rosny LIVE updates: Charles Perrottet resumes evidence as inquiry enters week six
World.content:
Hello and welcome to the Herald’s live coverage of the ICAC’s Operation Rosny public hearings.

I’m state political reporter Jessica McSweeney and along with the Herald’s senior writers, we’ll be bringing you all the news as it happens from the hearing room.

Today Charles Perrottet returns to the witness box to answer questions about his relationship with fugitive property developer Jean Nassif.

First, let’s take a look at what we covered last week:

Anita Perrottet has denied covering for her husband Charles after the ICAC heard evidence she was paid $660,999 in just over two years for her “strategic and marketing advice” but could not produce any written evidence of doing any work. She insisted she was paid what she was worth, and told the ICAC she gave her advice in person, over the phone or via disappearing messages.

Anita Perrottet said business expenses showing trips to Sydney were likely times she met with her client Jeremy Greenwood, but she couldn’t recall specifically where they met or what they met about. The ICAC then heard evidence that places not Anita, but her husband Charles as the one taking those trips when he would sometimes meet with Jean Nassif. Perrottet said he would “humour” Nassif because he had an ulterior motive and wanted to extract some information out of him – we expect to hear more about those motives this week.

The husband and wife texted about Liberal Party political machinations, and discussed if Charles’s brother Dominic would dump David Elliott from his cabinet as premier. The ICAC is investigating if Charles Perrottet, among others, worked to damage Elliott’s career on behalf of Nassif, who they anticipated receiving a share of $2 million from.

Former building commissioner David Chandler said Nassif called him to make the threat: “If you harm my developments, I’ll harm you”. Outside the hearing room Chandler said the home owners left to live in Toplace developments were living in “hell on earth”.

You can watch the hearing live stream here.

World.title: Why Thursday’s final will dictate Freo’s fortune and shape the entire series
World.content:
NationalWAAFL 2026 Why Thursday’s final will dictate Freo’s fortune and shape the entire series Paddy Sweeney August 31, 2026 — 11:10am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Finals. It’s where footy fantasies are made and broken. Stars of the game are formed, history created, legacies forged. It’s the time of year every team wants to be a part of and when all fans dare to dream. Alex Pearce will lead the Fremantle Dockers into the finals on Thursday. Getty Images Ten teams are already planning for 2027, leaving eight sides in the race for premiership glory.



Fremantle sits just three wins away from an elusive premiership, their first in the club’s 32-year existence. On Thursday night they’re presented with a golden opportunity to take a massive leap towards breaking the drought. But should they lose, the doubt, negativity and bad thoughts of more than three decades could again wash over them. It’s why the qualifying final won’t just dictate Fremantle’s fortunes, but shape the entire series. The Dockers should be confident.



As minor premiers, they’ve been the benchmark for 24 rounds - proof that every part of their game stands up. Their playing list is in great health with only Brennan Cox unavailable from their first choice team. They’ve won all 12 games at Optus Stadium in 2026 - their last loss at the venue coming in last year’s elimination final against Gold Coast. View post on X This season they’ve averaged 51,923 supporters per game at home, setting new crowd records across the competition.



However, defeating Hawthorn won’t be an easy equation. Sam Mitchell loves being the underdog and he’s tactically very good - and he would have spent the week off studying how to improve from the earlier loss to Fremantle this season. He’ll see the exposure to ‘Wharfie Time’ as a positive - from being overwhelmed, they’ve now trained for it, equipping themselves for the same moment if it arises. Mitchell is ruthless, when he wants something, he goes and gets it - one look at who they’ve acquired through recent trade periods shows you this. There’s no four points up for grabs this week, instead a much bigger carrot dangles - the perfect platform for a premiership charge.



Victory and they have a break before again being at home on what many consider the “better side” of the draw. View post on X With Brisbane expected to take care of the depleted Swans, a home preliminary final against either Sydney, Adelaide or the Western Bulldogs is up for grabs. Lose, and they’re then on a path to a potential showdown against the Lions at the Gabba as they chase a three-peat. Last week, four-time premiership player Luke Hodge said the Dockers were “perfectly placed” to win their first flag, citing their calm heads, as a key reason why they can go all the way.



The Hawks legend was speaking at the launch of the Premiership Cup Tour at Fremantle Boat Fishing Harbour. While the iconic location was its first “stop”, the Dockers also want it to be the final destination. Since day one of pre-season last year, Fremantle has been working towards creating a chance like the one Thursday presents. Destiny is in their own hands and they now need to deliver - turning promise into performance - and then a premiership.
